title: Mid-Way With Fields In The Extraordinary Saga Of A Comedy Genius And Legendary Iconcoclast
text:
As with vol. 1, one star comes off because of the price--close to $100 Amazon. This continues to be a real detriment to all (except the publisher), as Wertheim's magnificent study transcends Fields, in presenting an extremely balanced and well-written account of the rapidly-changing entertainment industry in 20th century America.

Vol. 2 picks up with Fields joining the premier Broadway stage revue of the early 1900's, the "Ziegfield Follies." As the author is a distinguished scholar of Ziegfield, Will Rogers and the "Follies" in general, homing in on the Fields work is a natural extension. Ziegfield had a great run as a show biz impresario, specializing in selecting his famed "Follies Girls," micro-managing the staging, costuming and choreographing of them in sparkling ways, and injecting comedic bits, with Will Rogers his favorite and Fields someone he viewed as a necessary evil. Fields and Ziegfield never got along; Fields, always resisting authority, chafed at Ziegfield's controlling influence and domineering personality. Of the two silent short films Ziegfield allowed Fields to make in the 19-teens, one is "lost," and the other, "The Pool Sharks," while noteworthy for its early special effects, is hardly a showcase for Fields's pantomime and sleight-of-hand skills. it will be 10 years before he returns to the cinema--and as Wertheim meticulously shows, Fields used every one of those years to explore and expand his versatility.

Of the "Ziegfield Follies" personalities, black comedian Bert Williams is of extraordinary appeal. He and Fields were very fond of one another. Williams dealt with incredible indignities. Revealingly, Wertheim writes of Fields's activity as an early stage actor-worker union organizer (the pay disparities, job insecurity and working conditions were deplorable). Among other progressive actions, Fields fought for equal access for Williams. At the same time, Fields was capable of playing an antisemitic prank on Eddie Cantor (Williams rescued Cantor); yet, Fields chastised wife Hattie for disparaging Jews.

Fields's tremendous insecurity and fear of failure contributed to his alcohol addiction. Wertheim also traces a very strong genetic link from both parents, along with his complex emotional disposition stemming from his conflicted family life, as strong contributing factors. Abstaining from booze while earning his living by juggling and pantomime, liquor fast became Fields's "escape" as his stage character broadened. Growing up in Philadelphia, "a hotbed" of drinking, son of an incorrigible bar manager, and "the association of drunkenness and debauchery with actors" also fueled Fields's habit. Doubtless, we will read more, including the insidious effects on his health, in vol. 3. Wertheim anticipates this: "The two remedies--alcohol and comedy--generated different endings to the same life. If alcohol precipitated Fields's death, Bill's comedy bestowed a gift to the world."

As in vol. 1, Wertheim masterfully weaves in the on-going saga of Fields, wife Hattie and son Claude; Hattie, a devout Catholic, refused a divorce, and Fields held her hostage to his weekly payments and peeves (granted, she had her difficulties also). When Ziegfield "chorine" Bessie Poole has a child by Fields, and Wertheim relates the couple's literal hand-off of the baby to an adoptive couple (with sporadic visits for a while, and $6,000 in contributions), Fields's callousness is palpable.

The essential character broadening--the sub-title "Becoming A Character Comedian"--was a slow work-in-progress, but Wertheim's book is a real page-turner at that point. The 1925 stage hit "Poppy," with Fields as Poppy's adoptive father and carnival con-man, was a break-through, and the rascally-but-benevolent con man character became a character-in-growth through the 1940's.

Thanks to writer J.P. McEvoy and a stage revue called "The Comic Supplement," Fields in this stage period also refined a character Wertheim variously describes as a middle-class, angry, put-upon yet somehow triumphant husband and father, nagged at by wife and mother-in-law, ridiculed by unwelcome children...the "Dysfunctional Family." Thanks to Wertheim's skill, we see just how closely this character came to parallel Fields's (1) upbringing and (2) relations with Hattie and Claude.

The stage births of Model-T family outings, picnics--and in particular, "The Sleeping Porch" routine where every-day noises, sights and vendors wreak havoc on Fields's attempts to sleep--are fascinating. Think: "It's A Gift," one of the two Fields films (along with "The Bank Dick") preserved in perpetuity by the Library of Congress. What we see in that film (and will learn about in more detail in vol. 3) is the hilarious culmination of nearly 15 years of careful refinement.

A few reservations. Substantively, Wertheim seems to strain to draw parallels between Fields and H.L. Mencken, yet the side-by-side quotations fall a bit flat. Technically, the book is chock-full of typos-- things that would evade spell-check, but not an interested reader. They distract from an otherwise splendid work. Ditto for the binding; it's weakening already. On the other hand, the photos--many never seen widely, and provided mostly from the family archives--are A+, as is Wertheim's varied sourcing.

At vol. 2's conclusion, D.W. Griffith casts Fields for the screen silent remake of "Poppy" ("Sally of the Sawdust") and the notices are spectacular. Fields essentially leaves the "footlights" for movies and signs a lucrative multi-film contract. "Perhaps I can be so successful as to make three million in the hinterland laugh. If I can make them laugh and through that laughter make this old world seem just a little brighter, then I am satisfied."

Thus we eagerly await vol. 3!

title: That would be Bore Island
text:
There is an essential thing for mystery novels. If there is a mystery, the reader must not solve it before the hero. If you are paying attention, you will know who Boat Boy is and who the cyberstalker is by p. 200, 20 pages ahead of Anna and company for Boat Boy and 150 ahead of them for the stalker.

Another less essential thing is that the reader must not be expecting the same old things. Specifically, I am utterly fed up (having read all the AP books, and the good ones frequently) with the battering of Anna Pigeon. In this one she gets poisoned, drowned, and mummified in duct tape (with a baby strapped to her chest). After all the beatings she's taken, she should look like Ernie Borgnine. It was old many books ago.

The other less essential thing is that the book should deliver the basics the previous novels depend on. As other reviewers have pointed out, Acadia National Park is just a stamp on the cover. I'm not sure Anna ever actually enters the park, aside from the ranger housing. One of the appeals of these books is that the setting is interestingly explored. Barr has ignored this requirement before (Burn, I'm looking at you) to her peril. when you finish High Country, you feel as if you've visited RMNP. In the Isle Royale books, the setting is the most interesting character. Here, it's not even window dressing.

Lastly, the killer (there is one almost in a subplot, although she gets to abuse Anna twice) is, frankly, not interesting. She's not a mystery; you know who she is from the beginning. Her motivation is a stew of disease-created mental illness, and her craziness is sad and sickening but not in any way interesting. Maybe it's a brilliant portrait of Huntington's, but as fodder for a thriller, it's just moldy hamburger.

This is the first Anna Pigeon I've picked up in the library instead of purchasing. Now Nevada Barr joins Lee Child and James Lee Burke on that list of writers whose books I'll read on a "try before you buy" basis.

title: "It turns out that when you are looking for your father you are also looking for other things."
text:
After reading Hisham Matar's two novels, each featuring a protagonist who is a young Libyan boy whose life is disrupted by the abduction/disappearance of a father or father figure from his life, it almost comes as a relief to turn to this memoir in which Matar finally confronts head on the central trauma of his life: the abduction of his own father, a prominent Libyan dissident, by the Qadaffi regime, when he was a 19-year-old university student.

By then, Matar and his family had been living in exile for a decade, an experience that he recounts in this book. At boarding school in England, the future novelist had to pretend to be the son of an Egyptian mother and an American mother, and his classmates included the son of a Qadaffi government minister. It was a strange, strained existence, as they watched their fellow exiles murdered or kidnapped, but Jaballa Matar only became more determined to fight the Libyan regime. When he vanished, it was years before his wife and two sons learned that he was still alive and held in a Libyan prison, and a few years later, word stopped coming altogether. But did he die in jail, or had he just vanished into an even deeper form of imprisonment, from which it was impossible to bribe a jailer to get word out? Until the fall of Qadaffi -- in which some of Hisham Matar's relatives participated, as he recounts here -- they would never even have a chance to find out, even though this memoir includes some creepy encounters with Qadaffi's son, Seif el-Islam, who promises to try to find out (as if he doesn't know already...)

But once Qadaffi is dead, Hisham can finally try to find out whether his father has survived. It's that quest that is the backbone of this memoir, although the narrative ranges back and forth in time, touching on family history, relationships between fathers and sons, and Libyan history. It's a devastating tale of the damage wreaked on that country by its Italian occupiers and by its own home-grown tyrants and a powerful and thoughtful story of what it means to be a lifelong exile and then to return to the country of one's birth, violently released from tyranny and trying to rediscover the meaning of a "civil society" in the aftermath of oppression. By all means, read Matar's novels, but this dwarfs them in terms of accomplishment.

title: Powerful and Evocative
text:
A powerful and evocative biography of Hillary Clinton the person, and her 2016 groundbreaking campaign to become the first woman President of the United States.

SUMMARY
Hillary showed tremendous strength and courage in the 2016 election, and she doubled down on these qualities by writing this compelling post-campaign analysis. She identified her challenges and takes responsibility for her decisions in the controversial campaign. She details her thought process in her decision to run, her challenges in the primary campaign with Bernie Sanders, and her failure to adapt to Donald Trump’s gorilla tactics. She discusses the email issue, the FBI investigation, James Comey, the media, Putin’s interference, Russian hacking, sexism, fake news and many other issues. She was the most competent democratic nominee to ever run for the presidency, her version of what happened in the campaign, is an important part of history that we can and should all learn from. Not just because the most competent candidate lost, but because most importantly, the integrity of our election process and in fact, our democracy was compromised in many ways.

“I never imagined that he [Putin] would have the audacity to launch a massive covert attack against our own democracy, right under our noses -- and that he'd get away with it."

"I think it's fair to say that I didn't realize how quickly the ground was shifting under all our feet. I was running a traditional presidential campaign with carefully thought-out policies and painstakingly built coalitions, while Trump was running a reality TV show that expertly and relentlessly stoked Americans' anger and resentment."

REVIEW
WHAT HAPPENED is a honest and enlightening book, not only about the campaign but about next steps for all of us. It’s about moving forward and healing the division in this country. Hillary is a brilliant writer who eloquently reveals her most personal thoughts during one of the most challenging times of her life. I listened to the Audible book and hearing it in her voice was just perfect. This intimate review of Hillary’s experiences will serve as a tremendous guidebook for us all, but perhaps particularly for the young women who desire to follow in her footsteps and attempt to once again break through that ultimate glass ceiling. Keep Going!

“And maybe if I showed that I wasn’t giving up, other people would take heart and keep fighting, too.”

title: Review for Too Beautiful to Break by Tessa Bailey
text:
***Review posted on The Eater of Books! blog***

Too Beautiful to Break by Tessa Bailey
Book Four of the Romancing the Clarksons series
Publisher: Forever Romance
Publication Date: September 26, 2017
Rating: 2 stars
Source: eARC from NetGalley

Summary (from Goodreads):

A love of a lifetime . . .

Leaving Belmont Clarkson is the hardest thing Sage Alexander has ever done. From the moment they met, she knew Belmont was the one, and getting up close and personal with him on his family's epic road trip has taken her desire to a new, even hotter level. But there's no way she can go there---not without revealing secrets that could devastate them both.

Losing Sage is not an option. Belmont's heart is hers, has always been hers. He knows she's hiding something from him, but nothing will stand in his way of telling her just how much she means to him. Finding her is easy---saving her from her past could cost him everything.

What I Liked:

I have so many mixed feelings about this book. On the one hand, it wasn't horrible, and I can see readers enjoying it. On the other hand, I didn't really like it. I love Tessa Bailey's books, and I have been a huge fan of hers for a long time. But this book just didn't do it for me.

This is the fourth and final novel in the Romancing the Clarksons series, and it features Belmont Clarkson and Sage Alexander. They have been circling each other during this entire series, but never together romantically. At the start of this book, it's just Belmont and Sage, since the other three Clarksons have taken detours during the trip, and will meet Belmont in New York for the Plunge. But Sage knows she can't stay with Belmont for this trip - she needs to take care of some business at home. Business that she knows Belmont won't like. She uses their dependency on each other as an excuse, but really, she needs to go back to her sad, terrible life in Sibley, Louisiana, so she can make things right. But Belmont will follow Sage to the ends of the earth, and he stops at nothing to help her when he learns of her situation. They both have a lot standing between them, but their love is stronger than they know.

Things I liked about this book: the characterization. I may not have loved Belmont like most readers of this series, but I can really appreciate how unique and different he is. Bailey has made him stand out completely, compared to the rest of her heroes of her various romance books, and in the romance world in general. Belmont is one of a kind. We can clearly see his character development in this story; he goes from putting Sage on a pedestal, to understanding her and loving her all the same. He overcomes some of his fears, and begins to understand his own self better.

The same can be said about Sage. She goes through a lot in this book, and she learns a lot about herself, and about Belmont. From start to finish, she is working towards a healthier, stronger relationship with Belmont. She also works through a lot of feelings she had stored up from her past, dealing with her parents and her childhood. She didn't have a traumatic or "terrible" childhood, but let's just say she had to come to terms with forgiving her parents, for a lot.

As always, Bailey writes a good romance. The chemistry between these two was always there, from the beginning of the series. This romance was interesting because Belmont and Sage clearly already love each other, but they were never together, so it's not a second-chance romance. They are a simmering fire together, and there is a pretty awesome part of the romance that I loved (but I won't say because it's something cool to discover). I wouldn't say this is one of Tessa's hottest books, but the chemistry is still good.

I liked how the book ended, for Belmont and Sage, and for the rest of the characters. We always expect a HEA from romance novels, but this book (and series) had a great HEA, and for everyone. This book was a quick read and while I didn't totally love it, I'm glad I gave it a chance.

What I Did Not Like:

If I'm being honest (which I always am!), I never really loved Belmont, like most readers I've seen. People were dying to read his story and I was just... kind of ambivalent? I didn't really care to read his story. The whole I'm-so-devoted-to-her thing that Belmont has going on was strange and sometimes a turn-off, because it was too intense. You'd have to read one of the books to know what I mean. Belmont is obsessed with Sage's well-being, her happiness, her family's situation. All of this sounds good on paper, but it's weird and a little unhealthy.

Cue my next complaint: how Belmont decides to take on Sage's burden himself (and the fact that she let him). The whole thing is that Sage goes home because her father is physically unwell, because his mining job is too demanding. So Sage goes to his employer (a mean, spiteful man) and offers to work in her father's place. And guess what Belmont does, when he shows up to Sibley? He offers to take Sage's place. I hated this. Keep in mind, Sage felt responsible because she borrowed money years ago from the man in order to get out of Sibley and to San Diego, and didn't pay him back. Her father took on her debt, as well as added his own, and he worked for the man in the deep of the mines.

It seemed incredibly unfair and unrealistic that Belmont would take Sage's place in the mines. And the fact that she let him? That's honestly ridiculous. I would never in 1000 years let a friend or a friend's brother do that (which was what Belmont was to her, at the time - not "boyfriend" yet). I definitely wouldn't let my boyfriend or husband do that. It's my responsibility, and no one would talk me out of it. Not even creepy Belmont who was obsessed with Sage's well-being. He'd have to suck it up and deal with the fact that I will pay off my and my family's debts. By myself. I would never endanger my partner like that, especially knowing he hates underground.

And to begin with - there were SOOOO many options such that Sage wouldn't have to take her father's place and work in the mines? Like, get a loan from a larger bank? From Sallie Mae? Bring in law enforcement or a legal team? Better yet - take your family and move? Or even better - pay your debts? It would be hard to leave family to suffer, but that's an option too (not a good one, obviously). My point is, there were so many better options than offering to take someone's place in the mines. And then there is the fact that Sage got a day's worth of training, before going into the mines. You need licenses and certifications to operate heavy equipment and machinery and whatnot... Sage couldn't have obtained any of that in a day. That just isn't plausible. And even if the owner were doing some illegal/shady business by letting Sage go into the mines with one day of training, that's when I would bring the law into it. You see how this makes no sense?

AND there is the fact that Belmont ended up working for MONTHS in the mines, while Sage went back to San Diego to do her wedding planning business thing. (I think? This wasn't entirely clear but that was the impression I got.) You're joking, right? I wouldn't let anyone replace me for any of my debt to begin with, but even if I did, I wouldn't just leave the man in my hometown and go? I would stay with him? This literally made no sense.

In essence, nothing about the plot made sense. This whole plot could have been dismissed, had Sage paid the debts back, or called the police, or simply walked out of there and let her parents reap what they sowed (most of the debt came from her parents and their alcohol addiction).

Would I Recommend It:

I don't really recommend this book. It's not a steamy, swoony love story. It's not even a satisfying story in general. The story frustrated me to no end and I couldn't connect with Belmont, or Sage. I liked how Tessa Bailey developed their characters and shed a lot of insight into their personalities and minds, but I just didn't connect. This romance novel didn't do anything for me. It wasn't enjoyable and I don't even know how I would recommend the book (like, in what situation or context). I feel like only fans of Tessa Bailey would try this book? It's not that compelling of a story if you're not a die-hard Bailey fan. Which I am. I'm so sad I didn't really like this book.

Rating:

2.5 stars -> rounded down to 2 stars. It's a shame. I started the review thinking that I would give this book a 3-star rating. But the more I think about it, the less I enjoyed the book. I wanted to like it, but I pretty much knew, as soon as Sage offered to take her father's place, that I wouldn't enjoy this book (because I knew that Belmont would offer to take hers, and the whole story was doomed from there). At least the story ends well... to a point. I'm glad this series is over because I don't think I would read the next book (if there were a fifth book).

title: Getting Intimate with the Mozarts
text: What better way to learn about Mozart than from his letters? His father goes from being a stock, domineering patriarch to a very human man, concerned about the well-being of his son and intent on helping the young man to make what he sees as the right decisions--though whether father knows best is up for debate. The letters reveal Europe in the second half of the 18th century. Travels by carriage, bad inns, frightening illnesses. It's fascinating to see the way Mozart's genius is questioned, and how he puts all the arguments of the naysayers to rest when given a chance. We see the famously dirty sense of humor in all members of his family. This wonderful edition of the letters contains brief introductions to various letters, strong footnotes, and a context-setting introduction. The letters themselves allow us an unadulterated view into the lives of one of the greatest composers. This book is well worth the price and your attention.

title: Obvious but not helpful
text:
The authors describe problems that anyone who works in, or who has spent much time, in hospitals can see as being obvious. In fact, the book could have been much longer had they gotten below the surface on such issues as the tremendous complexity of creating systems of electronic health records (which underlies some of the more superficially apparent problems they describe). What they call a scandal is really more a reflection of the fact that, as Peter Drucker himself once wrote, hospitals are the most complex entities in our economy.

Unfortunately, the authors don't offer any meaningful solutions for the horribly complex problems they describe. Many thousands of very intelligent healthcare executives, policy makers, academicians, suppliers, and others have tried to find solutions for these problems. This 66 page booklet offers nothing new.

Another problem with this book is that there is no information about who the authors are, what organization (if any) they represent and what ax (if any) they have to grind. Are they injured patients screaming at the system? Disgruntled employees or ex-employees? Academic researchers? Consultants promoting their business with a book? There is a clue about 2/3 of the way through the book (consultants) but it's only a clue.

I give the book two stars instead of just one because the authors (whoever they are) are clearly passionate about the problems. I hope their next book will offer solutions.

title: Not perfect, but close.
text:
This books starts with the basics like what milk alternatives are available.

After giving you an overview of alternatives, it jumps into three weeks of menu plans that includes breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
An example day would be:
Sunday:
Breakfast - Wholesome Apple-Cinnamon Muffins frosted with nut or seed butter
Lunch - Roasted Carrot Bisque, Whole Grain quick bread or Nuthin’ but cornbread cups, sliced option
Dinner - Teriyaki sliders (or burgers) with a side salad and Awesome Asian Vinaigrette.

Each plan tells you what page to find the recipes on.

There are also menus for a birthday party, for when you’re having company, or for a BBQ.

The first recipe section is drinks and includes things like 1-minute milk beverage and a carrot cake breakfast shake.

The second recipe sections is bakeshop breakfasts and includes things like Whole grain quick bread and vanilla cream scones.

The third recipe section is any-day brunch and includes things like a strawberry short stack and better with bacon fried rice (includes a vegan option).

The fourth recipe section is snackables and includes things like peanut power protein bars and dreamy chocolate banana snack cake.

The fifth recipe section is veggies first and includes things like mighty tasty broccoli and cream of portobello soup.

The sixth recipe section is American comfort cuisine and includes things like nacho pasta and chipotle back bean burgers.

The seventh recipe section is Mediterranean meals and includes things like a mushroom pesto pizza and a meatless Moroccan skillet.

The eighth recipe section is Asian eats and includes things like un-sushi salad wraps and Korean beed with Bok Choy.

The ninth recipe section is sweet rewards and includes things like no-bake pumpkin pie cups and Elvis bonbons.

The tenth recipe section is essential extras and includes things like rancher’s dressing, Paleo cauli-rice, and quick and easy pizza crust.

A guide at the beginning of the section tells you if each item is Vegan, Egg free, gluten free, tree nut free, peanut free, soy free, uses coconut, or if it includes an option to be any of those things.

Some of the recipes seem like filler. For example the Sous Chef’s Salad which is pretty much just a basic salad you already know how to make but includes packaged lunch meats and a warning that they may not actually be dairy free (and fails to mention there are vegan alternatives).

Some of the vegan options assume you’d know how to make the alternatives work. For example the vegan option for the un-sushi Salad wraps just suggests diced organic tempeh and extra firm tofu. Do you cook the tempeh exactly the same as you cook the shrimp? No clue, doesn’t say.

Overall I like this book. It’s ideal for people like me who don’t want to do anything too fancy. Some books I’ve encountered think you want to use a mile long list of ingredients, fry some ingredients up, boil some others, bake, and that’s just the sides. This book isn’t that complicated and most of the ingredients, if not all, are now standard at most grocery stores. There’s a bit too much meat for meat-free me, but there’s still things here that work for me with little or no modification. The layout is really nice and easy to use.

*Disclaimer* The publisher provided me a copy free for review. I only request books I think I'll like and I give them the same review I'd give them if I had purchased them.

The author has a very readable narrative writing style.

However the book does not cite any sources. This lack of academic rigor gives the fusillade of assertions the tone of an unkempt pensioner holding forth from an economy hotel bar along Roxas Blvd.

America spilled blood and treasure to remove Spanish rule and grant the Philippines its sovereignty for the first time in many centuries. A few decades later America again spilled blood and treasure to remove Japanese rule and grant the Philippines its sovereignty a second time.

Funny way to build an "empire"

Regardless the author refers to American imperialism in the Philippines at least once a page. No tariffs on American goods is cited as evidence of American imperialist villainy. Apparently Analyn can only be truly free from American imperialism if she pays the government a 33% surcharge for Levi's and Coca-Cola . . . Restoring the Philippines' proud heritage of dungarees and carbonated soft drinks.

Interestingly while American imperialism is continually decried and derided, the author laments the Philippines achieved independence from US rule before FDR could impose his wonderfully effective policies upon the Philippines.

This lament is not only self-contradictory and drenched with irony, but is also incorrect. December 1941 found the US and Philippines reaping the tragic consequences of FDR's economic, military, and foreign policy failures.

title: Professional Overview with Fabulous Bibliography
text:
asdf
I study sociobiology in general, and the sociobiology of Homo sapiens in particular. The population genetics of the New Synthesis is now verging on a century old, and it is firmly grounded in a conception of genetic information transmission that is clearly out of date. I have been studying epigenetics and epistasis to understand the complex nature of multicellular organisms and social species. The most important thing I have learned so far is that the traditional idea of how information is passed from a biological entity to its daughter copies goes far beyond Mendelian segregation.

This book describes contemporary genetic research in to complex information transfer mechanisms in the genome. It requires that the reader know something about molecular biology, but not that much. The description is very well done, and the bibliography is extensive and well directed.

Most fascinating is the author's argument that the complexities of the genome require that we go beyond the "reductionism" that has guided microbiological research and theory for more than a century. It is not clear what the alternative is, but some of the readings in the bibliography do give some indications.

At this point, the reader proceeds with trepidation.  Will expectations be dashed, realized, or exceeded?  If the reader has seen the movie before reading the book and liked the motion picture, I think the movie viewer will be disappointed with reading the novel.  I will not reveal the differences between the two, the prospective reader will have to discover them for oneself.  The book itself is an easy and short read.  The narrative is in a simple, straightforward style.  The two main characters are consistent in both the book and the film.  I thought the actors in the picture realized beautifully the author's description of her main characters.  The "Ghost"  has the best quotes!  Reading the book made me appreciate the process of translating a book to the screen. Since it is a short book, the screenwriter had to flesh out the story to make a full length feature film. text:
After having enjoyed PBS's Poldark series, reading the books intrigued me. "Reading" this series has become code for "immersing" myself in the fascinating 18th century world of Cornwall that I might have never discovered but for PBS's spot-on interpretation of Winston Graham's ambitious work. Let me state that I am "older" and am done with all my literary heavy-lifting. This doesn't mean I've consigned myself to pap either. Somewhere in the middle are books like the Poldark series (and Trollope) that reflect historical accuracy while providing societal and cultural commentary and entertaining with, simply stated, a good story.

At this juncture, I shall leave more sophisticated and intellectual literary critique to those who enjoy this kind of analytical word-smithing. I'm here to sell the point that the Poldark series is both stimulating and entertaining.

Insofar as being satisfied reading just Book 1, I suggest that you do not fool yourself that this paltry effort will sate your appetite. Buy the first three...or the first six...but plan on savoring the dozen.

title: Angst, romance, and more!
text:
***I received an ebook copy from the author at no charge***

Jewel E. Ann has always got me with her words, but Look the Part put her on my one-click list.

Flint Hopkins carries a secret with him that puts the weight of the world on his shoulders. His life revolves around his son, Harrison, and his law practice. Then Ellen Rodgers shows up at his office, looking to rent the space upstairs. It doesn’t take long for her to start driving Flint crazy—sexually and in general.

I was initially drawn to this book because it’s based in Minneapolis, and I’m a Minnesota native, and I don’t often see contemporary romance books that are set in my hometown. The blurb got me too, because it sounded like there would be so much sexual tension … and man oh man was there. Flint is sex on a stick, or “sex in a suit,” as Ellen likes to call him. This man is irresistible, but he has such a rock solid wall around himself that it’s impossible to know if anyone will ever be able to break through it. He’s arrogant, successful, has money, and is 100% dedicated to his autistic son. I fell in love with him before I was even three chapters in the book, and I just kept falling harder and harder as I read. This man is so broken, held captive by past mistakes that cost him everything, but also deserving of forgiveness and a chance at happiness in life. Jewel hit the character development with Flint right on the head, and as the book moved on, there was a beautiful transformation in him. And the transformation was organic and real, it wasn’t rushed and it didn’t feel forced.

Ellen might be my favorite female lead of a book I’ve read so far this year. She’s this beautiful and lively free spirit, who marches to the beat of her own drum (literally) and lives her life like the next second could be the last. She has some skeletons in her own closet too, though they aren’t quite as big as Flint’s. She’s strong, independent, and is completely comfortable in her own skin, despite how weird others might think she is. I loved that Ellen didn’t take anything from Flint, and that she wasn’t afraid to put the man in his place when it was warranted. And the compassion she showed to Harrison had my heart melting all over the place.

Look the Part is fantastically written. There’s constantly something happening in the plot, and I didn’t want to stop reading once I started. It actually only took me two days total to finish the book. I was chomping at the bit when it came to the sexual tension between Ellen and Flint. Every heated glance and innuendo had me practically climbing up the wall. This story is a slow burn, nothing happens overnight, and those are my favorite kind of romance novels to read. I love when authors let me savor every minute leading up to a couple coming together, and there was plenty to savor with this book.

Flint captured my heart for good, and easily earned himself a spot on my Top Book Boyfriends of 2018 list. I can’t say enough good things about this story, and I would recommend it to anyone who loves a good romance with lots of UST, angst, and comical moments.

title: A good companion to Paul Mariani's biography of Lowell
text:
I didn't rush to get this book. I've read Mariani's biography of Lowell many times, as well as biographies of his first and third wife, and I eagerly await a bio of the second Mrs. Robert Lowell, Elizabeth Hardwick. Yet, with the poet's daughter Harriet Lowell making new information available to this author, I finally had to see what this book had to offer.

The author makes it clear that this book is NOT a biography. Is it a bit repetitive? Sure -- and I skimmed over the Lowell family history and the minutiae regarding bipolar illness in general. What blew me away was her summary of his work at every stage. I didn't particularly notice any annoying psychobabble but instead appreciated her placing of the poetry within the context of his life -- including his spiritual life, which is not ignored. This is the first writer, to my knowledge, who has made the High Church Anglican influence on Lowell's work (and, of course, his funeral) crystal clear.

But the best part, for me, was the new understanding of Lowell's relationship with the amazing Hardwick and of Lowell as a father. For the first time, I began to understand why Hardwick stayed with Lowell despite his mental illness and why she "took him back" after his shameful desertion and the breakup of his third marriage. His daughter's assessment of him as a good father, despite everything, is echoed by the stepdaughters from his third marriage. The author's effort to pull together this new information will make this book a good companion to a biography of Elizabeth Hardwick when it appears.

title: A wonderful, captivating story that entertains and offers insight. A must read!
text:
With something as simple as a song, the authors immediately pull us into Jasmine’s seat in the car and her place in the world. We quickly get to know Jazzy and we feel for her. She is an interesting and sympathic soul. Each initial discovery raises many questions in the readers’ minds. Music bonds her adoptive family together as The Amazing Armstrongs and makes her feel left out, and so it is not without irony that her nickname evokes jazz. Even the dog’s name, Sing, becomes a compromise between her family’s musical interest and Jasmine’s love of Star Wars characters. The dog Sing howls when Jasmine tries to sing. Jazzy’s quest to find her talent is a quest to find her place in her family, to be amazing along with them. This caring child also feel concern that others, like her wheelchair-bound friend Alec, might feel left out or truly get left out by others. People can feel alien in many different ways, for many different reasons. People can connect, however, when they realize that feeling alien is something they have in common.

Feeling alien makes the characters in the fiction Jasmine loves appeal to her all the more. Aliens fill Star Wars, so much so that “alien” is normal. Princess Leia, also adopted in her infancy by a loving family, provides Jasmine with a role model: a fellow adoptee and a girl who grows up to become a strong leader and maybe even a Jedi.

Fiction is a powerful thing - on several levels, in this case. Fiction from the real world inspires this delightful girl in her fictional world, and her story can, in turn, inspire many people in our world.

This is a wonderful, captivating story. When it ended, I did not want to stop reading. The writing style is vivid. The story offers insight into childhood, adoption, and family life. Readers can learn a few things about adoption itself, including open adoption. This is an important work for all readers: children and adults, families of many kinds, oh so many people who feel like square pegs in round holes, and also the round pegs who can benefit from a glimpse into lives whose shapes have corners.

title: Such amazing stories. Though the second one ruined me.
text:
I was not ready for these two short stories. I have been meaning to read them for months, but ended up waiting until I could read Two Dark Reigns as well. I'm glad I did so. Because, gosh, these two stories ruined me. Five stars for sure. But my heart may not recover. I truly did not expect all of this heartbreak, to be honest.

Both short stories are just over a hundred pages, and took some time to read. I loved that. Loved that they were not so short. That they were hard to read. And they were both written so perfectly. I very much love this world that Kendare has created. It's done so well and so evil. I love reading every moment of it. Mostly, haha.

I shall not be sharing too much about these short stories. Only a few of my thoughts about them. And you must read both of these stories after Three Dark Crowns and One Dark Throne. They are both in such a stunning paperback edition too. Very much worth buying. I cannot wait to read book three next, and book four next year. Ack. I am beyond worried, though, especially after reading The Oracle Queen. I need these books to have a happy ending. I want a happy ending for all three queens and Jules too. And gosh, how I am nervous that I will not get my happy endings. Hmph. So excited to know everything, though, even if it ends up breaking my soul. Which I am sure it will, no matter if the endings are happy or not, haha. All the books so far have been very rude.

The first story is The Young Queens. It tells more about Arsinoe and Katharine and Mirabella as children. Not too much about their six years together, but a little bit of that too. And it was so sweet to read about. They were such loving sisters for six years. Until they were forced apart, having to live in different places, until being forced to kill each other ten years later. Gosh. The story in these books are so heartbreaking. Yet beyond interesting to read about and I love all the details so very much. It was all written so well too.

This first short story is about all three young queens, when they were taken away from each other. I loved reading more about all of them. Still like Mirabella the least, haha, but I did love her in this short story. Her love for her sisters was so good but sad. And those years she had to spend locked away. Gosh. Reading about that killed me a little. So yeah. I liked Mirabella in this short story. And Katharine. My love. My heart aches just thinking about her, and how she had to grow up. She did not have a lot of happy in her life. Oh.

But Arsinoe did. She grew up in a good place, with Jules, and I am so happy about that. Though reading about Arsinoe and Jules in this short story broke my heart. How very rude. We learn more about Jules's family. I loved her aunt so very much. And what happened with her, well. I shall not get past it. Especially remembering what happened in the previous books too. She deserved much better. Gosh. My poor heart. But yeah. Very much loved reading The Young Queens. Such a strong short story. Such great characters.

Then there was The Oracle Queen. I fear I shall never forget this story. It completely ruined me. I loved every moment of it, but I am not sure my heart will ever recover. It is set five hundred years earlier, and tells the story of the oracle queen Elsabet. I will not be sharing her story in my review. It would hurt too much. But I will say that her story killed me. And it was so heartbreaking from start to finish and it never got any better. That story did not have a happy ending. At all. But it was so so very much worth reading.

My heart is breaking for Elsabet, though. Oh. Her story was the very best. Written so well. But it was the saddest thing I have read in ages. Gosh. And with a sad ending too. How very rude. She had two great friends, though, and I adored reading about them. Until that ending. Ahh. She has been queen for three years. Her king consort is not a good person. And I cannot. It was so painful to read about. So good, but so painful. Shall not be sharing more from her story. I can't. But oh. It was so very good. You must read it.

I'm so thrilled that I finally made myself read Queens of Fennbirn. These two stories were worth reading. And even though the second story ruined me, I would still have read it, knowing all that happened. And I think you should all read it too. It's important. In these novellas we learn more about the island too. Which was awesome. Both stories were incredible. And I loved them so. If you still have not read these books by Kendare, then you really must get started. They are incredibly painful at times, but so very good. Worth it.

---

This review was first posted on my blog, Carina's Books.

title: A fascinating and unpredictable read
text:
This was an awesome read that was more like walking a tightrope without a net. At first I had some trouble falling into the author's voice and couldn't zip through it as I do with most books. I appreciate that. It's called having a distinctive style, and I felt the style was in perfect synch with the nature of the novel. Once I got into the grove and into the dark with this author, it was amazing. At no time could I anticipate what was going to happen, what had happened, or if I was going to be dropped below the surface of what *seems* to be reality into a bizarre world of smoke and mirrors without light. It scared the jeepers out of me most of the time; tapped into my worst fears and jangled my carefree enjoyment of thrillers. This book isn't for sissies.

Last Words. What does that mean? Right out of the gate, Mark Novak, the protagonist is haunted by the last words he spoke to his wife before she was murdered. He carries this weight with him to the cold, wet, disturbing winter of Garrison, Indiana to investigate what happened to Sarah Martin in the Trapdoor Caverns ten years earlier. He's an investigator for a group that works to make sure those found guilty of murder are truly guilty. He's as baffled by this assignment as the reader might be, and unprepared for the bitter cold of a landscape far away from his home in Florida and the depth of what lies beneath, and the deception that stands above. Ah-hem, it's why we practice whatever we want to master the most. We never know when we'll need it.

Novak is dealing with his own demons, and isn't it odd that he's sent to investigate the death of someone with a date attached to the death of a loss in his own life that's as bitter and cold as the caves? He's a lost and haunted soul, above and below ground, and damn if this author doesn't pull the reader right down into that pit with him. Ridley Barnes is a wonderfully complex character who knows the underground world like no other, and yet he's so lost within his own mind that he's not sure which side of good and evil he stands on. Do any of us. Really? What tunnels of darkness run through us that we fight to deny? Just skim the names given each section of the book and see if it doesn't give you the heebie-jeebies, make you want to turn away because it might throw light on what you'd prefer to keep hidden. Who asks to have this very cold case looked into is even more disturbing. How about this line? "His life had been saved by the look in a stranger's eyes. Would he ever know that? Ever understand how close he had come?" How close have we all come without knowing? Is there a Dark Man in front of us, behind us? If so, who is he?

I could go on and on about this book, but it's one of those reads where the author gives you the characters, the narrative, and the voice, then leaves you alone to make of it what you will. You can go as deep down into the twisting, squeezing, freezing caves that lie below the John Mellencamp little pink houses as you want. Or you can stay above ground and and enjoy the complexities of an author taking you on an unusual journey and introducing you to a cast of characters that you somehow recognize, but can't quite remember why.

In a world of prescriptive writing, this book writes its own prescription. What a relief.

title: Very Poorly Edited
text:
I recently got my first air fryer and I have been looking for good cookbooks to give me ideas of what I can do with it. I have had some limited success with it, but without a couple of good recipes to get me started I am a little limited. In looking for cookbooks I found this title, and based on the mostly positive reviews I decided to order it (I have ordered others as well). It might be a good book but it has to be one of the most poorly edited books I have ever seen (not just among cookbooks - any books). I never enjoy writing critical reviews, particularly about books because a lot of time and effort goes into writing them, but this is one of those occasion where I need to do so.

Let me cover the good parts first, before I get into my complaints.

This book has a nice collection of recipes, logically broken up into sections: Breakfast, Meat, Poultry, Seafood, Sides, Snacks/Appetizers and Desserts. While that’s a reasonable breakdown, I probably would have sectioned it a bit differently. That’s a personal preference, though - the sections make sense, and each contains a good collection of recipes.

The book starts with a discussion about air fryers and how to choose one, even offering up a selection of summary write-ups about several different brands. That’s a great start and while not meant to be exhaustive it will get you going in the right direction.

A lot of these recipes require a larger model air fryer that can handle baking trays and the like. I have not seen any collection that gives you any kind of indicator of what size fryer you need with the recipes, this book included. It would be a nice addition to include such, which would be a great time saver and would elevate the collection over the competition.

This is a self-published book, which is not a problem if you either take the time to polish your work or if you have a decent editor that takes the time to go through and make corrections. It appears that the only editing that this book received was getting fed through an automatic spell checker. There are so many typographical errors, but not misspellings - this is a case of the wrong word being used. For example, in the recipe for Pesto Sirloin Steak, the instructions say “Preheat flyer to 350 degrees F.” The recipe for Orange Pecan Crusted Lamb says “Season the lamb into the fryer...” (more subtle). Some recipes have all the ingredient names capitalized, most do not. Page 1 of the introduction starts a sentence with “The unfortunate truth us that...”. There’s even an error on the back cover - an extra blank line in the middle of a paragraph. I could go on for a while here, naming many more errors, but that’s not productive. None of these render the book useless or unreadable but they make the book seem more like an uncorrected proof than a completed book.

In light of the numerous errors I am having trouble recommending this book. It’s not bad, and it’s clear a lot of effort went into the writing, but it is so riddled with errors that it’s difficult to rate it any higher. There are better edited, more polished books on air frying available. I can only hope the Kindle version is better than the paperback.

title: Fantastic combination of human and supernatural events!
text:
THE SIREN AND THE SPECTER, by Jonathan Janz, is one of his most complex and "layered" novels to date. In any book, your focus is on either the supernatural OR the human element during certain points. However, in this one, Janz has blended these two components together so well that they are nearly inseparable from each other.

"You can't reason away the unreasonable . . ."

We begin with David Caine, a man known for his books ultimately debunking believed supernatural phenomenon. His old college friend, Chris Gardiner, along with his overly intrusive wife, Katherine Mayr, have purchased The Alexander House: possibly "the oldest haunted house in America" . Katherine is quite adamant that David will write a book that goes against his natural predisposition and admit that this house is haunted; thereby, giving her idea of hosting a 'haunted attraction' quite a large boost in credence.

Chris' motives are not quite as clear.

". . . I don't presume to know the truth about the Alexander House. The fact of the matter is that no one knows the truth."

David's character is as detailed as they get. Mentally haunted by an incident in his past where he pushed away a woman he loved, he is literally full of contradictions and conflicts in both his mental thoughts and physical actions. Janz could not have created a better, more "perfect" character for this role if he tried. This is a man you can't help but feel for, whether you like or dislike his motions. He is simply too real, too human, to look at as mere words on a page. He quickly becomes an actual person to the readers, flaws and all. (Perhaps more because of his flaws . . .)

". . . there comes a point when disbelief turns into stupidity . . ."

The legends state that a huge, sadistic man--Judson Alexander--was given that out of the way house to indulge in his acts of depravity away from the town.

". . . They gave him this territory to limit what he could do . . . "

Even though the man himself has been dead for centuries, this doesn't stop Janz from creating an atmosphere--both in the Alexander house, itself, and the surrounding area--even more menacing and fear-provoking than before. Every small detail, from the layout of the rooms to the lifestyles and emotions of the two homes closest in proximity, add to this distinctive unease. A sense of almost palpable dread transfers itself from off the pages directly into the reader's mind. I can honestly say that I caught myself either shivering or gaping open-mouthed at many points during the course of this novel, so real were the feelings it evoked within me.

". . . Homes have personalities . . . some are sullen, some are cheerful. This one-- . . . --is less predictable . . . "

"It's like it was . . . hiding from me . . . even walked the property in all directions . . . And I never saw the Alexander House."

As the book progresses we begin to glimpse the depths at which this superstitious legacy has touched all in its vicinity. Without giving away any spoilers, I can safely say that few--if any--readers would be able to even guess as to the lengths Janz goes with these individuals and locations. You'll not find any two the same--ALL original and some . . . damaged . . . in various ways. Despite the number of divergent threads, I never once felt "lost" or confused. I merely couldn't stop turning page after page to read the next episode about to unfold.

". . . Saying words that end up being true . . . is not the same as being honest."

From the centuries old Alexander House, the mysterious Rappahannock River, small Oxrun Park, and neighboring homes, there is a distinctive feel to this novel that if ever there was a place for the "impossible" to become the "everyday", this was it.

". . . You believe certain things your whole life. Those beliefs, they dig grooves into your brain, like a record player, and the needle doesn't leave the grooves. For many years you don't see anything . . . to knock the needle out of place . . . "

Overall, one of the best novels I've ever read that infuses the supernatural so seamlessly with human nature--and I don't necessarily mean the "best" of what humans have to give. Janz didn't just rely on either one element or the other in THE SIREN AND THE SPECTER (which would have been fairly predictable to some), but rather brought the combination to an entirely new level. Throughout "most" novels, I am able to predict some parts long before the ending. However, due to the powerful blending of details here, the few "suspicions" I had missed the mark completely. Despite the literary complexity of this story, Janz' skill made it easy to follow along for the entire duration. The only real complaint I had was when it ended.

I still wanted more.

"That place is deceased . . . "

Highest recommendation!

title: So he's used a bit of "poetic licence" to tell a good tale. It's certainly worth a read
text:
John Shors says 65% of this novel is based on hard facts - all the royal characters were real people and acted as they did in the book. So he's used a bit of "poetic licence" to tell a good tale. It's certainly worth a read, so long as you are not pedantic about historical fiction being 100% accurate.

But this novel is more than historical fiction I think. Beautifully written (in the first person narrative through the eyes of Princess Jahanara), with evocative imagery, it is an epic story depicting the downfall of a royal empire. In a similar vein to Ken Follett's Pillars of the Earth (but much shorter), it covers powerful emotions - greed, lust, power, resilience, love - between siblings, parents and children and of course, men and women. I enjoyed it more than I expected to. I also felt it has relevance to today's world, by illustrating the societal impact of liberal versus orthodox perspectives in religion and using the latter to justify discrimination, war and genocide.

It's a captivating read. I highly recommend it

Book: Remnants, Season of Glory by by Lisa T. Bergren, Blink, 2015
Genre: Post-Apoctalyptic, Allegory
Target Audience: Girls 15+
Subjects: Love, Family Relationships, Good vs. Evil, Hope, Truth
Summary: Together again the Ailith rejoice in the strength that comes from their togetherness. And they rejoice at how a hostile city humbles itself before it’s Maker. Even more cause for rejoicing comes when the elders recognize that the Maker is doing things differently than the traditions and lighten one of the burdens placed on the Ailith. The trails aren’t over, however. Right as they return home, triumphant and exaltant, a newcomer to the Valley meets them. A man born to be a brother but turned traitor: Kellach. He wants them to believe he has changed, that being a part of the Ailith is his greatest desire. Adrianna knows the Maker’s call is on his life, but she and the others also know that Sethos’ call is on his life as well. Their season of glory is also one of tests and trials. Wisdom, strength and discernment are in high demand.
Notes: Season of Glory is the third in the Remnants series. This series shows a world after a great war, a world where much knowledge and products have been destroyed. A prophecy came forth that some day the Ailith would come and free the people from the evil ones who enslave the world. On the day they were born, it was felt all over and these called were hidden away and trained for seventeen years. Then on the same day, all around a call came that it was time to venture into the world and unite with the others. They come in sets of two: a “Remnant” – one who has a special talent or skill and a “Knight” who lives to protect the Remnant. All knowledge is given on a need-to-know basis, to the characters and to the reader. The spiritual element is that all the good guys in the story believe in an all-powerful Maker. He gives strength and gifts to His followers. There is no discussion of who He is – the salvation He brings, but He is worshipped and believed to be capable of providing power. There is also words that represent the Bible. Actual physical books are lost due to the war but the words of Scripture are passed down and learned by those who follow the Maker.
In book two, these is an element of questioning the call to walk into danger rather than stay and hide in safety. The desire of all is for the lost to be reached, but some believe the lost will just come to them. The Ailith believe themselves to be called to go out into the hurting world and bring the Maker to them.
There is also a very strong element of who is in control of your life. Kellach and Adrianna both wrestle with control. At one point, Ronan explains the struggles as the simplest, yet most difficult thing to do – let go of your own control and allow the Maker to be in charge. Kellach is determined to do what he, himself wants, not Sethos or the Maker or anyone else.
Overall, this book did a good job portraying the idea of someone called by God to save the world and attempting to follow His leading and rely on Him for strength to do the task.
Spiritual Content Recommendation Scale: 4.5/5

title: A great read; among the best of the genre. Only one small complaint...
text:
Tyson is one of the truly great science insiders, advocates and educators of our time and this is an engaging read. It is a series of essays that covers the era of space exploration in an enlightening and entertaining way. It is book of great stories of our progress, not a mere catalogue of events. It contains all of the main fare for space junkies and it is served up well. It is almost as funny in places as the best bits of Mary Roach's "Packing for Mars", and (appropriately, for a more general book) does not provide as detailed a pathway to human (cf robotic) exploration as Buzz Aldrin in his "Mission to Mars". It is certainly much easier to read for the less technophilic, more emotionally involved reader than Shayler, Shayler and Salmon's "Marswalk One". Its honest but really quite troubling description of the difficulties facing manned exploration of space beyond low Earth orbit will be appreciated by enthusiasts. Tyson comments that much ground-breaking early technology appears quaint when compared to more developed versions. His observation that the now-old Saturn V rockets still evoke the reverence due to the 'latest and greatest', was a powerful lament.
I would recommend this book to any space enthusiast; it is amongst the best of the genre. However I do have a complaint. Like it or not, space exploration is now a thoroughly international mission, just as it also now involves private enterprise and robotics. Tyson himself is valued internationally and his (like Aldrin's) nationalistic wish for continued American supremacy in space is itself somewhat quaint and backward-looking. It also risks blindness to, and threatens lack of support for, some of the optimism and exciting achievements of other players such as the Europeans, Indians and Chinese.

As a child of the Cold War era, I often wondered, "Why do they harbor such ill feelings toward the US in Central America and the Caribbean?" And "Why does Europe hold us at arms' length despite our saving the continent in two world wars?" These were issues too new for the history books, yet beyond the contemporary news. Many of the answers lie within the pages of this book. It is a story of power and privilege. And for my money, outright treason.

I sincerely hope the prediction of James Jesus Angleton in the closing pages is correct. As Mark Twain once said, "Patriotism is supporting your country at all times. And your government when it deserves it." If ever a book gave one pause to consider his words, this is it.

title: An insider perspective
text:
I took courses from RBM in undergrad--at least 2 or 3, as she is one of the primary professors at Sacramento State. She informed us that this book is written itself to cater to individuals with alternative learning styles, particularly those with ADHD. That's why much of the chapter is in a bullet-point format. As a person with ADHD, this was the most easily digestible book in both undergrad and grad school, pretty much the polar opposite to the blue/purple bible (general assessment/treatment of children... It's at work, so I can't remember the name) which I found impossible to read.

The reason I give this book four stars instead of five is because of my experience of the general world view of the author. Although she likes to study and understand other cultures, she has a pretty narrow, prescriptive mindset herself. RBM's experience in the Philippines as a child was that of the daughter of missionaries. She is devoutly Christian herself and still has that missionary mindset--she thinks everyone should be Christian (evidenced by calling the annual Holiday party a "Christmas Party" and referring to winter break as "Christmas Break.") RBM likes to put people from other cultures into boxes--for instance, she often discussed "welfare families" in class; generations of African Americans who "push their way to the front of the food-stamps line" and feel "entitled to help from the government."

Definitely take what she says with a grain of salt, but there is still excellent information in here that will help you to understand the families of children with special needs, and to prevent misdiagnosis of children from cultures other than your own.

title: The Corean Chronicles Get More Complex...
text: One of the nice things about this series -- and it becomes quite noticeable by Book 2 -- is both the Reader's and the Character's Discovery Process in the sense that the Post-Cataclysmic World that the characters in the book inhabit, must survive in, and must make sense of is built-off of a remainder of a grander civilization that once was meaning that there's quite a lot to rediscover and/or to learn for the first time.  In terms of L.E. Modesitt's Fantasy Series this is an unusually complex structure for the storyline in that there's a lot more for both the Reader and the Characters to have to learn and to make sense of whereas in The Imager Portfolio and The Saga of Recluce things are pretty well layed-out and there's not so much that's unknown except for new and expanded applications of the characters powers.  I was definitely more satisfied with and was able to enjoy this second book of the series far more than I was able to the first book. Wendra developing Talent was a bit of a stretch but, for the moment, I'm prepared to suspend judgement and see where Modesitt takes the story.  One thing the author does quite well in his Serialized Series -- and Robert Jordan did this as well -- is give each book a point, a beginning, a middle, and an "ending" that satisfy whilst also leaving enough up in the air that follow-up books will be required to resolve The Bigger Storyline.  Where Modesitt differs is that -- through Prequelization of Developed Themes + Details -- he enjoys going backwards and showcasing how D led to C, C led to B, and B led to A.

title: This Book Needs a Movie Deal
text:
It’s not very often that a book impresses me enough for me to give it five stars, but this novel achieved that feat.

Iron Mike is an awesome story that starts with a widespread technological attack that takes out over 99% of the population. Left to look after his little sister, natural survivor Mike Sanderlin takes the reigns of chaos and struggles, with great difficultly, to tame the wild new world that threatens what little he has left. Teaming up with a host of other survivors, he learns that everything has changed, including himself.

Every character in this book is detailed and original. There are moments of bone-cracking action, sizzling emotion, and cinematic tension. It’s a typical end-of-the-world story but it’s been executed with a writing style so fresh and an imagination so sharp that it rises far above more mediocre stories in its genre.

I often end my book reviews with a critical point, suggesting something that I think could have been improved. Not this time. Quite simply, this is the best sci-fi novel I’ve read in a while. I was blown away. If a sequel appears – and I’m sure it will – I’ll be one of the first to buy it.

title: Depressing to know who we--the U.S.A.--may be. Damn the Constitution!
text:
Tim Weiner's, Legacy of Ashes is 600 pp. with an additional 180 pp. of notes. It is is a comprehensive and lengthy writing of the history of the C.I.A. The book is divided into six (6) parts that block out the years covered into six (6) segments. The writing is straightforward, simple, and clear.

For the reader who needs to know each of those six segments of years, I say, read on. However, I found the theme was so repetitive that one section would have sufficed.

I appreciated gaining an understanding of our C.I.A., it's unconstitutional and illegal activities as well as dishonest actions taken simply to "cover their butts," or to suppress something negative about the C.I.A. itself. I, and many others no doubt, question the real purpose of the C.I.A. as it relates to U.S. core values. I'm beginning to wonder how important those Constitutional values are to our leaders, or, for that matter, the American public​.

Possibly this book helps us to understand how we've gotten where we are today. Our Presidential Cabinet figures are "forgetting" important disclosures, and many congressmen and women show little or no concern. Maybe Weiner's book begins to show us the early stage cancer now metastasizing.

Legacy of Ashes is a valuable read for those wanting greater depth of understanding of who we are in the U.S. and where we may be going based on our history of a key intelligence agency. For most of us, the points made about the C.I.A. take too long to be expressed and are repeated far too many times.

title: Informative but dry and dense. Also, the future of the Earth as a viable planet isn't looking so hot.
text:
This book is relatively short, but dense. I'm not quite sure who the audience is for this book--if Wadhams is aiming at the layperson, this book is way too technical and difficult, but if he is aiming for fellow scientists, academics, and students of geology/science in general, then I think it is appropriately written. Me, well, I'm no scientist, though I did take Ice Age Earth way back in undergrad so thankfully not all the concepts introduced in this book were new to me. Honestly, that little bit of background really helped me understand some of Wadhams discussions. Other parts, I found generally accessible and some parts were mind numbingly boring. (I kind of understand why he dedicated his first chapters on the chemical make up of ice and how it grows but woo boy, was that boring. On the plus side, I can now describe something growing "dendritically.")

Though he does use a lot of technical language and you may not understand everything he is saying (especially when describing arctic processes or c-axes, pancake ice, albedo, or whatever) Wadhams' point is clear. He is sounding an alarm about global warming, the melting arctic ice and the catastrophic effects this could and likely will have. He lays out how carbon dioxide and methane act as greenhouse gases and how once released in the atmosphere, they stay there for upwards of a 100 years and that we are very near a point that even if we stop all emissions (which is not ever going to happen) that the warming cycle will continue. That is, it's about to pass a tipping point from which the results are irreversible. He does a good job of laying out all the issues this could create--famine as the temperatures in the agricultural lands change an extreme weather affects yields, increasing hurricanes as the warm ocean water doesn't get cooled by colder water currents from the arctic, increased desertification into current arable land, etc. He certainly doesn't paint a rosy picture. At the end of the book he does lay out different strategies currently on the table for reducing carbon or cooling the planet, though he also goes through all the problem with the possible solutions currently on the table. It's all very bleak.

The part I found most interesting, apart from how we're all going to die, is that he isn't addressing climate change deniers in this book (apart from mentioning them in the final chapter) but rather is focusing his ire on the current climate change "Establishment" -- the IPCC and many of the scientists whose predictions on ice melt and temperature rise he feels are wildly inaccurate and way too conservative. He is particularly critical of their dedication to computer modelling and their dismissal of results from scientific observations and work that are not based on modelling. He calls the Paris Accords something that should have been undertaken 20 years ago and constantly criticizes the IPCC's warming projections. As someone who believes in climate change, but has generally accepted the standard line from the IPCC and others Wadhams book makes me think twice about their projections (and it's not like their projections are sunny) and realize that things are perhaps much worse than we realize. He does have acall to arms at the end encouraging people to do something--to stand up and fight, really--but everything before it is so depressing it almost makes one feel, "What's the point? We're all doomed."

text:

He's an excellent writer, and I only gave him four stars instead of five because I preferred one of his other books to this one. David Sloane, a top-notch attorney, is recovering from the loss of his wife. In the midst of his work on previous cases, he comes across a very smart, attractive defending attorney who was against him on one of those cases. She quickly becomes involved in his life, almost too quickly. Then Sloane finds out that this woman is being targeted for her work in bringing down a drug trafficker who managed to kill her daughter. When a trafficker is found murdered, she becomes a suspect, and asks Sloane to represent her in court.

Sloane seems to be a bit oblivious to this woman's agenda, but the people who work for him and even his step-son are growing wise to possible problems in the case, and in this woman's involvement in Sloane's life. Sloane is forced to separate his personal life from the case, and look at what is really going on before it is too late.

title: There was a number of of Communist enclaves which were resistant to easy eradication. Year after year
text:
This book is one of the few in English to cover this very little known period in Chinese history. The book starts with 1928, which is usually considered the end of the Warlord era, and ends with 1937 when the major war began with Japan. The Nationalist Party of China (Guomindang) in theory united the country in 1928 after about a decade of the internecine wars among the various Warlords which rendered China what we would call today a failed state. Through diplomacy, threats, bribes and military force, the Nationalists achieved a tentative unity; however, old habits die hard. The former Warlords wanted business as usual. In 1929 and 1930 several of the most powerful Warlords rebelled in the Central Plains War, threatening to devolve the country back into a failed state. This was eventually put down. However, other rebellions by former Warlords, or newly appointed generals ensued almost continuously to 1937. If not rebellions against the central government, there were outbreaks of provincial armies warring against each other. The Nationalists' most recalcitrant internal threat were the Communists. There was a number of of Communist enclaves which were resistant to easy eradication. Year after year, the Chiang Kai Shek government sent massive armies to crush them, especially the enclave led by Mao Tse-tung, but could not. In addition to these internal threats, there were the external threats by the Soviet Union, Japan and Tibet. Almost immediately upon achieving unity in 1928, war ensued with the Soviet Union over the East Manchurian Railway, a strip of territory along the railway controlled by the Soviet Union across the northern tip of China. The war ended disastrously for China. Japan followed suit in 1931, or rather the rogue Japanese Kwantung Army did, overrunning what was then called Manchuria, the three northeastern provinces. It escalated into an attack on Shanghai. Chiang Kai Shek did not declare war at that time, a pragmatic but controversial decision. The Kwantung Army continued to slice off one territory after another in northern China, sometimes using puppet armies such as the Manchukuoan and Inner Mongolian. The Soviets exploited the resentment of the Islamic population of far west Sinkiang to intervene militarily and rendered the province a Soviet satellite starting 1934. Tibet used local Buddhist monastery disputes to attempt to take over territory in China which had ethnic Tibetans. This last was the only foreign encroachment that was met with a counter offensive, and it was successful. The appeasement policy regarding Japan created such resentment that the general charged with another attack on the Communist enclave kidnapped Chiang Kai Shek and forced him into a united front of Nationalists and Communists against the Japanese, The next Japanese aggression will be met with war. The book ends here.

I would have liked to have given this book a higher rating. Unfortunately, there are problems. One is the editing, or the lack thereof. Many, many misspellings of simple words and proper names. The latter causes confusion since there are many similar Chinese names; one does not know if the different spelling indicates a new character or just a misspelling. There are grammatical problems. Two seemingly conflicting facts are given sometimes in the same paragraph. Paragraphs contradict each other. When it says Fengtien Army in one place and Mukden Army in another, how many readers would know they refer to the same thing? Fengtien is the Chinese name, Mukden is the Manchu name. Good editing could have resolved these issues. Then, there is the lack of detailed maps. Very general maps of the whole country are given at the beginning of the book. One obscure Chinese town is cited after another; without detailed maps it is hard to follow the actions described in the text. There are no footnotes and the only sources are in English. The best part of the book are the photographs of which there are many.
