title: Believe It I You Dare
text:
It's painful to say this, but this book is almost totally a work of fiction.
I do believe that the author's name was Belton Cooper. However, anything beyond that is iffy, to say the least.
Somehow, I find it more than a little incredible to believe the action, as he describes it:
Supposedly, one man, along with his driver, in a combat zone, drove from the front lines to the rear echelon area, 30 to 60 miles each way, routinely, at night, under complete blackout, at 65 mph, in a jeep, with absolutely no lights, through enemy territory, with no map, to get information on battle-damaged tanks back to the rear, having memorized the route completely by heart, and did this on a daily, routine basis, just as a bread truck driver would run his route, strikes me as something less than totally believable.
In the first place, how could you memorize a route, "completely by heart," when you would be in a different place each night?
Plus, assuming you could even get a jeep up to 65 mph, what do you think would happen if, in total darkness, you hit a tree squarely in the middle of the front bumper? Forget 30 to 60 miles: You'd be lucky to make it 100 yards.
Yet, he somehow was able to get 65 mph out of a jeep, which tops out at maybe 45-50 mph - and he did it in total darkness, 30 to 60 miles, through enemy territory.
Really?
It may have actually happened, but then, Bigfoot may also be alive and well in the Oregon woods, too.
This was on top of first having tracked down and located and examined and inventoried each battle-damaged tank, writing a report of the physical damage, while disregarding any dead crew members still remaining in the tank, and delivered the finished report 30-60 miles to the rear, through enemy territory, at night, and then, the next day, led a procession of replacement tanks back to the front to replenish the ones they lost the day before.
Does this strike anyone as being credible, or even possible?
Does this sound like a TV episode of the "A-Team?"
I'm wondering, if underneath his fatigue jacket, he was wearing a blue sweatshirt with a big red letter "S" in the middle of his chest?
There are so many details he doesn't bother to mention, let alone explain, that nothing about the whole tale has any credibility.
Such as: How would he know where to even begin looking for tanks that had been knocked out in battle? Did just he and his driver poke around in battle areas trying to find tanks that had been killed, or did he have any sort of armed protection? What would keep him from being attacked by the enemy, as he looked for damaged tanks?
If you've ever seen a battle-damaged tank, you would know that it takes a whole lot more than a few hand tools and some paint to get them back into operational condition. In most cases, they're little more than a pile of scrap metal.
Plus, how did this all happen out in the battle areas?
Where did he find crewmen to get the refurbished tanks back to the front? What about ammo for the tanks? What about gasoline? If this was in a combat zone, what would keep the refurbished tanks from being attacked on their way back to the front? Did the tanks have just a driver, or did they also have a full crew; tank commander, driver, loader, and gunner?
If the tanks only had a driver to get it back to the front, how would the tank defend itself if it was attacked, without a gunner and loader, and someone, such as a tank commander, to direct the action and man the .50 cal. machine gun? Where is the front, anyway? Which way did they go? The front today is not in the same location it was in yesterday.
BTW: The "front" implies an imaginary line drawn between the good guys and the enemy - where people are shooting at each other - to kill - with real bullets. Hardly the place for a delivery transaction to occur.
As far as that goes, how did the battle-damaged tanks get back to the rear echelon to be repaired in the first place?
What about the crewmen who were killed in the battle action, and were still in the tanks? Have you ever smelled the interior of a tank in which people were killed a day or two before, and were still in the tank?
How did these people get back to the rear echelon, once they had delivered their tanks? How would he find the front, anyway, inasmuch as it would have advanced, ever more forward (or maybe they even had to fall back) - how many miles? In which direction?
Would the enemy kindly just refrain from attacking them while he drove the newly refurbished tanks back to the front - wherever it might be - and allow him to bring the tanks up, and turn them over to the front-line commander?
To have accomplished what he claims to have accomplished is very laudable, and he would certainly deserve much credit, but the whole story sounds more than highly suspect to me.
I sort of lost interest after the first couple of chapters, because I'm really not interested in reading someone's idea of heroic escapades, especially when they are the ones supposedly doing it. This is the kind of stuff you read in war novels - or Action Comics.
I think he missed his calling - as an action/adventure fiction writer.
I was afraid to read any further, because if this all happened just in the first two chapters, there is no telling how much more incredible information he would impart in the next, many chapters until the end.
In fact, several years ago, I had a friend who was very enjoyable to be around, and he had so many incredible stories about his escapades and adventures, that I eagerly lapped them up every time I saw him, and believed every word.
One day, however, it struck me that his stories were so fantastic that they couldn't possibly be true, and I finally concluded that probably everything he had ever told me was a product of his incredible imagination, and he had made it up on the fly, as he spoke.
This is precisely the feeling I get in reading Mr. Cooper's story, because hardly any of it rings true.
But as to those few experts at spinning tales, such as I strongly suspect Mr. Cooper was one of the premier members, they tell it so skillfully that it all sounds completely credible, and you are never tempted to doubt anything they say.
Just to give you an idea of how knowledgeable Mr. Cooper was, he beefs about the American tanks being named for Southern generals, but was unaware that our tanks were actually named by the British, which usually got first crack at our tanks even before we did, since they were in the war before us, and we supplied much of their armor, long before we even entered the war.
The British named all of our tanks - all after American Generals - which is admittedly a little strange - but it's a fact.
Frankly, I think he made it up as he went, just as the thoughts occurred to him in his very vivid imagination.
It has all the touches of some of the tales surrounding the Adventures of Bigfoot, with much fantastic action, but little or no explanation of exactly how it could possibly have happened, here in the real world.

title: Wondering about Washington?  Here's a book for you!
text:
As this book was recommended by the President of Mount Vernon as the best single-volume book about George Washington, I had to read it, especially in an effort to update my own book “George Washington’s Liberty Key.” I found the book a gem to hold, beautifully bound and printed. Rhodehamel's story of Washington reads as well as any of the best of dozens of other books about him I had read before. I was especially pleased that the author introduced numerous, uncommon insights as to why things happened the way they did. For example, General Clinton’s familiarity with New York from when his father was royal governor allowed him to propose (and lead) the pivotal flanking movement through Jamaica Pass during the Battle of Long Island. Other authors often give credit to a “loyalist spy” making the suggestion to General Howe, at least as to the Pass being lightly defended and leaving out any mention of Clinton's background or, for that matter, Howe's never-to-be-forgotten horrible experience with direct attacks at Bunker Hill. Unfortunately, one is surprised by a couple minor typos and inaccuracies in a book so otherwise well-written and researched. One inaccuracy, made by many august others, is having King George III call Washington, upon his relinquishing command of the army at the end of the Revolutionary War, “the greatest man in the world.” No, George III called Washington “the greatest character of the age.” All in all, however, the book is extremely well done and highly recommended.

Check out one of William J. Bahr’s books: [[ASIN:1537323377 George Washington's Liberty Key: Mount Vernon's Bastille Key – the Mystery and Magic of Its Body, Mind, and Soul]], a best seller at Mount Vernon.

title: Inaccurate law
text:
First, in the CivPro section, one of the answers states that a plaintiff can maintain a diversity suit because the damages was “at least” 75,000. Every law student and lawyer knows that it must “exceed” 75,000. Even the FRCP uses “exceeds”.

Second, the statements of law for ConLaw are partial and not complete. For instance, the intermediate standard of review requires the law be substantially related to an important governmental interest and the rational basis review requires the law be rationally related to a legitimate interest. The book omits substantially related and rationally related.

Third, if an MEE subject is also an MBE subject, then that outline is not in this book. You have to buy the MBE volumes 1 and 2 for those subjects. This was not mentioned on the amazon page.

Update:

Review of the Family Law outline has revealed more inaccurate statements of the law:

The book states that a valid premarital agreement is:

"...full disclosure of all the spouses' assets and liabilities, reasonable opportunity for both parties to seek independent counsel, and the parties must be acting in good faith without fraud or coercion."

While some of this is correct, it is worded incorrectly, used out of context, uses words not used in the official model answer, and is still missing important elements. From the NCBE:

"...such agreements are enforceable unless procured by fraud, duress, or coercion. A premarital agreement must be in writing and signed by both parties. A premarital agreement is not enforceable if the spouse whom enforcement is sought proves that (a) the agreement was made involuntarily, OR (b) it was unconscionable when executed and before execution the spouse was (i) not provided fair disclosure of financial information, (ii) did not waive disclosure, and (iii) did not have knowledge of such information. Elements that courts will look to for voluntariness is (1) presence of independent legal counsel, (2) length of the time between the date of the agreement and the wedding, (3) the party's abilities to understand the agreement, and (4) other reasons"

While much longer, this statement is accurate and complete. The statement from the Rigos book lacks voluntariness, which was tested on the Feb 2016 MEE. So, you would have gotten the wrong answer if you had followed the Rigos statement. The Rigos statement lacks unconscionable, waiver, and the fact that independent counsel is part of voluntariness. Also, a premarital agreement does not require "full" disclosure nor does it require "good faith".

title: Insight into horror
text:
After having enjoyed the iconic horror of the landmark film for many years, I decided to delve into the novel on which it’s based. And while I’m an ardent believer that the book is always better than the movie (in almost all cases), in this case, it’s impossible to state unequivocally which is the superior work of art.

The film is, of course, a classic. I need make no argument for that here. The novel? Probably less so. It is, however, noteworthy for a number of elements that the film seems to lack. In the film, the most memorable scenes are those of the possessed Regan spewing out obscenities and vomit while levitating her bed and telekinetically moving furniture. These scenes create comparable horror in the novel, yet the climactic event itself—the exorcism—lasts just 30 pages or so. The novel also offers greater development of Damien Karras, the young Jesuit whose professional interest in Regan’s case troubles him and challenges his faith. Through him, we learn more about the history of demonic possession. Furthermore, minor characters like Kinderman, the police detective, and Karl and Winnie, the McNeil household staff, are more fully developed through subplots.

Blatty’s prose style is rather pedestrian and unremarkable, but it serves the story adequately. The artistry of this novel does not lie in its use of the language but in its power to portray the terror of the supernatural.

title: I just love the ideas
text:
(some very light spoilers here)

To keep it short : this is almost exactly the book I wanted to read.

I'm an ancient Chinese philosophy/history geek. I just love the ideas, the old religions and spiritual practices, the writing system(s) the crazy stuff that happened, the impressive inventions, etc... In short, I think China is (at least culturally) one the most interesting place on Earth. I simply love reading about the different dynasties and the various books that came to us from that time. Confucius of course, but also Mencius (so very modern), Mo Zi and his scary utilitarian politics, or (my favourites) the more poetical Lao Zi and Zhuang Zi.

I'm also a huge science fiction and fantasy geek. I studied literature (from Shakespeare to Dickens, from Pynchon to Steven Millhauser) at university, but it's with Tolkien's fantasy or Iain Banks' science fiction that I'll read myself to sleep.

It's not a surprise that I had been looking for a book like The Grace of Kings for a long time, then. Ever since I got into Chinese culture, I wanted to read a fantasy retelling of its history in the same vein as Tolkien is the reimagining of Ancient England, Game of Thrones the recycling of the War of the Roses, or Delany's Neveryona a sort of retelling of prehistoric Europe/Near-East. Reading Zhuangzi, I could tell that there was a world of wonders in China, and I wanted to be amazed by them too. This is exactly what happened with Ken Liu's novel.

There are plenty of references to historical events, more or less recycled to fit the story of the book, and I was always very happy to catch them. I'm sure many went over my head, but they will come to me along the years while I continue to study China and read the following books in The Dandelion Dynasty. The world invented by Ken Liu is very coherent as well as rich.

I haven't really felt the Chinese spiritual heritage rewritten in the book, which was a surprise. I guess that I expected a more "Taoist" mystical world, something like I find in Ursula Le Guin's books. But the surprise was actually very good, as the treatment of the gods was great. The parts that concerned them were probably my favourites, and I hope we'll get to know more about them in the following books. I'd love to know from where they ultimately come from, both in their world and in our own.

Something I really loved was the various war chapters. It's easy : I just couldn't let go of my reading device during these parts. I was completely hooked by them, and absolutely devoured these chapters. I usually get bored by the way battles are told in other other fantasy books... but not here. Not only did I care about the characters involved, but how they managed their successes and failures was made very interesting by the writing. I feel like the rhythm of these sections was perfect, and would sometimes feel like I was in front of a detective novel, and had a great time playing with the book and trying to second-guess the various strategies used by the characters.

As always with Ken Liu's fiction, the writing was great. When I read his fiction, I always have a "sense of flowing" which is immensely pleasant, its balance is perfect. Grace of Kings, apart from some very rare exceptions, was no exception. My only regret here is that I would have loved to have more "sense of wonder" moments. They do come, sometimes, but I felt they were too short.

Only two things I didn't care much about. First, I had a hard time with the names. They sometimes sounded quite silly in the languages I speak (French and Spanish), and I didn't feel like they were evocative enough. I sometimes forgot who was who, and often had to go back to the beginning to check.

My other problem was with the way romance was used in the novel. Quite simply, I didn't believe in its (few) love stories.

I had a great time with that novel, and I highly recommend it.

title: Heart-Pulsing.
text:
The year is 1976. An air France plane with 248 passengers has been hijacked by Palestinian and German terrorists. The aircraft has been landed in Entebbe, Uganda (over 2500 miles from Israel) where tyrant Idi Amin offers sanctuary to the terrorists.

Their demands: release of 40 Palestinian terrorists from Israeli prisons, and an additional few from other free nations. Or else.

What would you do? Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin is in a bind, as there is understandable pressure on him from the families of the loved ones held captive in an airport terminal in Uganda. Does he negotiate with the terrorists, acquiescing to their demands? Or does he look into riskier options?

Giving into the terrorists will undoubtedly cause Israel’s national prestige to plummet—as well as encourage more hijackings in the future. Release of deadly terrorists from prisons will almost guarantee more loss of life in the future. For statesman Shimon Peres there is only one option. “If we give into the terrorists, not even the faintest memory of us will remain.”

Operation Thunderbolt is a brilliantly written narrative of the 1976 hijacking and the famous Special Forces raid that followed. It follows closely the personal accounts of passengers on the Air France plane, ministers of Israeli Defense, soldiers of the Unit, as well as many other global figures--giving the reader an incredible behind the scenes look as the drama unfolds.

The book as a whole is: unbelievably tense, overwhelmingly tragic, absolutely immense. A truly enjoyable read.

title: Not what I was hoping for
text:
I picked up a used copy from another store online, in good condition.

The sample pages (from the Kindle version) don't actually show the weekly recipes. They only show the introductory information. the intro information is fine, but what you really want from this book is the weekly cook-up directions: recipes, shopping lists, and plans. And these were a bit of a disappointment to me. If they had been visible in the preview, I wouldn't have bought the book. I will likely be donating the book to one of my local charities, after I finish going through the recipes to see if there's anything worth saving.

Two main problems, for me. First, I don't see how the weekly cook-up actually produces enough food for one week. Lunch and Dinner are grouped together as "Lunch/Dinner" and there's only two main recipes there (with the sides switched out). Even if we're only cooking for 5 days (assuming you're eating out on the weekends), that's 10 meals that you need to make... with two recipes. It seems repetitive, boring, and not very healthy. The author doesn't mention fasting, so I don't think you're supposed to skip lunch (which might make the recipes make more sense).

For example, here's what's listed for week 1 (page xvii in the hard cover edition):

Breakfast:
- 1-2 Paleo Energy Muffins
- 1 Piece of Breakfast Casserole

Snacks:
- Raw Veggie Snack Bag and Paleo Hummus
- Raw Veggie Snack Bag
- 1-2 Paleo Energy Muffins
- 1 slice of Breakfast Casserole

Lunch/Dinner:
- Collard Greens Sandwich Wrap
- Collard Greens Sandwich Wrap and Raw Veggie Snack Bag
- Collard Greens Sandwich Wrap and Raw Veggie Snack Bag and Paleo Hummus
- Paleo Winter Ragu (1c/225g per serving)
- Paleo Winter Ragu (1c/225g as topping for spaghetti squash or spiralized veggies)

That's it. That's your menu for the week. And as a side note, for 4 weeks, there's only two meals with seafood (fish tacos in week 3 and tuna salad in week 4). I'm surprised... I generally try to eat several servings of fish per week.

The second issue for me is that the meals/snacks contain extra sugar. The Paleo Energy Muffins in week one, for example, include maple syrup and cacao nibs. This might not be an issue for everyone, but I'm trying to reduce my sugar intake for health purposes. Adding syrup to a meal (or chocolate to breakfast) isn't something that's helpful for me. It would be less of an issue if there were more meals provided (it would be easier to swap something out), but there's not. But, I understand that this might not be an issue for everyone (and I may try some of the muffins as a way to wean myself off the other sugary snacks that I'm struggling with.)

Some of the meals are also not really "recipe worthy". The Collard Greens wrap for week 1, for example, is literally just bacon, luncheon meat, and whatever vegetables you want - wrapped in a collard green. The pictures show tomatoes and onions. The notes give examples of "paleo pickle slices, tomato slices, sliced red onion, etc.". Again, this is listed as one of only two meals for a week's worth of lunches and dinners, and it's essentially two slices of luncheon meat, bacon, tomatoes, onions wrapped in a collard leaf. That doesn't seem like enough to carry 6 meals (the recipe calls for making about 6 servings, with 2 pieces of luncheon meet per serving).

I was so excited when I saw this book, and though it might fill in some of my cooking and meal prep gaps. I've been doing weekly meal prep for the last few months, but still struggle with making enough food to get through the week and trying to decrease my sugar. The book was a pretty big disappointment and waste of money for me :( . I think the idea is phenomenal, I'd love to see a really good "paleo bootcamp" plan... but this just wasn't what I was hoping for, personally.

Here is the recipe listing for the remaining weeks, since I wish I had seen it before ordering:

Week 2 (page xviii):

Breakfast:

title: Noah calls April a goddess and paints a perfect picture of the girl he sees
text:
Published writer and former lawyer, Noah Callaway lives a seemingly quiet life. Tucked away in his late aunt’s cottage, Noah just wants to write about crime and forget his past. He wants to forget about his obsession with April Moon which started in high school. Noah calls April a goddess and paints a perfect picture of the girl he sees. Throughout their lives, Noah and April have an on again off again relationship and are even engaged to be married at one point. However, the perfect girl that Noah has dreamt up has a dark past that he’s chosen not to notice. Finally, free of the obsession, Noah receives a phone call from his estranged friend, Will who says April is the prime suspect in a murder and suicide attempt. The Beauty of the End follows Noah as he attempts to uncover years’ worth of secrets left behind by a woman he thought he knew, in order to prove her innocence.

I was quite impressed with the way this story started out and unfolded. The Beauty of the End is a gripping tale and I found myself flipping through the pages quite quickly. There are (mostly) believable characters and the style of writing is easy to follow. This is my first book written by Debbie Howells and I can’t wait to read more. That being said, I absolutely hated how naïve Noah’s character is. I can understand how April was able to keep some secrets from him, however, (without giving away spoilers) there were a few things that he SHOULD have noticed. I find it hard to believe that he was so wrapped up in the person he wanted her to be that he missed completely who she really was.

I had several of the clues pinpointed from the beginning but I wasn’t able to solve all the mysteries that April laid out until the very end. Also, the ending didn’t quite add up for me. It was not as smooth as the rest of the story was. Even though this wasn’t my favorite psychological thriller, Howells is still a brilliant writer and I urge you to give her a shot.

title: Beautiful Love Story
text:
First of all I'd like to give credit to the author, Paula Quinene, for writing a subject that is barely ever, if at all used in historical fictions: Guam during World War II. I've studied history - a lot - and have never read about Guam's experience during the war. Secondly, Paula is a native of Guam, and writing this book in English has taken her ten years to write and produce. She never gave up her dream to have her story told. For that alone, I praise you Paula. Lastly, I know first hand how difficult it is to write a war-based romance and pull it off. Men want the blood and guts, soldiers will correct you on the right wording (like the difference between C-ration and MREs), and women just want the romance... that's what problems I went through when writing Beneath the Wall, a Vietnam War historical romance. In the end, it's what the author wants the story to be that makes it wonderful. 

With all that said, this was a pretty darn good book. I loved the history, loved learning about a subject I never read before, and loved the romance between Johan and Jesi. It has a very real-life feel to it. You can feel the heat, taste the coconut (and there's a lot of coconut), and see the world that Jesi lives in very clearly. 

Like I mentioned above, though, the author's second language is English, so there is a bit of a barrier there. It makes for a little difficult reading, but to me, it makes the story more authentic, like Jesi is telling the story herself. 

So if you like a beautiful love story, and history on a barely seen time in the world, then please check it out. 

PS. I realize the cover says that it's an erotic tale... I don't know who came up with that one, but it's not erotic - at least not in my eyes. Erotic to me is kinky stuff, 50 Shades junk... this is not that at all or anything close to that. The characters do have a loving and healthy relationship, but nothing erotic.  If it were a movie, it would be rated R, not in the NC-17 or X range. Sexy, but not disgusting.

title: Best Book of 2016
text:
This is the book to beat this year.

| Best in the mystery genre of 2016 |

A jolly good treasure hunt.

The twisting and turning alleys of plots, subplots and the art of moving through them.

Rohan, got the ring right on the jackpot.

The story opens with the protagonist loosing his manuscript. And his vehicle. Thankfully a godsend helps him retrieve what's his.

But not the novel.

So here we go on a roll.

Ashwin is a laid back real estate broker whose ditched by his girlfriend. Russian Girlfriend. And he takes it upon himself to generalize that sour taste by one Russian Federation citizen.

Landing up in his place, yes GOA, are four of his friends for vacation. Only that it is serious. Dead serious.

Pratik, tells them a historical story of a treasure that was long hidden and forgotten. No, it is not mythology stuff, rather solid gold we are talking about. Worth 200 Crores INR. And he has the map. Also, he is a descendant of the guy who put it in earth somewhere in Goa.

The chase begins. With not 5 but 6 people, including Maya. Well, Ashwin would not like Iftikar's girlfriend's being left out of my review for obvious reasons.

Because she was Russian. And Iftikar pours the entire story of 2000 Crores to his soulmate.

The story wobbles from one end to another, like a drunken old man. Then energizes itself from the Red Bull and we welcome the entry of not one but two more claimants to the grand lottery prize.

They have their own version of stories to append to the initial one. You do not know what is true.

One of them is a local don. Russian Don.
To make matters worse.
And the second one is the owner of the house where the treasure is believed to be buried.

I am not spoiling this one for you.

But to intrigue you further in the name of giving you some clues, here's something you'll love.

One. The treasure does exist.

Two. It is taken out multiple times.

Three And buried back.

Four The police arrives in time.

The punchlines are hilariously placed and it comes across as one brilliant book with perfectly well nourished characters (pun : intended) in Bhavesh.

The mystery is so finely knit that author does something out of the box.

He sits down cross-legged and discusses plot holes with you. Come on, no one did that with the reader.

And mind you, there are no plot holes.

One Word Verdict : Masterclass

Best in the mystery genre this 2016. Loaded to the brim.

title: A Carroll Festival of Footnotes
text:
When I was a child, I pored over my mother’s handed-down copies of “Alice in Wonderland” and “Through the Looking Glass”. I was delighted by the other worlds down the rabbit hole and on the other side of the mirror, enthralled by the Cheshire Cat’s magical grin, the live playing cards and chessmen, the further adventures of my old friend Humpty Dumpty, and the antics of the Mad Hatter and March Hare. At the same time I felt some of the frustration that a child feels while sitting in on grown-ups’ conversation – I got the gist of the story, but I somehow knew that there was a lot that I wasn’t getting, grownup humor that was going on over my head. Even later, when I re-read Alice as a grown-up, I knew I wasn’t getting the point of a lot of the satire.

In “The Annotated Alice” Martin Gardner solves that problem completely and charmingly, with affectionate and witty footnote explanations of Carrollian wit that are almost as much fun to read as the original text, especially if you are a trivia nerd like me. Are you curious about the inspiration for “How doth the little crocodile/ improve his shining tail”? Here is the complete text of Rev. Isaac Watts poem “How doth the little busy bee/ improve each shining hour.” Is it true that John Tenniel’s drawings of the Mad Hatter were meant to represent British Prime Minister Gladstone? Gardner lays that myth to rest. Other notes explain in-jokes – allusions to incidents and people in Oxford and the family of Alice Liddell that would be clearly understood by his target audience, the real Alice and her sisters.

If you first met “Alice” in your youth and would like to know her better, I recommend you snuggle up with “The Annotated Alice” as your bedside companion. You will find unsuspected sophistication in this old treasure, you will feel younger with every page, and your dreams will be haunted by nothing worse than the Jabberwock.

title: Wildlife Co-Existence California Style: Upbeat Stories
text:
California and its people are amazing. Despite its huge human population and its 12-lane freeways, Californians are co-existing with their wildlife and enjoying it. Although P-22 is on the cover, the book is about much more than the story of the solitary male puma living in a park in the middle of LA. Where else would motorists patiently wait while two deer trot across the Golden Gate Bridge at the height of rush hour? Where would endangered San Joaquin kit foxes folic on lawns within the city limits of Bakersfield? Where would gray foxes live on Facebook’s campus in Silicon Valley, entertaining Mark Zuckerberg? The book is full of stories like this.

But most amazing to me was the announcement by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife in 2014: “Re-establishment of native species is a long-term goal that excites the department. This is true for the gray wolf.” At the time, wolves weren’t even residents of the state, but the wildlife commissioners voted in advance of their arrival to give them protection under the California Endangered Species Act. How many other states have done that?

I am a native of California. I don’t live there anymore--the crowds and the massive freeways drove me away--but the stories in this book make me proud to have been a resident. I only wish more people in other states were as tolerant.

title: Delightfully strange, dark fun.
text:
In "Palindrome," EZ Rinsky has crafted a compelling read that is a bit of Michael Chabon and a bit of Gary Shteyngart mashed up with old-school noir. The storyline and the characters are weird without seeming kooky, which is a fine line to trod. My biggest pet peeve when reading mystery/detective novels is an ending that either leaves too many frayed ends or tries to wrap up the story too neatly. Not to worry here - the ending to Palindrome was satisfying in more ways than one!

In all, this book is full of fun and suspense. Rinsky balances the dark and sometimes twisted plot with the main character's smirking humor. After finishing the book, it hovered in my thoughts for a few days, replaying itself at random intervals. That's the mark of a good story!

title: Creepy, cruel killer makes for high suspense, but has odd heroine's daughter & little mystery
text:
"The Bones Will Speak" is a Christian suspense novel. This is the second book in a series. This book didn't spoil the previous mystery, but I'd recommend starting with that one. I didn't always understand why Gwen and her daughter acted like they did, and the first book might have helped flesh that out.

Gwen was resourceful, but she deeply resented her ex-husband and that effected her judgment (and her driving) at times. Her best friend urged her to forgive her husband so she could heal. Gwen's daughter really confused me. At times, the 14-year-old acted like she resented her mother and was in full rebellion. She knew she was in danger, but she didn't lock the doors when told to and even refused to jump into a river because "it's cold." But then she'd act like a naive, trusting 5-year-old who just knows mommy will make things all better. She trustingly opened the door to a stranger. There was a reason to open the door, but a teen would have realized a potential flaw with that reason.

The mystery was clue-based. Whodunit deliberately left obvious clues and Gwen pointed out others, so it was easy to put together whodunit. There were two possible people for the unknown challenge-coin holder, but clues quickly cleared that mystery up, too. So the story hinged on its high level of suspense. This was a creepy story with a sick whodunit who cruelly killed many animals and people. There was danger at every turn.

Still, I had a hard time believing how easily the killer was able to find girls whose facial structure looked just like Gwen's daughter and who had a genetic disease or disfigurement. There was no sex or bad language. The crime scene gore was not graphically described.

I received an ebook review copy of this book from the publisher through NetGalley.

title: Ignore the middle - the first and l last are truly worth the read!
text:
I was one of the few who have only read this one novel by Pam Jenoff. I'm glad I read this one first. It grabs you from the beginning and makes it hard to put it done. WWII Nazi Germany, Poland Jews being completely wiped out, the Polish resistance doing whatever they can do to counter the terrorism and genocide by the Nazis. The special camp that resistance captives were sent for daily tortures to give up info is where we meet Marta, our heroine. From the beginning you are captivated by her strength and resolve - you only hope for that same gumption had you been in her place. You fall for the American soldier that liberated her from the death camp just as hard as she did, as well as grieve with her when she loses Rose.

Now comes the part where Jenoff must have let someone else write for her. She had to! All of a sudden our heroine is weak minded and cowardly, making poor decisions and becoming a robot who can't make up her own mind about anything. What happened to our Marta?

Then the author wakes up from her nap and brings back the first Marta - thank God. Because I was about to quit reading the rest of it. Talk about a scathing review on its way! SPOILER ALERT - skip this sentence.....though bringing Paul back from the dead was a bit over the top....it did make my heart flutter a bit after the dead space in the middle. The rest of the book becomes an espionage thriller full of Russian spies (one of which is a shocker) and escapes that you simply can't put down.

So, like I said - if there was a way to forget the middle part, I'd of given this book a 5 star, but alas it must settle for a 3. A good read - you MUST read it. And, yes, I will probably read the Kommandants Girl to see if Jenoff did, indeed, write a full novel before this fiasco.

Instead this is a book about a not-so-little boy’s bedtime and the bedtime story he makes up with one of his moms about a dragon who doesn’t want to be fierce any more.

I was so excited for family diversity that is just a fact of life and not something to be examined or questioned. I really liked the illustrations as well, and the fact that dragons (like boys and girls) can be any way they want to be, and don’t only have to be what folks expect of them.

title: Now that I understand you, is it OK to hate you?
text: The first step toward accepting others' views is willingness to concede that they are worth considering at all. We Americans spend a great deal of time talking past one another, rarely stopping to consider where the other person is "coming from." There has always been a lot of this in our society, but my perception--like that of many others--is that it is getting worse. By writing off the other's claim to legitimacy, we write him off as a human being. Having lived in Argentina during the last military dictatorship, I know all too well where this can lead. I recognize many things in today's America that I saw developing in the runup to the Argentine dirty war forty-odd years ago, and they terrify me. This book is an attempt to understand the underlying psychology that leads to polarization on what are essentially moral questions. It deploys a mix of social-science methods, philosophical argument, and cognitive neuroscience toward that end. Its conclusions are not so novel as the author thinks: many thoughtful people have arrived at similar analyses without the trappings of scientific rigor. But it is still good for inspiring serious thought about how we might get out of our dilemma before it leads us on to violent attempts at "resolution." One cavil: the "elephant" metaphor doesn't really work, and it gets annoying. It reminds me of George Lakoff's "Don't Think of an Elephant." Haidt does cite two of Lakoff's books, which have similar take-homes to his own.

title: Okay - For Banks Completists
text:
This slim volume of short SF by the master novelist is currently hard to acquire in the USA - no ebook or in-print hardcopy version - so the question is should you pay the premium in price and delivery time to get one of the available used copies? My suggestion is to do this only if you're determined to acquire all of Banks' Culture-setting fiction, all his SF or all his novels (speculative and non).

The big draw here is the title novella, in which Diziet Sma, the Special-Circumstances officer from the amazing novel, The Use of Weapons, comes to late 20th-Century Earth with a Culture mission deciding whether to contact Terran civilization or not. That sounds like a can't-miss premise before you read the story. In the event, I found just about every aspect of the novella spectacularly misconceived. Why set it in 1977 mostly in the West rather than 1989 mostly in the East, for example? (The story was written in 1989, per the copyright date.) Why concentrate on a period of human capitalism in its doldrums when it would be more interesting to get the Culture's - and by extension Banks' - perspective on the simultaneous and greater doldrums of human socialism? Why present all the action as the SC agents' summaries of their interaction with Terrans without actually showing any of those interactions. (I don't think any Earth-human gets a real speaking role.) The novella is also very, very. very. very talky. Overall, it feels like not just a failure, but a failure of nerve.

The other pieces set in or relating to the Culture are better. "A Gift from the Culture" is a good story about blackmail and terrorism. "Descendent" is a nice piece about a human and his intelligent space-suit trying to survive the aftermath of an ambush. "A Few Notes on the Culture" is a good piece of nonfiction, but reprints an old usenet post readily available on http://www.vavatch.co.uk/. The non-Culture stories range from "nice enough I suppose" (Road of Skulls, Odd Attachment, Cleaning Up) to awful (Piece). I don't think any of them will stick with me for their positive qualities.

In advance of tracking down this book, I feared I'd be missing something if I let it pass me by. Having read it, I learn that I'd have been fine. Banks wrote some great novels, but short fiction doesn't seem to have been his idiom.

text:
This is the second collection of Sin’s poetry that I’ve read and, like Algedonic, I enjoyed it quite a bit. It is formatted in the ever more prevalent style of writing very short poems or simple phrases rather than longer, multiple stanza poetry that most people are used to. It is a particularly tricky style to write well, as that type of poetry can come across as disjointed or shallow more easily than longer poems. However, when it is done well, it can be surprisingly powerful and touching. Though it did not captivate me in the way that Algedonic did, I still had a rather positive experience with Rest in the Mourning.

I have spoken in my other review about r.h. Sin’s talent for writing, and that shines through once again in this collection. His main focus is on the strength of women, but this still makes for a universally relatable read due to his beautiful writing and depiction of the common highs and lows of life. Sin knows how to simplify what can be very complex emotions, and the message he conveys is that of affirmation and strength. Just like the first experience I had with his work, I felt that he did a nice job of focusing on every human’s power to heal themselves in the midst or aftermath of hardship.

However, this collection, compared to his last, was not very unique. Every poem focuses either on women—or, less frequently, on himself—finding their true worth, and removing themselves from toxic relationships. There is nothing inherently wrong with the topic, but I feel that there needs to be some sort of variation, however small. You can still connect your topics together in some way to give the collection as a whole one theme, but I found none of that here. So while the way he worded things was beautiful, overall, every poem felt a little repetitive. I am still interested in reading more of his work, so I definitely will continue to do so.

title: “A New History of Life”  by P. Ward and J. Kirschvink
text:
The authors, Peter Ward, a professor of biology and earth & space sciences, and Joe Kirschvink, a professor of geobiology, get high marks for presenting an account of science at work, with competing interpretations and theories, explanations of just what is measured and how it is interpreted—in other words the gory details of how science actually works. Their topic—the geological, biological, chemical and physical history of the evolution of the earth and life upon it--- is of great interest to everyone. The material presented should be understandable by any serious reader, but a great deal of effort will be required to remember the plethora of categories and dates and causes for this and that from chapter to chapter. A summary chart of the names and times of the periods of geological time and for mass extinctions and their causes, and the major events that happened within each geological period would have been helpful. I made such a chart, which unfortunately does not format on Amazon, to help myself and others who lack this familiarity

I would also fault the authors for cluttering the book with unnecessary details about which scientist working for which university discovered this or believes that. The necessary technical details of how fossils are dated, how the carbon cycles work, etc. are well-described, but could be better highlighted and indexed for the continual reference that will be necessary by reader’s unfamiliar with the subjects. However, the wealth of information contained in the book makes it well worth reading.

The first question to be addressed in a history of life is what do we mean by life? This has been dealt with by philosophers since time in memoriam, but this is a science book and more precise definitions are needed. The 2nd Law of Thermodynamics states that over time the state of order of a system in isolation will decay into a state of disorder; i.e. entropy will increase. A living organism harvests energy from the external world and uses it to maintain its order (metabolism) and reproduce. Life could be understood as a series of chemical machines, all packed together and integrated, expending energy to maintain order. For life on earth, the primary source of energy are light photons from the Sun which through photosynthesis convert carbon dioxide and water into complex carbon compounds with many bonds in which energy is stored (another source is the thermal energy from the earth’s core). Life may occur in single cells and in man and in everything in between. It should not be surprising that life started at the single cell level, probably first evolved into a thin layer of green slime and then into more complicated forms, a story well told by the authors. Nor is it surprising that conditions were not propitious for the formation life on the surface of the earth for the first 700 million years after the formation of earth and that the first life probably formed in more hospitable thermal vents in the deep ocean 3850 million years ago. What is surprising is that life may have started, evolved and been wiped out by cataclysmic mass extinctions a number of times over the intervening 3.85 billion years to the present.

Creating and maintaining the conditions amenable to the origination and sustenance of life is the key to the story of life on earth, and these conditions are related to the carbon cycles, both of them. The short-term carbon cycle is dominated by plant life. Carbon dioxide is taken up during photosynthesis in plants, which releases oxygen into the environment, and energy-rich carbon compounds are locked into the plant tissue, which is either eaten by something or transferred to the soil when the plant decays, where the carbon compounds, oxidized with a gain of energy by small organisms, are then recycled through this process again. The long-term (millions of years) carbon cycle involves transfer of carbon to and from rocks. Carbon dioxide is transformed into living tissue which decays or is eaten to form other animals and plants, which eventually form rocks and later fuse into the lava and gas deep in the earth, which is ultimately brought back to the surface by volcanic action and leakage through deep sea vents. The long-term carbon cycle has a huge effect on the carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere, hence on the greenhouse effect and global temperature. This carbon cycle gone awry has produced total glacierization of the earth more than once and has produced several mass extinctions of species. After each mass extinction, there has been an explosion of new species of life that, together with the survivors of the mass extinction, evolve into incredible complexity over the many millions of years until the next mass extinction. In the atmosphere of the early earth there was little or no oxygen, much more carbon dioxide and about the same nitrogen as today.

This is a fascinating story of life on earth, of how the measurements are made of conditions that existed a million and a billion years ago, how we know the age of fossils so old and the competing and evolving interpretations of what caused it all.

title: One of the best of its genre.
text:
This book's title is catchy but but misleading in its lack of ambition: yes, Stolzenburg tells the story of the "Connecticut Lion," improbable and tragic as it was---about a young male cougar who walked from the Black Hills of South Dakota to the manicured yards of Greenwich, Connecticut, presumably searching for a mate. As the author shows in gripping detail, the animal stirred the hearts and imaginations of many people who encountered him in his travels; Stolzenburg describes, too, the disappointment many of them felt upon learning of the lion's death on a Greenwich freeway.

But this book is so much more than that. Interwoven with the lion's story are several other stories, big and small, including those of the scientists and citizens who tracked him and were otherwise committed to his kind. We learn the story of wildlife advocates invested in the return of this once-native species to the eastern U.S., where forests have been overbrowsed by the lion's former quarry, white-tailed deer. We learn a great deal, too, about a a subset of the public that is convinced (sometimes with evidence, sometimes without) that eastern lions are indeed alive and well--maybe even abundant, maybe even delivered clandestinely by the American government in furtherance of some plot whose rationale beggars the mind. We learn about the natural history of cougars dating back to the Pleistocene. We learn about the culture of hunting and its proponents, some who would preserve cougars and others (unfortunately representing the majority of political will in many western states) who would obliterate them as a pest or a menace. Indeed, we also learn quite a bit about the history of our irrational fear of the cougar---an animal that (in places like L.A.) lurks silently among millions of humans whom it could kill effortlessly yet almost never does. As the author points out, our beloved pet dogs present a much greater risk.

I've lost count of how many natural history books I've read, but this is easily one of the best. Engagingly written, studiously researched, and spun like a modern epic that charges energetically to an emotionally vexed conclusion: yes, the lion was a model of fortitude and his story can give hope to those who yearn for the wilderness that was, but his journey was quite literally a dead end.

title: Best Dekker Novel So Far
text:
“When you surrender your clinging to all attachments, all masks, all judgment, you awaken to a staggering love. In that love, you hold no record of wrong, and you escape all fear because there is no fear in love. Isn’t that what you want, 49th?”

How could one man have possibly answered all of life’s deepest, hardest questions in a single novel?

Ted Dekker did it.

Or at least, he answered all of mine.

Rise of the Mystics is the second book in Ted Dekker’s 49th Mystic duology, the sequel to The 49th Mystic. It is the continuation of the story of Rachelle Matthews, a young woman on a journey from blindness to sight in more ways than one. The 49th Mystic finds Rachelle in a sheltered paradise called Eden, Utah, physically blind but able to see far more than her father or the town leaders ever could. Since her earliest years, she has dreamt of a terrifying being she calls Shadow Man, never imagining that he would materialize into the tightly-secured Eden as the cunning Vlad Smith to pursue her and take control of the city. With his appearance, however, comes another new experience for Rachelle: when she dreams, she wakes up in another world.

Other Earth.

In that world, she awakens to her true potential and destiny, sent on a mission by the wondrous and beautiful man Justin (who is much, much more than a man) to find five Seals that will reveal truth and reality to both Earth and Other Earth. She is the 49th Mystic of the great prophecy.

Rise of the Mystics brings readers further into Rachelle’s journey, revealing that three of the five Seals have been found, but the fourth and fifth Seals will be the most difficult to discover because they will come at a time of the most crisis, not only in Rachelle’s life, but in the history of both worlds she is destined to awaken. On Earth, the world’s security leaders are preparing to gather for a summit, not having a clue that Vlad has crafted a plan that could wipe out the global economy, and whether Vlad activates this plan all hinges on whether he succeeds or fails in his mission to destroy what Rachelle seeks to save.

And he is sure he will succeed.

In Other Earth, the armies of every great kingdom—the Horde, the Elyonites, the Eramites, and the Circle—are preparing to clash, all aiming in their own way to eradicate the Realm of Mystics—charged with heresy by every other belief system—and using Rachelle as the means to do so.

Rachelle’s strange but deeply wise mentor, Talya, guides her and her companion, Jacob, the Horde warrior who has abandoned the ways of his people in pursuit of helping the 49th, toward a greater understanding of the forgotten way of Justin, but to fully achieve this understanding, both Jacob and Rachelle must go through the most dangerous and frightening challenges of their lives, with the future of both realms dependent on what they learn in the process.

Rise of the Mystics is my favorite book by Ted Dekker so far, and I would also say it is his best work. Everything that fans love about Dekker’s work culminates in this novel—the suspense, the vivid and life-like characters, the complex and twisting plots, and especially the depth of spiritual wisdom.

One of the most defining aspects of an excellent work of literature is how it presents and answers universal questions—Why am I here? What is the point of life? If there is a point, how do I find victory and peace in this life instead of pushing through constant struggle, fear, and pain? Who is God and what does He look like?

Am I worthy of love? Am I approved of?

Dekker succeeds in answering these questions through the stories and wisdom of each character, plumbing spiritual depths and tying science with spirituality to create a stunning and true picture of a reality that I knew was there but couldn’t put into words or images. This book came to me during a “dark night of the soul,” as some spiritual teachers call it—a time in which I have been disillusioned about what to believe, a time in which everything I think I know is constantly turned on its head. When I read Rise of the Mystics, I felt hope that there was a way for me to find truth, the truth that spilled over in its pages.

Rise of the Mystics is a masterful and beautiful work that I believe will take the world by storm. Hungry souls are longing for the love that sings to them through its words.

Read it and find love.

title: Wisdom for Waiting:  Ten Lessons from the Life of Joseph
text:
It’s become a cliché, really.
“Wait on God.”
In the glib heart, it’s an all purpose non-answer. It’s what we say when we don’t know what to say.

In Waiting on God: What to Do When God Does Nothing, Wayne Stiles opens the lens of Scripture to take in the Old Testament life of Joseph and de-formulizes that formulaic phrase. Because Joseph spent so much of his life waiting for God to do something, Wayne helps us to see that “we apply sovereignty by waiting on God,” and that every single fruit of the Spirit can be linked in some way to waiting. He offers much practical wisdom in every chapter, but I plucked ten fruitful principles for my own heart to remember when I’m waiting for God to act:
1.Mind the gaps! What we don’t see in biblical narrative is the large gaps of time between the great moments. Biblical lives were not non-stop action any more than ours are, and it is during these God-orchestrated gaps that we do our waiting . . . and wondering. For better insight into Joseph’s life, be sure to follow Joseph’s story found in Genesis 37-50, and available with just a click at Biblegateway.com (#bgbg2).
2.If you’ve spent a lifetime in a family that puts the “fun” in dysfunctional, it takes more than promises to keep from repeating their failures. God is at work in this kind of challenging commitment to change. He rescued Joseph from resorting to unhealthy patterns, and He will meet us in our waiting times to bring about changes that will move our hearts away from generational sin. (Genesis 37:19,20)
3.The hunger that gnaws at your heart during times of waiting will not be satisfied by a quick fix. Don’t short-circuit God’s good plan by settling for Satan’s short-cut. (Genesis 39:9)
4.Judah, Joseph’s brother, left home and used sex as a sedative for a disappointing life. Joseph’s denial of Potiphar’s wife was a decision NOT to gratify himself, but, instead, to wait. Like Joseph, we may have to wait (long and hard) for a glimpse of God’s reasoning behind His assignment of waiting, (Genesis 39:20, 21).
5.The pit of waiting is God’s stop-light where we build character for what lies ahead. Deep rootedness is a higher priority than present-day productivity. (Psalm 105:18,19)
6.Obscure faithfulness in our daily walk with God is not a path to immediate maturity or success. Joseph may have felt forgotten for two years, but he did not forget God. While Joseph’s abilities were on the shelf, God was preparing him for later success. (Luke 16:10)
7.While we think of waiting as the problem, God intends the time of waiting to REVEAL the problem. God used time to create space for forgiveness among the sons of Jacob and also to open their father Jacob’s own heart. (Genesis 43:14) Wayne Stiles challenges his readers to “consider the joy you would have if you surrendered the life you want and embraced the life God is waiting to give you.”
8.God devotes three chapters to the twenty-four hour waiting period before Joseph reveals his identity to his brothers. It was the climax of a twenty-two year wait for reconciliation. In his father Jacob’s case, he did not even realize that he had been waiting — the blessing of seeing his son alive again was completely unexpected! (Ephesians 3:20)
9.Joseph was quick to give God credit for the plot-line of his life:
“God will interpret your dream, Pharaoh.”
“God meant your evil for good, brothers.”
Recognizing God at work made it possible for Joseph to forgive whole-heartedly. Reconciliation followed even after all the lost years.
10.By the time Jacob passed away, the long view had proved him joyously wrong in his lament that “all things are against me!” Hopelessness has no place in our lives, even in the midst of agony like Jacob experienced. When his sons buried him, these Old Testament saints died “without receiving the promises.” We, too, live with continual hope of promises that we have yet to see.

And so we wait. The Christian life is one of obedience which requires an eternal perspective during the moments when it appears that God is inactive. Joseph’s story is our story, but it is also true that his hope is our hope. As we wait individually, in whatever tiny narrative is unfolding on the home front, we wait for the fulfillment of Jesus’ words: “Surely, I am coming quickly.”
To this, we reply from our deepest heart: “Amen. Come quickly, Lord Jesus.”
And while we wait? “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.”

title: Great Book
text: I haven't quite been all through the book as yet but I have read and used enough to know that it is well worth the price.  I am largely a self taught trumpet player although I did have lessons when I was a youngster about 75 years ago and was first-chair trumpet in my high school band nearly seventy years ago.  After laying the trumpet aside after college I took it up again about fifteen years ago.  I play primarily for my own pleasure and occasional specials at church and other functions.  Having said all that to define my category I will say that it's not to late for an old dog to learn new tricks. The book is the most comprehensive of any that I have seen.  It covers everything from trumpet history to accessories and everything in between.  Range, endurance, special effects, you name it, the topic is addressed.  I think it would be invaluable not only for a beginner but also for a long-time amateur like myself.  In only a few days I have learned much I didn't know.  The author presents everything in a light-hearted, friendly and and even funny manner so it's not like the usual instruction book.  I've even learned how to blow a horse whinny, I doubt if I find and occasion to blow that in church but now I know how it's done :).  With his detailed instruction how to "clean up your axe" I was inspired yesterday to take my Yamaha apart and wash the horn and parts in soap and water in my laundry tub.  Of course I knew how to clean a trumpet but I had never seen such detailed and thorough instructions.  All-in-all, It's just a fun and useful book for trumpet players and teachers of all levels of experience.

title: A close look at a Supreme Court Justice.
text:
My Grandfather's Son is a great book, though, I will let you know that I am a boring person who loves to read about the law.
Obviously the book has been copy-edited, but Justice Thomas' personality does shine through from the rough draft. Note to publishers:
people do not care about typos and internal consistency as you would like to believe. Try not to edit.

The story starts in the South, with Justice Thomas having a deprived upbringing. He talks about what it was like to grow up black
in the USA in those days. Justice Thomas is a Republican, so his views are refreshing, in that if I wanted to learn what Democrats
think, I would read the newspaper.

Justice Thomas talks about his days as an angry young man, attending Yale Law School, and the Catholic faith that he finally
recovered.

Then there is the slow and steady rise to the top. Working for the Department of Education, then judge, and then very quickly being
nominated to the Supreme Court of the US.

If there is one thing that I took from this book, is that Justice Thomas deserves to sit on the Supreme Court, not because he is black
(all things considered I think that is a good enough reason) but because he has earned it. Meaning the merit argument.

title: Green energy is not an illusion; it's just not the reality that Zehner wants.
text:
*Green illusions* is simply one more in a long series of attempts to promote the idea of a future built around contraction and decline, and to
insist that any other future is either implausible or even worse than the one the book's author has in mind. To convince you of this, Ozzie
Zehner spares no effort in putting forth a series of arguments that are at best misrepresentations, and at worst simply factually incorrect.

Let's start by acknowledging what the book does get right. Zehner tells us that we can achieve our desires for a better environment much
better, and with vastly less expense, by some simple, practical measures that don't require a lot of advanced technology. It's pretty hard to
quarrel with less junk mail and useless packaging, with not idolizing green lawns, or with measures that make it easier to use bicycles (or our
feet) to get around. At the same time, though, we are told that technological improvements that increase efficiency are largely futile because
of the "rebound effect," often called the Jevons paradox. The basic idea is that if you find ways to use a resource more efficiently, in an
effort to save that resource, you end up defeating yourself because people will just end up using even more of the resource than before, with
no cost saving. Various authors propose this, usually phrased as if it were some kind of iron law, even though the principle has never been
proved--and when anyone has studied the question, it has generally resulted in "rebound coefficients" that are considerably less than 1.0. In
other words, more of the energy service (air conditioning or lighting, for example) is used if better efficiency allows less coal, oil, or
whatever resource to be used, but not enough to completely negate the reduction in resource use.

Here, at least, Zehner does clarify something in a way I have not seen other authors doing: He acknowledges that appetites for resource use are
limited. For example, no one is likely to install five times as many light bulbs in a residence just because the bulbs become five times as
efficient. But that's not the problem: The savings are simply used elsewhere in the economy, so the rebound is indirect. Well, if you think
about it, this is a fairly stunning admission. You see, the problem is not that efficiency improvements are futile. In fact, generally the
argument for emphasizing efficiency (as made by Amory Lovins, for example) has never been that it will lead to a major decline in overall
energy use; rather, the point is that this is *the most cost-effective way* of reducing the cost and environmental consequences of energy use;
efficiency lets us grab the low-hanging fruit, if you like.

Another point is strikingly obvious if you think about it: If efficiency improvements are subject to the rebound effect, then *any other way*
of making energy services cheaper is subject to the same effect. Whether it's fracking to get more natural gas, cost reduction in PV cells, LED
lighting, or small, modular nuclear reactors, anything that makes a unit of the ultimate energy service cheaper has the *same* potential for
triggering more use of that service, and that will negate some of the cost saving.

But here's the real revelation: If we adopt those simple measures that Zehner prefers, *those, too* are subject to the rebound effect. If you
ride a bike instead of driving the car, you might take those savings and apply them to a plane ticket to a vacation spot on another continent.
Or you might buy tickets to concerts at the local arts center--probably with a much smaller environmental footprint. But in general, a group of
consumers with increased disposable income due to one thing, will spend those savings on a variety of other things, and for a large group there
will be fairly predictable results. The rebound effect can be used to argue against almost any solution.

At this point, it appears that what Zehner has a problem with is economic growth itself. Never mind that economic growth can be defined in ways
that don't necessarily involve more use of physical resources--for example, if you link economic value to hours of labor needed for one class
of goods and services, then if you find ways to provide the same goods and services with less work, that amounts to growth, because other goods and services have more value. Even if you assume that growth means more physical goods, it does not follow that the environmental impact is greater. And here is where we start to really glimpse the essence of Zehner's way of viewing the world.

The future implicit in the analysis that *Green Illusions* put forth is one of contraction, of doing less. If you've read Heinberg, Kunstler,
Ruppert, and their ilk, then you already know the kind of thinking involved. The difference with Zehner is the sharp focus on disparaging the
prospects for clean, carbon-free, and most of all abundant, energy. This is the make-or-break issue for Zehner. It's never clearer than in the
middle of the book, where he mentions the prospects for nuclear fusion: "If by some stroke of luck [of course, Zehner would have you believe it
is a matter of luck] fusion should ever prove to become the cheap and available energy source its proponents insist it will become, you are
invited to pull this book from your shelf and throw it in the trash—along with the rest of your nonfiction books [presumably, as you stand at
your window and gawk at the passing flocks of pigs on the wing]. A world with inexpensive and scalable fusion would initiate a reset on every
level of human and environmental interaction (along with some unintended consequences to be sure)." He can feel safe saying this because it's a virtual certainty that fusion energy is not going to remake the energy world in any time frame he needs to be concerned about. What he's really
concerned about, and what he devotes the most intense effort to, is the threat of wind and solar. He finds the current, supposed infatuation
with solar to be such folly as to describe it in overtly sneering terms: "Perhaps it's all too easy for us to miss the limitations of
alternative energy as we drop to our knees at the foot of the clean energy spectacle, gasping in rapture. The spectacle has become a divine
deity around which duty-bound citizens gravitate to chant objectives without always reflecting on fundamental goals." He cannot abide a
successful transition to the kind of solar future that some have in mind. If that were to happen in the next two or three decades, indeed we
may as well throw his book in the trash. He said so himself.

Let's get down to specifics. Zehner says that the estimated cost to power the whole planet with PV cells is $123 trillion, plus 694 billion per
year for maintenance--although, as he admits, this assumes no cost reductions, even though those reductions have been happening fairly steadily all through the history of the technology. He does not elaborate on the source of his cost estimate, although he does footnote it. But he puts forth another estimate, "based on California solar projects," of $14000 trillion--which is about $1000 per watt of capacity, clearly
unrelated to any widespread reality. He also says that "everyone would have to move to the desert, otherwise transmission losses would make the plan unworkable," even though that assumes all the power would be generated in the sunniest region of the country, a very unlikely scenario for just the reason he gives. (The average solar influx between the sunniest regions and most of the rest of the continental US is not all that
huge, and the more solar is installed at one time, the more it drives down the cost of future deployment.) He says that it's hard to get economies of scale because investments vary with such things as oil prices—but PV deployment since 1992 has nevertheless been quite steady if
you look over a span of more than a year or two.

There are other objections put forth. Toxic emissions are said to be a worry, though no quantitative figures are given, and no information on
how hard it would be to fix such problems. Thieves are going to rip off your solar modules! And people fall off roofs when they have to clean
solar cells. Seriously?! Are we supposed to believe that, having developed the advanced technology involved in our modern energy
infrastructure, we cannot come up with a practical way to clean solar cells without having to climb up onto our roofs?

(BTW Zehner says "If the text on this page represented total US power supply, the photovoltaic portion would fit inside the period at the end
of this sentence." That would be a ratio of at least 10,000, as he later acknowledges implicitly by putting it as "less than one hundredth of a
percent." Such an orders-of-magnitude error should not pass without notice. It's reminiscent of Gwyneth Cravens's dollhouse analogy (in the
pro-nuclear book *Power to Save the World*, in which she, like Zehner, completely misrepresents the amount of solar PV that is out there.)

Then there is the cost of inverters. We're told that these inverters cost $8000 (for a system of what size, he doesn't say), and that they last
5 to 8 years. The implication is that at the end of eight years, the inverter is just a useless pile of scrap metal. More likely is that a single component might fail or, in the worst case, the unit might need a more general refurbishing. IAC are we supposed to believe that the
inverter has only a fraction of the lifetime of the PV arrays themselves? That just doesn't make sense.

We're told that solar PV systems "[are] sensitive to extreme temperatures, oblige owners to perform *constant maintenance*, and require
*extremely expensive* components to keep them going for their *comparatively short* lifespan." [emphases mine] I don't see a single number in
that paragraph; do you?

Solar PV is *not* a fairy tale. No, it's Ozzie Zehner's worst nightmare, and it's coming more true, night after night (even when the Sun is not shining).

Wind gets a similar treatment, though more briefly. There's discussion of deforestation in Brazil to set up wind turbines although, again,
nothing quantitative is given; more of what is often called "anecdotal" evidence. And whence comes the idea that you need 18000 MW of wind
power to replace 1000 MW of coal-derived power? This so-called reliability factor (differing from the simpler "capacity factor") is never made
clear.

Finally, once again, we come to the real source of the concern: "Hype surrounding wind energy might even shield the fossil-fuel establishment—
if clean and abundant energy is just over the horizon, then there is less motivation to clean up existing energy production or use energy more
wisely." It's just like the way more efficiency leads to more energy use, negating the benefits. In the end, you could raise such an objection
to anything! If there is no punishment, people will behave badly.

What this ultimately seems to come down to is a kind of New Puritanism. This time, we're not "sinners in the hands of an angry God," we're just
a ship of fools, doing this to ourselves; but whatever led to this apocalypse staring us in the face, we have to stop all our sinnin', and
realize that, as Heinberg tells us, the party is over, and we have to clean up our mess and start acting like adults.

And if you've been reading a lot of this kind of literature, you knew it had to eventually come around to [cue drum roll] *The Population Explosion*. Think of Ehrlich's famous equation I = PAT, where I is environmental impact, P is population, A is "affluence" (how much sinnin'
each of us does), and T is technology. Never mind that P is pretty much a done deal (with the global fertility rate now roughly at replacement
rate, having been cut in half in about the last 50 years). Never mind that A, the measure of our wasteful habits, is likewise very hard to
change, especially for the majority of the world's people who have never had much ability to waste until very recently. What we can change, and
what we're changing rapidly now, is that T factor.

It's the promise of cutting that T factor that Zehner conspicuously disparages. In fact, it's ironic: Energy-saving technology is said to not
be an effective solution to environmental problems, because people will not exercise restraint, but will instead just waste resources
(especially energy) in other areas. Yet Zehner's preferred solution, the one needed if we're to drive carbon emissions to zero, rather than
just stopping the increase, is what? It's for people to exercise *even more* restraint (though, of course, this will have to be aided greatly
by changes in public policy, which will require either much persuasion or much coercion, something that seems especially hard to achieve in the
current political climate).

Let's leave that discussion with a real gem: "The staunchest defenders of population growth enthusiastically point out that all of the world's
inhabitants could easily fit within a landmass the size of Texas with enough space for each family to have a modest apartment." This may be the
ultimate in straw men. Is there anyone, at least anyone with a wide audience, who is claiming such a thing? (All right, I haven't listened to much talk radio lately, so I may be on shaky ground there.) But more pertinently: What serious person is a "defender of population growth"? I'm not sure even the Pope could be put in that group any more. It's getting harder all the time to see population as a global issue (although in parts of
the world, for specific countries, it still is). For some, though, it seems the population explosion is still *the* issue. It's one side of the New Puritanism.

I'll finish with a rundown of the factual errors I noticed in one pass through this book:

1. "If successful, these various strategies could continue to draw lifespans closer to, or some say beyond, the 'Hayflick limit' of roughly 120
years…" --The Hayflick limit is not a limit to lifespan, but to cell doublings, in most cells of most multicellular organisms.

2. "Recent estimates [of US population] range from 420 to 500 million by 2050 and up to billion by 2100."
--That would require 1.3%/yr, almost double the current rate. But that's total growth, not just natural increase; we're well below replacement rate.
--WRT births relative to death; IAC the intent seems unclear, unless it's just a desperate attempt to hype a population problem
--Growth due to natural increase is about 0.3% (and declining).

3. No, the US government did not build Hanford to "enrich" plutonium. U-235 is what is enriched for some purposes.

4. Fusion power does not "work on the principle of the hydrogen bomb"; for one thing, no fission is involved, whereas in the H-bomb the fusion is used to boost fission.

5. (regarding fusion power) From completion of ITER to start of DEMO construction is NOT expected to take 20 years; the plan is more like 10.

title: A Soaring Sci-Fi Adventure
text:
I was absolutely enthralled by this Young Adult sci-fi adventure, Defy the Stars by Claudia Gray. I could barely put it down for the three days it took to read it (and if real life had not insisted on repeatedly making demands on my time, I'd likely have read it in a single day).

The story is about a 17-year-old female soldier from a planet called Genesis, which has rebelled against Earth authority in an effort to avoid becoming another heavily polluted Earth. This has led to a form of government which is very Luddite-sounding. That is, anti-technology. Leaving them open to Earth's efforts to reassert its authority. Obviously, the Genesis fleet is old and not up to the task.

This leaves young Noemi Vidal volunteering for a suicide mission along with many other young people, to close the gate linking Earth to their planet, in order to buy time to re-arm. It is as a result of preparing for this mission that Noemi meets the other main character, Abel, who is a 19-year-old appearing robot who has been stranded in a spacecraft for 30 years at the site of an earlier battle between the two planets.

The interaction between the two is very well done, as Noemi realizes there have been repercussions to her planets rebellion that affects all of human space in ways she could not have imagined, and Abel realizes that he has evolved during the 30 years he spent alone and waiting. Both of them make discoveries about themselves and about their worlds, having their assumptions challenged on a fundamental level.

I could easily see this becoming a movie. It's that good. If the author failed as a waitress, she has succeeded as a sci-fi author. This book may be targeted for a young adult audience, but it has very adult themes - and I don't mean sex and violence but rather what it is to be human, and one of philosophy's oldest questions: how we know what we know.

Noemi and Abel are in for some surprises, and so is the reader as the story soars at break-neck speed from planet to planet and a story that ends up being about far more than either of them at first imagined. Five stars.
