title: Travel Tips and Treasures for the Andes
text:
A Sierra Club production gem, I came across this book while preparing for my backpacking trip to the realm of the Andes. In just 250 pages it provided me with information galore on my intended route through Ecuador, Bolivia and Peru including excerpts on culture and places not covered in the usual plethora of guide books used by professional vagabonds. One such example was the little village of Coroico, Bolivia which turned out to be one of the highlights of my three month journey through the Andes. Had I not read about it in Frazier's book I might never have gone there.
There are photos, maps, tables, a Spanish language glossary and most valuable of all to me---a Quechua language glossary--the language of the Andes--which I tore out and carried in my back pocket the entire trip. At the end, a bibliography proved to be a valuable resource for other related books.
Great book for those Andes-bound--concise and well laid-out. In paperback it is small, light and compact--perfect for stuffing in your pack.

title: Beautiful Lake Como
text:
This book obviously has a wonderful setting and so you'll be sucked right into Italy as soon as you pick this up. The book follows two characters and so we have a dual narrative structure that I love. Both characters have skeletons hiding in their closet that we don't know about and all is revealed as the book continues. Despite the fact that I really wanted to find out what each of these women were hiding I did find the pace of the book a little slow and struggled to bond with the characters initially because I knew they were hiding something, nevertheless I wanted to know what that is and I enjoyed reading about the Italian food and the Italian landscape.

The characters were really quite different and so I can see why this author chose to have their stories come together in this way. I really liked Taggie and respected the way she composed herself and her reasons behind being in Lake Como before and after finding out what they were. I didn't like Lucy as much. I found that I really didn't get along with the way she had so many doubts about things but she didn't follow up on them. She was a little indecisive and it really began to grate on me. Later on in the novel she definitely finds a little more back bone but I wasn't entirely happy with the ending that she got.

The secrets that both these women have and even those they don't fully appreciate are what kept me reading through this book and the structure definitely made me keep turning the pages. Because I struggled to identify with one of the characters I think I struggled to keep up the pace during her sections of the story. Overall though this was a good read and I really enjoyed spending time in Lake Como.

title: Summary of R. N. Swanson's Fine Overview
text:
This book appears in the series titled Cambridge Medieval Textbooks. Swanson, a British scholar who specializes in Medieval History, explains that his survey focuses on Latin Christendom, which was centered in western Europe, although it extended well beyond that region. This is a study, then, of that church defined as "the whole company of baptised Christians who acknowledge the papacy as their earthly head" (7). The time frame, c. 1215-c. 1515, roughly corresponds to the three hundred years between the Fourth and Fifth Lateran Councils. Admittedly, the author tends to use his locale of specialty, England, as representative of all Europe (xiii). Of course, this is not always possible, a fact he clearly appreciates.

Having introduced his work and identified its scale, Swanson treats eight general topics in successive chapters. Chapter 2, "The Faith and its demands," defines the boundaries of orthodox teaching in Latin Christendom of the time. The author notes how groups like the Cathars and Waldensians indirectly put pressure on the Church to clarify its doctrine. The period also witnessed the long-standing tension between reason and revelation.

Chapter 3, "Access to the Faith," details how the Church communicated its message, and how it was acquired by believers. Significantly, the author points to families and popular songs as well as to the Bible, other books, icons, drama, and church architecture as important sources.

Chapter 4, "Religious Life," relates common liturgical experiences, especially the mass, of course. It also explores the fact that leading up to the period under study, many people had concluded that it wasn't only religious professionals who could participate in the apostolic life and be saved. Lay people could live such lives as well.

Chapter 5 looks at the "'non-Purgatorial' aspects of devotion" (137). These included, again, the mass, as well as a wide array of personal and impersonal intercessors, including Christ, Mary, other saints, relics, images, guardian angels, etc. In addition to these traditional avenues, Swanson notes less common ways, like mysticism, and ways identified as "superstition" or, perhaps less prejudicial, "lay Christianity."

Chapter 6, "The pilgrimage of life and death," focuses on distinctly "Purgatorial" aspects of devotion. Swanson highlights the popular metaphor of pilgrimage, the demands of caritas (Christian charity), and the preoccupation with death and one's well-being in the hereafter.

Chapter 7, "Priests, people, and power," explores priestly roles and lay expectations. Here, Swanson provides an especially helpful discussion of "anticlericalism," which, he observes, is an imprecise term. In order to define the idea more clearly, he offers three possible categories: (a) simple antipathy to individual clerics, (b) generalized hostility to the clerical class, and (c) active opposition to all sacerdotalism, which was rare (248).

Chapter 8, "Inclusion and exclusion," deals with a set of questions that every religious tradition must answer: Who should be included or excluded from membership? Upon what basis? How should this tradition think of and treat other ones? These questions obviously circle back to some of the general topics dealt with in Chapter 2, but Chapter 8 includes specific sections on heretics, Jews, Muslims, demonology, etc.

Finally, in Chapter 9, "The reality of religion," Swanson offers a few generalizations. He notes, for example, that unlike the situation in 1215, by 1515 "all of western and central Europe was included within the catholic church" (341), and religion was "more a part of the cultural baggage of more people, and more deeply embedded, that it had been" (340). Had the tradition become so deep and wide by 1515 that reform impulses, backed by large numbers of people, inevitably led to a rupture? To what degree did the advent of printing generate the Reformation? What would have happened if the church had managed to contain and handle reform impulses? Of course, we'll never know.

Okay, that's a lot of information, much of it presented in that dry format followed by most textbooks. Here's one of the book's saving graces: it has an an extensive table of contents, plus an index that runs to about 18 pages. So, if there's something about the subject that you want to look up, you should be able to find it easily, read the three or four pages of relevant material, and go on.

title: WONDERFUL FLOWING CHRISTMAS ARRANGEMENTS
text:
Normally I would take a great deal of time to savor new music, before writing an evaluation. Not only would I practice it for a number of weeks, but use it at church before writing about it, in order to estimate our people's responsiveness to what they are hearing. I am making an exception in the case of the book, first because it is Christmas music and cannot be played at church for some months, not giving enough time for other church musicians who might wish to select it for the 2017 holiday season. Second, having just received the book today, and having played through most of the individual pieces immediately, I feel unusually enthusiastic.

I have no other music arranged by Faye López. I heard of her on a sample CD sent out by Lorenz and Lillenas publishers. I must confess, I had discarded a number of 2016 and 2017 catalogs, but brought the sample CD's enclosed in each one to my car player, listening sporadically as the narrator would announce a composer/arranger and then play samples of a number of works by each. Since I am not a music major, but one of those church organists/pianists who studied little yet played for congregations for many decades, I'm always uncertain what books will actually prove usable, within the limitations of my ability, and feel most comfortable at the upper-intermediate level. I feel a huge high when I can use something at the advanced level, but doing so without lots of practice is usually dependent upon the style of the arranger. For example, I can almost always play music by Tom Fettke, perhaps my favorite Evangelical piano arranger. I also do well with most of the Alfred sacred music series. For organ, Lani Smith is probably my favorite arranger. Faye López was totally new to me, but the lilting, winsome nature of what I heard on that sample CD led me to look for her music on Amazon, and I was delighted to see this book as one of the Alfred Sacred performer series. I will most likely look for more of her work in the future.

All this being said, I am thoroughly delighted with the book from a number of perspectives. First, the music is both worshipful and playable. I can read through it at first glance, and know with a little polishing almost every piece in this generously-sized compilation will be of use at our Sunday evening services during Advent. Second, the music flows; it will be enjoyable to play, inspiring to both the musician and the congregation. Finally, though there are challenging key changes and sufficient variations to make it interesting, most of the pieces do not contain pitfalls of small, tricky sections that can discourage a non-professional pianist. It irks me especially when I get to the very last few measures of something beautiful, only to find them unplayable, forcing me either to adapt the ending, or to discard the piece entirely. Faye López's music seems consistently usable, with endings that are satisfying, but not unduly challenging. I am excited at the prospect of practicing this new Christmas music, a worship experience in itself, then using it to bring people Christmas joy, drawing them closer to the Lord.

title: "They're being shot at!"
text:
"The Final Mission Of Extortion 17" is subtitled "Special Ops, Helicopter Support, Seal Team Six, and the Deadliest Day of the US War In Afghanistan". From my perspective, there just isn't enough of those things to make this book worthwhile for the military history reader.

The author begins with a typical support mission flown by army helicopter pilots in Afghanistan and moves from there to the men who crewed the CH-47D Chinook twin-rotor helicopter. The author spends time on a previous mission in which a Chinook went down - cause not known for certain, but possibly by enemy action before going back to crew biographies before ending with the final mission in which Chinook call sign "Extortion one-seven" was shot down with the loss of all passengers and crew.

I think the author does a fine job of writing a memorial to the men who were piloting and serving on "One-Seven", their humble origins and their desire to serve their country as well as a love of flying and serving in Army aviation. We find out the kind of men these servicemen were who put themselves in harm's way. Along the way, we learn a lot about the helicopter they flew, the CH-47D Chinook, as well as army aviation and the brotherhood of arms.

Having said that, there's simply too little of the other things the military history reader, like myself, is interested in. The shootdown takes only one chapter - a short one at that. There's little discussion of the tactics used on these insertions. There's no discussion of the vulnerability of rotary wing (helicopter) transports that historically have shown themselves to be extremely useful, but also very vulnerable to even small-arms fire. How does the high-altitude of Afghanistan dictate what kinds of helicopters can be used effectively? The entire ground force was put in one Chinook. Is that putting all the eggs in one basket so to speak?

The author does a great job of bringing the lives and characters of these young men to the fore, and rightly so. But, for me, there wasn't enough here that couldn't have been covered in a magazine article.

title: "Do I contradict myself? Very well then, I contradict myself: I am large. I contain multitudes." Walt Whitman
text:
The Whitman observation reminds me of the lyrics Joni Mitchell composed for one of her most popular songs:

"I've looked at life from both sides now,
from win and lose, and still somehow
it's life's illusions I recall.
I really don't know life at all."

I wish had a dollar for every time I have heard the comment, "What you see is what you get." Møre often than not, what we see is what others allow to be seen and it is also true that many (most?) people are unwilling and/or unable to examine what is in what Todd Kashdan and Robert Biswas-Diener characterize as a "human psychological knapsack" and then integrating into their lives what has been "previously ignored and underappreciated parts of who [they] are." They wrote this book to help as many people as possible to bring wholeness within reach, "perhaps for the first time."

These are among the dozens of passages of greatest interest and value to me, also listed to suggest the scope of Kashdan and Biswas-Diener's coverage:

o Why the Way We've Been Pursuing Happiness Won't Make Us Happy (Pages 2-10)
o What Wholeness Looks Like, Beyond the Impostor Syndrome, and The Virtues of Throwing in the Towel (13-17)
o The Benefits of Fantasy (17-18)
o The Origins of Comfort Addiction (29-37)
o What's the Alternative? and Psychology's Holy Grail (44-51)
o Why Bad Can Be More Powerful Than Good (54-59)
o A Tour of Three Dreaded Emotions: Anger, Guilt, and Shame (66-84)
o Effectively Harnessing and Using Anxiety (92-93)
o Has Happiness Been Taken Too Far? (100-116)
o Three Mindless Paths to Success and Well-Being (128-147)
o Understanding the Three Parts of the Teddy Effect (159-163)
o All the World's a Stage (177-181)
o Recognizing Your Positivity Bias (192-200)
o Broad Strokes or Fine-Toothed Comb (214-220)
o Beyond Happiness (220-221)

I agree with Todd Kashdan and Robert Biswas-Diener: "To progress on your journey of personal growth, love, and meaning and purpose in life, you need to become aware of all aspects of yourself, including your darker tendencies, and be agile enough to integrate them into your behavioral repertoire as needed. Do not repress, ignore, or hide the darker gifts [and they really are gifts]. Be aware of them, appreciate them, and then you're ready harness them. When you do this, you'll find you've gained greater access to well-being. To do otherwise is to be enslaved by fear, to set an artificial limit on what you experience and accomplish in this, the one and only life we know for sure that you'll have. Make the most of it. Become whole."

Easier said then done? Of course. Will reading and then perhaps re-reading this book make anyone whole? Perhaps less incomplete, somewhat more fulfilled, but hardly whole. Each of us really is a "work in progress." However, I am certain that the information, insights, and counsel provided in this book will help many of those who read it to gain access to everything or at least much of what they are hauling in their "psychological knapsack [by] unpacking and integrating previously ignored and underappreciated parts of who [they] are."

title: Peeking Through the Window
text: This book contains a collection of stories about the tea ceremony first published in 1804.  It's fascinating for a modern Western reader to study its history in Japan and the high regard in which the tea utensils themselves were held.  Individual implements were famous and even given names.  Interesting anecdotes include the tea guest who stole a coveted tea caddy right out from under the host and a warrior who smashed his tea kettle before his death rather than let the enemy have it.  Or how about the retainer who wanted his master's tea kettle really bad, but was told he'd have to score a big military victory before obtaining it?  (He did.)  Then there's the sharing of incense among tea guests by passing it from your left sleeve through your right one and on to the next person.  These and numerous other tidbits will hold your attention as you peruse this slim volume.  It has caused me to view my own tea belongings a bit differently - I've purchased several special handmade tea bowls and some fine teas as well!

title: INTERESTING READ....A Review by Beverly Bateman-Harper
text:
Wow! What an interesting look inside an individual's life by someone who apparently knew him better than he knew himself! The writer, his "office wife" did a superb job of projecting Rick's personality which was full of charm and charisma as well as stubbornness and complexity.

Truly, Rick Bateman lived fast, loved fast, fought brilliantly, sought adventure and enjoyed life in excess. Based on his lifestyle and never-ending search for the happiness, fame and fortune that he was always seeking, he lost the one battle that he likely never thought he needed to prepare for - his life.

Jude Burke's writing style is very engaging. You feel as though you know her characters personally as she has a way of putting "life" into them. Once I started the book, I realized I was more than half way through it before I put it down. Admittedly, I was most interested in learning about Rick Bateman as I was wondering, and still am, if somehow he is a distant relative of mine! He was certainly a colorful character and had a zest for life that was admirable at times and foolhardy at others.

I debated throughout the book as to which he was most proud of - his personal or his professional accomplishments! I choose to think that there were parts of both that he was pleased with.

Jude, well done.

title: Not a Smooth Ride
text:
One day, Nick Donaghue, an obituary writer for THE TIMES, is on his way to work, when he is involved in a horrible train crash where he is the only one escaping unharmed. While everybody else thinks Nick to be very fortunate, his life is turning into a literal nightmare. After months of sleepless nights, he moves from London to an old beach house in Cornwall where he runs into Sasha and has to give up his notion of living a quiet and secluded life.

(Warning: There is a minor spoiler in the upcoming paragraph)
It is hard to put this novel into a literary genre. The Obituary Writer starts out as a mystery with thriller elements, then it turns into a love story. This would have been okay. Unfortunately, the romance is soon sprinkled with paragraphs right out of an erotic novel that seem utterly out of place. And to top it all off, there’s a little bit of crime here, and some sick lit there. Don’t get me wrong – there is nothing wrong with mixing genres if the mix is homogeneous. In this case it isn’t and it seems like the author wanted to try out all these different genres to see how they worked for her.

Other than that, The Obituary Writer is an entertaining novel. It sucks you in right at the beginning and holds your attention for quite some time. The middle is a little slow, but the narrative takes up speed again in the last third of the book.

While we get to know Nick Donaghue’s character – his feelings, fears and doubts – very closely, most of the other characters stay in the background. It would have been nice to get a better understanding of Sasha, the woman who attracts Nick’s attention.

If you are as drawn to this novel by its beautiful cover as I was, you might as well give it a try, but it will not be a smooth ride, that’s for sure. And if you’ve already read The Obituary Writer, I’d like to know what you thought about the ending. But no spoilers please!

Also, his Clanmates were unhappy with his father and 'it was his destiny'.

In addition, I noticed that mistakes. First, cats prefer fresh food, so they wouldn't scavenge. Also, a group of red foxes is called a skulk, not a pack. On the other hand, I noticed that the authors got something right. For instance, they used the term dog fox, which applies to males.

That said, the biggest issue turned out to be Tigerheart's and Dovewing's relationship. It was just Dovewing arguing with him, hurling verbal abuse, worrying their kids (albeit she wasn't wrong to), and being nice to him when she was in a good mood. At least, she called herself a coward for forcing him to make an impossible decision.

On the other hand, it wasn't all bad. Spire greeted the two main characters, helped trap the foxes, lead them partway to the lake, and risked his life to save Lightkit and Pouncekit. He in turn received a warrior name and a kit named after him. I felt those were pretty good rewards.

title: A fresh read fortified with substance
text:
The book read like a modern version of Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman fused with an advent calendar. It takes place in 1990s Los Angeles during the holiday season. Ms. Cronin inserted awesome local and historic references. Felt like I was there.

I expect stories to offer messages on how to lead a better life, and The Gift Counselor didn’t disappoint. The protagonist is a single parent psychologist who moved to Southern California and reinvented her life after suffering a series of losses. At first I was thrown off by a couple of typos and an oddly spelled word in the Kindle edition. Ubiquitous in today’s environment yet disrupting nonetheless. That minor criticism aside, the author incorporated well placed threads that made the story gallop toward a surprising ending.

Akin to Michaela Quinn, we get to watch the main character nurture her career, ponder a potential love interest, and struggle to raise a socially responsible kid. I also liked the nod to community service. One of my favorite interpersonal conflicts revolves around a psycho co-worker. Who hasn’t had a job soured by one of those people? This is an authentic and human story peppered with humor.

From the perspective of a former single parent with sole responsibility who managed child-rearing plus a career, I wish I could have read this story earlier in life. I can’t wait for the main character to return.

However, after cracking it open, I found that it only carries the original English text of each tale and as most are foreign, their English translations usually didn't come out until the stories had already been watered down a bit. Each chapter is opened with an explanation of the history and various translations, which I found to be the most interesting part of the book along with the authors' introduction to folktales that describe a general history and the themes found in the tales.

Overall, I found it rather boring. It took me a while to get through it and I love reading the original fairy tales. The history behind them was interesting, but the stories themselves were not well explained. The authors kept the original language with a few minor footnotes to explain words or phrases, but often you are left to try and decipher Olde English for yourself. Granted, it's not super hard, but it would have been nice to have more clear and concise language.

If you're interested in the original wording and syntax of the stories, this is a good book for you. Otherwise, it's not great.

"Word for the Year" and the rest of the articles in the January section helped simplify and crystallize my thinking.

Each month has several short, seasonal articles to help you get back on track or stay on track, and there's space to jot down your own thinking or responses. The concepts are clear and uncomplicated, and help open up your mind. Although the articles are about writing, they are helping me think through other goals as well.

title: To clarify some falsehoods reported in this book I would like it to be known that the day the wolf ...
text:
my name is Rick Huteson. I am the person who's dog was taken by this Black Wolf. To clarify some falsehoods reported in this book I would like it to be known that the day the wolf hunted my dog I was NOT using a predator call to call out the wolf, I didn't want to have anything to do with the wolf.

Upon tracking this wolf the day after it took my dog, Barten and I agreed that the wolf was tracking my friends and I for at least 45 minutes before it called my dog out. What he reported or what was read that he reported and what actually happen seemed to be two different things. The blood was fresh, not from a hare, it was from my dog. I don't know if any of you have ever had your dog taken by a wild animal, but to hear my dog screaming in pain as its packed off into the woods by a wolf was the most terrifying and heart breaking moments I've ever experienced.

To make it clear: I was walking with my friends and my dogs on a trail we have been walking for years, I repeat, I WAS NOT LOOKING FOR THE WOLF, the wolf was HUNTING my dogs.

Fish and Game upon tracking the wolf with me, said it was evident the wolf was tracking us for at least 45 minutes. We seen where it lurked in the tree line right behind us then cut us off where it got my dogs attention then took my dog- what he reported was quite different.

only one person every asked me what happen and it wasn't the person who wrote this book, which makes sense as of to why this book claims so many false things as truth. There were 3 people and 2 dogs, only one person interviewed me and that was someone from Juneau Empire, which is notorious for weaving narratives to fit their agenda.

It was obvious to me that this wolf was a tourist attraction and fish and game felt as if the wolf was good for publicity so they did everything they could to protect it.

This wolf took several dogs after it took mine but people were too afraid to report it because they seen how much the press hammered on me with victim blaming.

I do not appreciate this narrative that makes me out to be a sketchy character who was up to no good when in-fact I was just walking my dogs with my friends like I always do. I just happen to be at the wrong place at the wrong time.

My dogs track ends where the blood trail and wolf tracks began.

I told Barten that I wanted that wolf re-located and if not then they should shoot it before it takes a small childs life. Fish and game had a chance to save that wolfs life but they chose to treat it as a tourist attraction instead of a life worth saving Now it seems someone took the law into their own hand and shot the wolf not too long after the wolf killed my and several other peoples dogs.

The author of this book and many like him contributed to the untimely death of this wolf by over romanticizing this wild creature by naming it Romeo the friendly wolf who loves dogs which of course drew a lot of attention. One thing most Alaskans know is that if a wild animal, a wild predator becomes familiar with humans, its an automatic death sentence for that animal and possibly the people they interact with.

If the author of this book did the right thing and advocated for the removal and re-location of this wolf, instead of profiteering and using it as a marketing ploy to sell books and use for photo ops, maybe this wolf would have lived a longer more satisfying life instead of getting shot somewhere around Juneau. This author is selfish and is just as responsible for the death of the black wolf as is the person who shot it.

I am a dog person, I am a outdoors man and lover of all wild animals. My initial response was to re-locate the wolf or shoot it before it continues to kill other animals or small children. I realized that wolves will be wolves, and that people will be people and once the word got out that this wolf is hanging out in town and killing dogs that it would be the certain death of this wolf sooner or later and I was right. Ultimately I wanted this wolf to live even though he killed my friend

title: AN ENJOYABLE MARITIME ADVENTURE
text:
CRUDE CARRIER REVIEW

I find nothing about Rex Burns, author of “Crude Carrier,” having experience aboard any type of ship. He mostly writes detective stories around the Denver area where he lives. Burns has moved from his normal writing tendencies to the pitching deck, claustrophobic confines of an ocean-going transport vessel, and the complexities of petroleum commerce. His knowledge and ability to write about on-board life aboard a crude oil ship is a radical change and indicates a devotion to intensive research.

Howard Pease (1894-1974) is a legend for his tramp steamer adventures written for young adults in the mid 20th century. As a young boy I was mesmerized by the sinister confines and intrigue found aboard freighters and still have every book he wrote in my library. But Pease had much to draw on as he presented his wondrous stories because he lived the life of a crewman on this type of vessel. I find Burns also has an authentic voice about adventures at sea, despite his lack of background, and I don’t find a false step in his writing. Perhaps his background as a Marine Captain helped a bit.

The details he describes about the workings, procedures, and life aboard a large vessel are enlightening. His casual allusions about claustrophobia aboard a steel can on surging endless waters are realistic enough to bring shivers to my sensitive core. My innards do not suffer confinement gladly. There is also authenticity in his descriptions of the electronics the protagonist must maintain aboard the ship. Again, I see dedication to research.

Critics might point out that getting a job as third officer on a ship of this size with zero maritime experience is an unlikely event. Also, to have the entire staff of command officers of a large-scale crude oil transport, including the Captain, be heavily involved in criminal activity including murder might be a stretch. And the disappearance of millions of gallons of crude would likely raise a few more eyebrows than are lifted in the story. But, as I have said many times, it’s the author’s book and he has license to write anything he feels comfortable with. I enjoyed the novel and didn’t feel a bit hoodwinked by these developments.

His use of a female sidekick is done with respect and careful consideration of the fact that sex does not have to be flaunted in every mystery story. She is not a superwoman but adds an important element to the story.

Burns writes in a terse and brawny style and his depictions are convincing and magnetic. This is an entertaining and illuminating report on the transportation of crude oil and the corruption surrounding its commerce. I enjoyed the book and heartily recommend it for an entertaining read.

Schuyler T Wallace
Author f TIN LIZARD TALES

The Smallest Part by Amy Harmon.
⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

There aren't enough stars in the sky for Amy Harmon's The Smallest Part. I wish I could lasso each one, give it a tug, and attach it to another outline on Amazon.

At 8%--only 8% into this book, I cared so much about Mercedes, Noah and sweet little Gia.

Harmon wraps you around her characters, she pushes and pulls at your limbs, your heart. She makes you see the other side. The other side of death. The other side of our upbringing, that we assume just bury into the night sky and let it fade away as the sun rises again. She also brought back memories of my childhood that I want to keep in the forefront of my mind for a long while.

She brought back Exclamation perfume.
Red, Red Wine by UB40.
She brought back John Stockton and Karl Malone.

She allows the characters to show you why they are the way the are, fractured, flawed, cracked.

This was my first book by Harmon.

Before I finished The Smallest Part, I went to Amazon and bought The Laws of Moses and A Different Blue. I didn't read the synopsis, I didn't have to. It didn't matter. What she writes, I'll read them. Open every last word, close it, tuck the memories, her words, in my back pocket and carry them with me. I'll carry the emotions she made me feel about my life, my upbringing, the woman I am today, until time fades them into a distant memory.

Thank you, Amy, for gifting us with your words.
This book, a phenomenal read, will stick with me for a very long time. ❤️

title: A pioneering work of media theory, The Image has somehow grown more relevant with time!
text:
A brilliant, stunningly prescient analysis of culture. It's thoroughly researched, comprehensively argued, and densely packed with proof of the bold notion that America is becoming a society of unreality that favors shadow over substance. Today we speak well of Baudrillard, Debord, Postman, Andy Warhol--all these men owe a great debt to this book, yet, in keeping with Boorstin's thesis, the book itself has been overshadowed by its imitators.

The Image has only become more relevant in modern society, and I suspect the trend will continue. It is one of a few essential texts for understanding modern America.

It's true that culture has lost sight of the real, but I wonder--is it only because of our media? Isn't this representative of a greater phenomenon, in which all bearing on a privileged narrative of reality has been lost? Is the 'The Image' perhaps an indication of our greater postmodern malaise?

title: A fine book for anyone wanting to try their hand at electronics for the first time
text:
I wish a book like this had been available when I first learned electronics many years ago. I might not have burned up quite so many of the parts I salvaged from old radios and TVs! "Easy Electronics" lives up to its title by offering 12 different projects with outstanding illustrations. The book also offers simple schematic diagrams and clear, step-by-step procedures that use easy-to-acquire resistors, capacitors, LEDs, phototransistors, a small integrated circuit chip, and a few other components, such as the ubiquitous 2N3904 NPN transistor and a mini-breadboard with jumper wires. Many of the book's projects can be wired up just by clipping small alligator-clip jumpers to component leads. But the circuits requiring both an integrated circuit (a 7555) and a 2N3904 transistor definitely are easier to wire up using a mini-breadboard and some jumper wires. The book explains resistance (including parallel and series) and capacitance, as well as how transistors, phototransistors, multi-pole switches, transducers and other components at a basic level. This is a fine book for anyone wanting to try their hand at electronics for the first time. The circuits are safe for kids (especially with adult supervision), and the projects use three AA batteries in series, producing only about 4.5 volts or so. The book includes a helpful shopping list with part numbers and suggested suppliers. A complete parts kit to accompany the book also is available from a supplier.

(My thanks to O'Reilly Media for providing an advance reading copy.)

title: Amazing book!
text:
“The Crimson Cord” by Jill Eileen Smith tells the story of Rahab. In the Bible Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho who helped Israelite spies. Rahab protected the Israelites and was promised safety when the Israelites took Jericho. She was told to hang a crimson cord on her window and when the time came she and anyone who resided in her house would be safe. “The Crimson Cord” takes us into Rahab’s world and brings the scriptures in the Bible to life. The Bible does not say why Rahab became a prostitute but this book gives us one possibility. This book also makes us think what her thoughts and feelings were during that dark time in her life. We also see how she moves from her past to a bright future and become an ancestor to Jesus. While we can only speculate about most of Rahab’s life, this book will bring her to life and make us wonder what this woman was truly like.

This is a wonderfully written book and that will draw you in from the first page and keep you turning until the last. Jill Eileen Smith does an amazing job in bringing the Bible to life and detailing what life was life back then. This is the ultimate story of redemption and forgiveness. We see that if we put our trust and faith in God He will forgive us of our sins if we are sincere and repent. Rahab’s story shows us that God can and will use anybody from any walk of life for a greater good. I received a complimentary copy of this book to review from Revell.

title: This felt very much like I sat down with the author and just sort ...
text:
This felt very much like I sat down with the author and just sort of talked randomly with him about his career. There were all kinds of interesting nuggets about the industry in here, and the author had no qualms about throwing names out there. None of it was particularly bad, so I don't think he'll get any backlash from it, but all the same it seemed a very gutsy move.

The only thing I will say I had a problem with was how odd it was to read. There didn't seem to be any form that was followed. It was kind of chronological, but there didn't seem to be any real narrative. This is what I mean about it feeling like I just sat down and chit chatted with the author. It was just very jumpy.

That doesn't pose as much of a problem as you might expect, though. Since the stories are all separate from each other, you don't really miss out on anything the way it is written. The only major feedback I would give to the author is to do another sweep--certain words were spelled wrong that shouldn't have been, that should have been easy to spot. The two that stick out the most in my mind are "eery" and "trakked".

title: That is one of a hell ride of FEELS. OH MY GOD. DAMN. This series never fails to give me palpitations
text:
The wait is freaking over and the Boss is here! The story focuses on Victor Faust a.k.a The Boss, the merciless killer and Izabel's lover. I'm excited and nervous what's going to happen next after that cliffhanger on The Black Wolf. Here, he bares his past and we get to know the real him.

"I open the doors wide to my past, and let in the sterilizing light."

The story starts as Victor and Izabel are on vacation at Venezuela. He has a purpose on that trip, it's his chance to confess everything to Izabel: the secrets he knew about her, the purpose of her mission with Niklas etc.. However, the moment has been interrupted because they're kidnapped by some people who wanted revenge on Victor for the longest time. They are prepared to unleash hell to hurt him and as well as the love of his life.

That is one of a hell ride of FEELS. OH MY GOD. DAMN. This series never fails to give me palpitations and I have absolutely no chill for all the surprising plot twists. There are new characters being introduced and I'm curious to get to know all of them. All of them are twisted in their own way, some of them are ruthless and not to be trusted yet.

"No one is immune to change, especially those who fear it. It comes for us first, and it destroys us swiftly because we fight it the hardest."

The character developments are hands down well written. Izabel endured all the pain and yet she survived. It makes her more determined, powerful and confident with herself. She wants to stand on her own feet and I love the direction she's taking in. It might be dangerous but I trust her and she's going to survive it. Victor made a huge transition. Love changed him in some ways. Even if he's not used to it, for Izabel, he embraced it.

I love it and it's definitely 5 stars for me. It's worth my obsession and I'm looking forward for the upcoming books in this series and I'm so pumped to read them all. Those preview to the upcoming books.. OMG. I. WANT. ASAP.
It's going to give me more mini heart attacks.

title: Lyric, character-driven coming of age story of expatriate life, revolution, family, and betrayal.
text: I loved this book.  It starts out slowly, so I had to start it more than once, and I'm glad I did.  The language grabbed me first - almost like poetry.  Then I began to connect with the characters.  The main character, Salim, is an introvert, like me, and I enjoyed his observations about people and human nature, the things he wondered about and the dots he connected between how people - individually and as a society - behaved and what they said about themselves.  I was particularly interested in his observations of the various political leaders, from the colonizers, to the locals who took control after the revolution, to the British when he moved to London.  I didn't detect a hint of a plot for the first 175 pages, but I was caught up in his experience as an expat of Zanzibar - Zanzibar! - living in London.  I noticed that the other reviews are not as favorable as mine.  Maybe I loved it more than I normally would have because a friend of mine is studying the African diaspora, and this little story helps me feel a part of that work.  I was curious about how he felt living in London, home of the colonial oppressors he despised and distrusted, his experience as a black man, an African man, a Muslim, a poor man, an immigrant in London, and how he felt about home - about where home is when no place feels like home.  The writing style and the depictions of character and family remind me of Sebastian Barry, a favorite author.  I wish now that I were more familiar with Shakespeare, who also plays an important part in the story.

title: Una exposición extraordinaria de pedofilia y obstrucción de la justicia tanto en México como en el Vaticano
text:
(La traducción al español sigue esta revisión de la lengua inglesa)

This book has its faults and its critics, but it is a good exposé of the misdeeds of the late Mexican cleric, Marciel Maciel, of the late 20th century and the devastating and far-reaching effects of the rampant pedophilia among his Cruzados de Cristo Rey (Legionnaires of Christ.)
My own research into this case shows that Pope Saint John Paul II, unfortunately (through ignorance of the truth, that was concealed from him) admired Marciel Maciel. Accordingly, Cardinal Ratzinger, who had the responsibility for bringing Maciel to trial (after far too many years of pleas by his victims)finally created a portfolio in the Vatican in 1997; however, he suppressed the prosecution of JP II's "friend" until JP II died. Ratzinger ascended to the papacy, and another high bishop took over from Ratzinger the office that was responsible for prosecuting such cases.
In a most unusual and disheartening move, the case was dropped just a few weeks after Benedict XVI took office. Some assumed that the accusations had been reviewed and considered insufficient for a trial. Others – even some hierarchs – protested the decision to drop the case. However, the new man in charge of the curia, acknowledging the objections he had received, noted that the decision had not been issued under his own official seal of authority, but that it had been issued by the Holy See itself, i.e. by order of none other than the new Benedict XVI himself. The struggle continues.
-----------------------------
Este libro tiene sus fallas y sus críticas, pero es una buena exposición de las fechorías del fallecido clérigo mexicano, Marciel Maciel, de finales del siglo XX y los devastadores y trascendentales efectos de la pedofilia rampante entre sus Cruzados de Cristo Rey. (Legionarios de Cristo)
Mi propia investigación sobre este caso muestra que el Papa San Juan Pablo II, desafortunadamente (por ignorancia de la verdad, que se le ocultó) admiraba a Marciel Maciel. En consecuencia, el Cardenal Ratzinger, que tenía la responsabilidad de enjuiciar a Maciel (después de demasiados años de súplicas por parte de sus víctimas) finalmente creó una cartera en el Vaticano en 1997; sin embargo, reprimió el enjuiciamiento del "amigo" de JP II hasta que murió JP II. Ratzinger ascendió al papado, y otro alto obispo sustituyó a Ratzinger en la oficina responsable de enjuiciar tales casos.
En un movimiento muy inusual y desalentador, el caso fue abandonado unas pocas semanas después de que Benedicto XVI asumió el cargo. Algunos supusieron que las acusaciones habían sido revisadas y consideradas insuficientes para un juicio. Otros, incluso algunos jerarcas, protestaron por la decisión de abandonar el caso. Sin embargo, el nuevo responsable de la curia, reconociendo las objeciones que había recibido, señaló que la decisión no había sido emitida bajo su propio sello de autoridad oficial, sino que había sido emitida por la Santa Sede misma, es decir, por orden de nada menos que el nuevo Benedicto XVI mismo. La lucha continúa.

title: An eye opening and fun read.
text: Quite a fun read for me. I think you would like this if you are curious about how things work. It is not a "survivalist" book. It is a book designed to inform people about how little we understand the foundations of our technology. I think we often are unaware of the actually brilliant efforts our ancestors made just to get us to the level of production we take for granted today. I sometimes get the impression from peers that they think people in the past were kind of dumb not to have cell phones and microwave popcorn. But the people saying that are completely ignorant of the complex path of development we have taken and would be hopeless about even how to begin to do these things if they had to start from scratch. So... a good book for those interested in the history of technology; but also a good book for the reader of science fiction as these concepts tie in with many works of that genre in an indirect way.  It was well written and edited.

title: Crappy story, great art, incredible characterization
text:
This classic story attempts to incorporate all the 1990’s Marvel horror titles into one cohesive whole, but fails utterly. Major enemies are dispatched with a single shot of hellfire, every battle is described as “the first encounter with the Lillin,” and Lilith herself is a joke. Still, this collection has that 90’s nostalgia that reminds me how Marvel used to be a great company.

Despite its many faults, this book is amazing. Blaze has never looked (or been depicted) better. He’s the chain-smoking badass that will do anything to protect his family. The Nightstalkers intro is one of the best ever, but the Morbius and Darkhold Redeemers are simply awful. The story itself isn’t much, but the characterization and feel of the book are spot on. I’d read a page from the Darkhold to find more comics like this.

As a bonus, this collection also contains the “Spirits of Venom” storyline which is an absolute blast. Hobgoblin, Demogoblin, Venom, Hag, Troll, and the Spidey Doppleganger together? Yes please.

Check out the original covers of Nightstalkers 1 and the Spirits of Venom art with Venom hanging from the ceiling, holding Ghost Rider’s skull. Outstanding. Add the infamous Johnny Blaze “Bang, yer dead” cover and you’ll never buy a 21st century Marvel comic again.

title: Another Great Rupert Annual.
text:
Often with Rupert Annuals Brits buy them for the year in which they or the person for whom the gift is for birthday.
This can lead to problems because the British have the habit of calling the Annual for the following year in which it was originally published.
So a book published and released for the Christmas market of 1963 would be entitled Rupert Annual 1964 and so on.

This is listed as No author and Alex Cubie!

Which seems to contradict the no author bit at least.

Here is the review,

Originally published in 1975 this book takes the title `Rupert Annual 1976 for it was for the Christmas Market and all annuals took the next year in their title.
This one has the Title Rupert and `The Daily Express Annual' on its cover.

The cover by Alex Cubie shows Rupert waving holding a large green, wooden, steam train with a parachute attached. The full impact of the books cover is when you hold it out and see that a gigantic gondola, perhaps suspended from an airship and carrying 3 clown? Passengers who are throwing various toys to the children of Nutwood. The presents are floating down on brightly coloured parachutes.
Ruperts chums are catching them on the rear of the cover and on the front others are running as fast as they can to `bag' a present.

Tiger Lily is depicted upon the rear holding a brightly painted top.
The cover looks `cluttered' and the figures seem too `heavy and thick' Cubie seems to have overdone the black outlines around his figures too much.
Indeed the animals in the background look to be the wrong scale and there is an overall lack of depth to the cover.

Thankfully we don't judge a book by its cover do we?

No?

Good for the contents are really good.

The book cost just 90p and my what a bargain that was and a really appreciated Christmas present at the times when we children got much less at Christmas that children do now.

The endpapers again by Alex Cubie is entitled `Rupert Awaits king Neptune'.

Again like it's cover it is not one of the better pictures. The figures again look too heavy- but the feel is of an evening or maybe early morning so Cubie may be given some leeway.

To the Contents.

I can reassure you that art work and colouring are beautiful truly works of art for all the stories are all wonderful and expertly drawn and so beautifully coloured.
Generally the artist drew the pictures and a talented colourist would use their skill to enhance the wonderful drawings. A bad colourist could ruin a great artists work. This is not the case here- far from it. The palette use is bright and jewel like- truly lovely.
Alex Cubie really has excelled with his artwork and the story writer whoever they may be have written wonderful stories.

Each has a wonderful story page starter picture with a short paragraph setting the scene.

The first story is called `Rupert and the Jumping Men'.
In it Rupert wishes to buy a board game called `Halma' I must admit I have never heard of the game myself I think it may be a little like Ludo.
There are no sets to be had in the Toyshop.
Rupert meets a Chinese Doll who ensures Rupert shrinks to small size so he can enter the land of Games.
Here chaos reigns! The pawns don't like to restricted to sliding across their boards- the Halma pieces wish to slide and the tiddlywinks want to jump and do all 3!

After a madcap gigantic board game the pieces revert back to their sets and peace is restored.
HOWEVER.... There is a prominent figure of a Golliw*g (sic) so this is a gentle warning.

Then the next story is `Rupert and Young Kevin'.
Here a new boy attends school but runs away. All the children at Rupert's school chase after him and he gives them a real song and dance of a chase. A gentle story with a really clever twist... Now you wouldn't want me to divulge the twist would you?

Of Course not!

On page 60 there is Rupert's Maze and puzzle.

The third Story `Rupert and the Hot Water' is really fabulous- Rupert goes to the seaside and promises to find something interesting for the Professor.
Water spouts appear and Rupert takes pail of water and finds that it is hot.
BUT it never ever cools down.
Imagine the savings on hot water bottles in the Winter- or boiling an egg??
He meets Tiger Lilly and her Daddy the Conjuror who has a visitor the Sorcerer.
He has travel all the way from China, through the earth in a magic `mole machine'.
Could this be the source of the `Hot Water'?

The final story is `Rupert and the Windy Day'.
Rupert has an adventure with the Scout Geoffrey and they discover a mysterious long lost brick tunnel. Where does it lead too?

The book is completed with

Make Rupert's Humming-bird and Rupert's three wise monkeys- origami folding.
There is
Rupert's Maze and Puzzle, Rupert's School-time Game and finally Rupert's Kite Puzzle.

Just four stories but all are wonderful.
No Christmassy ones alas.
But each is really good making this a wonderful Rupert Annual.

Enjoy.

title: Communism Is Decay and Death, EVERYWHERE It Is Tried
text:
Communism had a nine-figure body count in the twentieth century, and in this volume author Paul Kengor rightly excoriates it as the worst idea in history. It leads to crushing poverty, mass murder, loss of civil liberties, and, of course, no right of exit for those trapped in the evil regimes it establishes, wherever those regimes are established. America has faults, but they are minuscule compared to those of Communist societies. In the West the squalid Communist record has been buried and hidden, especially from our young, and Kengor admirably exposes it in this book.

Kengor provides the basic history of the Communist movement, illustrating that such a terrible system was produced by terrible individuals such as Marx, Lenin, Stalin, and others. He describes Soviet terror and quotes Soviet leaders who acknowledged the obvious, that mass violence and slaughter would be necessary to implement Communism. The author describes the damage that Communism wrought in Russia, China, and the Third World, and notes that such a hideous system actually had adherents in America (and, yes, the CPUSA was run from Moscow).

Because Communism tries to change human nature, it has failed in all of the cultures and climates where it has been tried, and not because "it wasn't real Communism" or "the wrong people were in charge," as the more unserious boosters of the system attempt to explain away its failures. Kengor notes that some young people today are so miseducated and naïve that they think that socialism and Communism are merely "people being kind," but there is nothing kind about Communism or its leaders—elites and the ruling classes in Communist societies never live under the conditions they inflict on everyone else, and the only morality the ruling classes observe is that which serves their own interests. The chief product of Communism, Kengor observes, is death.

Kengor examines socialism and the resurgent interest in Communism in the twenty-first century and describes the reminder (as if the world needed one) of how evil and unworkable Communism is by its recent affliction of Venezuela. The author covers Communism's modern associated cultural parallel movements, Cultural Marxism and the Frankfurt School.

The final test of Communism is what happens when the gates are raised. If those in the Soviet Union, Cuba, Vietnam, and China had been given a chance to leave in the twentieth century, millions would have fled. Conversely, apart from a tiny handful of eccentrics, no one would have left a capitalist country to go "live" under Communism. This book should be required reading for everyone under 30 today, and those who are interested in further reading can follow the book suggestions offered throughout, especially Kevin Williamson's "Politically Incorrect Guide to Socialism."

title: The Uneventful Event
text:
Go to page 261. If you read this and are enthralled get the book and spend time getting to know the protagonists. They are several. This book requires some knowledge of basketball and its techniques even though through serendipity one of the catalyst characters knew the inventor of the game; so there is a historical recounting of the game up to 1944. The book's major flaw is its anvil of the words used to describe American blacks: Negro or Colored. The author chooses to use these two terms throughout when describing era. Because racial description will continue to evolve, presently at African American, the author's choice while disturbing is appropriate. He presents violent and subtle acts of racism as equally powerful and segregating. He does not spare the reader, choosing not to gloss over anything. It is amazing that in our era these same things still happen. To get to the climatic point of the eventful non-event it is necessary to show how simply difficult it was to have a game between differing races in the North Carolina of the 1940s. It is not hard to imagine in other small towns throughout the South and other places in America similar gatherings of integration were occurring. This particular game was pivotal because of its link to the birth of basketball. The end of the book is more of a pause and somewhat anti-climatic. The NOTES section is as important reading as the rest of the book.
Even if you are not a fan of basketball or sports, and this is about a time when sports were not the central focus of America, this is a great capsule of the struggle for American unity and integration. It describes a time when segregation and subjugation of blacks was acceptable to most blacks and whites. It details how a small college prospered amid the horrific second class citizenship of the area. There are glimpses of the rise of black middle class America not through sports but business. This book gives understanding that being the same is not equal. Loosely related incidences are brought forward to paint this tableau in time with a sharp razor edge; there are parts that feel like walking on knives. After reading this, one wonders why have things changed but the results remain: unarmed black men shot and their killers acquitted. The book does offer insight, but of course no answers. Integration was a slow arduous process, even in the North although the book makes this seem different, but it was only a first step.

title: Masterful storytelling at its best.
text:
If there's a category for modern day fairytales, Carrie Ann Lahain's "Morgrim's Wood" fits the bill. When we first meet Pam, she's having a very bad day. A punch to her best friend's nose lands Pam in jail, and in classic fairytale fashion, the stranger in the cell gives us our first hint not everything is as it seems in Lahain's world.

Pam's own pain becomes clear when we learn she's still recovering from the loss of her daughter. But it's not just Pam, everyone in her family is suffering.

A trip into upstate New York soon changes everything. The mysterious woods from Pam's childhood haunt her once again, and this time, those dark places hold the key to her healing.

Morgrim's Wood runs along at a breakneck speed as Lahain masterfully reveals each twist and turn. This author has some storytelling chops and I'm eager to read her other books. The characters have depth. I admire Lahain's flair for creative antagonists, and the sticky situations the characters find themselves in. Who or what Morgrim actually is, keeps you guessing right up to the very end.

Bravo, Carrie Ann! Perhaps we'll see a sequel?

title: The Mafia queen has outdone herself!
text:
Reviewed by Rachel & Sharon Thérèse

Darhower took us by storm! Unarguably, Mafia genre is her forte and by offering us what we thought might be hoping too much for, made our day, or month… our year complete. One of the characters in Target on Our Backs, Lorenzo Gambini, that bad boy who left us greedy to know more, is back and in full force with his own series, Scarlet Scars. To our delight, he hasn’t changed his tune one little bit, either. Now then, what is interesting about this book is you don’t need to read the Monster in His Eyes series to appreciate why he’s like he is. The author has given little tips about his past experiences without confusing the new reader. If anything, what she has done is open up one’s appetite for those who haven’t had the pleasure of meeting him. Not only did she jog our memory, but she also titillated us in unimaginable ways. To write what she has took a lot of courage since she’s changed her storytelling style a tad. It’s darker. And how damn well it worked out!

We love stories told in present and from two perspectives which she has done in many of her previous books. Even though the narrative structure in this one was more than to our liking, it’s different in the respect that both protagonists ask the reader rhetorical questions making one ponder over what is going to come next. In some instances, we even found ourselves answering back in the middle of a battle of wits. However, there is nothing amusing about their story. This is serious stuff in capital letters underlined and highlighted. Not surprisingly, we loved their gritty mind games that kept us guessing right up until the end! We have to say that if there are was one character we couldn’t help but to succumb to at the drop of a hat was Lorenzo. He is our man! Yep, Darhower’s Mafia men we love to death and unashamedly so!

Lorenzo’s villainous persona, his understated comebacks regardless of the outcome, were second to none. His outlook on life’s little-huge setbacks never ruffled his feathers. He is understood by no-one. He’s scarred past is under wraps but to be revealed...slowly, and just how we like. He’s fearless and has a moral compass that only works to serve his imperfections brilliantly. His nuances and peculiar tastes, we connected to easily, Nonetheless, he made our hair stand on end. We adored him; we hated him, we agreed to disagree with him. His quirks, decisions and impatience made him the perfect adversary for Morgan who would cross his path when least expected. Finding someone such as her to stand up and tell him what she thought was our pleasure tenfold. Ah, but Morgan plays just as dirty as him. If anything, the game is lost before it’s even begun.

“. . . I’ll forgive you a lot of things, but if you tell me you don’t eat oranges, we’re going to have a problem.”

Morgan wasn’t on his agenda and would become a thorn in his side. Like an aching constant, he couldn’t get her out of his mind. Fathoming out this young woman who wanted to be left alone, who was so unpretentious, opens Pandora’s box. Ooh boy, do things get interesting in this read from there on in! Morgan confused us, worried us and her unpretentiousness even got the better of us. She selflessly carries out her quest for freedom making the reader ask why she has to go through such trauma. This young gal rocks and became our number one heroine without even trying to. Like Lorenzo, her past is complicated. There are moments extremely difficult to read in this book. Moments when our imagination ran riot, but here’s the huge but... you don’t know why until the last written word. We like to think that we can suss out the ending of a book. Not here folks, and we tried our hardest!

“You're mine. I won’t let you go. I can’t. I destroy any man who tries to take you away from me. . .”

The secondary character development was beyond our expectations. Lie. Darhower is an expert in such details and has yet to let us down. Frustratingly explicit descriptions of events regardless of whether or not they were in the bedroom, have without a doubt, defeated these two readers. We were left in a blubbering mess and can’t thank her enough for releasing Grievous soon. The outcome of such a nail-biting conclusion to this duet is so anticipated that we’d sell our souls for it! And that’s saying something! Bravo ma’am!

title: I love Candace Calvert's books and couldn't wait to get my ...
text:
I love Candace Calvert's books and couldn't wait to get my hands on this one! Step by Step was exactly what I've come to expect from Calvert's books. Wonderfully exciting medical drama with a good dose of romantic tension and an outside villain to keep things interesting. Her characters are always quite complex but I felt like this book had even more complexity than usual. Taylor's life is full of tension from work, crisis team, relationships, and grief. Then Seth shows up and complicates things even more! And the minor characters are dealing with issues too. Both the internal conflicts and the interpersonal ones in this book keep things interesting as you wonder when and where people will reconcile with their own personal issues as well as issues with each other.

The romance in this book was good! There was a lot of romantic tension since there are two men in Taylor's life and that definitely made things interesting more than once. I felt like the scenes with both the men were quite realistic and in fact maybe toned down from what would happen in real life if two guys were going for the same girl! I definitely found myself rooting for one of them :)

I am giving this book 3 1/2 stars because for me the pacing was off. It just didn't move as fast as I'm used to her books moving and I ended up reading this book in three sittings when I usually read her books in one. The medical drama part I still loved but I wonder if I wasn't hindered following so many interesting characters. I was really drawn to Kasie's character and I'm hoping she'll be the main character in her own book too. I also found myself more interested than I wanted to be in what would happen with Sloane. But I didn't care for being so distracted from Taylor's life.

I would especially recommend this book for anyone who enjoys medical dramas and also for pet lovers because pets played a huge role in this story (perhaps one of the reasons I wasn't as invested in the story since I'm not a huge pet person.)

So while overall this wasn't my favorite book by Calvert she is still among my favorite authors and I am very much looking forward to her next book!

title: The New Case For Gold is Rickards Manifesto!
text: In his newest book, The New Case For Gold, Jim Rickards has produced his most powerful and timely work yet.  In a very articulate narrative he explains all the reasons why the average person needs to acquire gold and acquire it NOW.  Rickards takes a very complex global monetary and economic subject and puts it into very simple and understandable terms.  Whether or not you are an experienced gold advocate or a complete newbie to the world of gold you will learn something.  Mr. Rickards is a very smart and accomplished expert in the world of global finance.  He uses that expertise to share the big picture and all the "moving parts" that are involved between the major players on the world stage.  Rickards gives a thorough historical background of the part gold has played in the world economies. His advice to regular folks who may not be investment savvy and looking for a simple strategy to protect their wealth is to own physical gold as insurance or a hedge against a potential monetary and economic crisis.  This book is not just recycling the old justifications for owning gold.  Rickards points out the majority of our money and wealth is in a digital form these days.  Consequently our portfolios and bank accounts are at very high risk of "cyber financial terrorism"!  He warns us that hackers from our international competition are perpetually attempting to break into our government and large financial institutions computer systems to bring them crashing down, reeking havoc and disaster.  Physical gold, says Rickards, is a tangible asset that can't be hacked.  These are only a few justifications in a long list that Rickards promotes. The New Case For Gold is the most comprehensive work about what's going on in the global economic, monetary and currency wars with the most rational financial strategy for us regular investors.  The message: Buy some physical gold NOW while it's still available and affordable.  Invest the $15 for the book.  It may be the best investment you ever made.  TC

title: Simply Wonderful Sepik Region PNG Art
text:
Hardcover, Pictorial Boards, (Issued less DJ), 11.5" x 9.75", 353 Pages. 228 Catalogue Items in Color.30 Field Photos. 2 x 2-Page Maps, 1 x 1-Page Map.1 X 2-Page German map of the Sepik region from 1924. 5-Page Bibliography. Title Translation (From German) : "Dance Of The Ancestors, Art From The Sepik (River Region) In Papua New Guinea". TEXT AND DESCRIPTIONS ENTIRELY IN GERMAN. Authors : Philippe Peltier, Markus Schindlbeck, Christian Kaufmann. Published by : Berliner Festpiele + Stadt Zurich + Musee Du Quai Branly + HIRMER, 2015.

As usual for me, the main point of an art book is the art itself, not what some undoubtedly wise PhD's have to say about the art. By this criteria this book is a treat, because the objects depicted are of a truly wonderful quality, and since my German is limited to ordering beer, I have an excuse not to read the text at all. Not only are the objects depicted sublime, but they are not the same old pieces featured in a hundred other Oceanic art books. The book is published to accompany exhibitions at Martin-Gropius-Bau, Berlin (March-June 2015), Museum Reitberg, Zurich (July-October 2015), and Musee Du Quai Branly, Paris (October 2015-February 2016).

Items featured include : Canoe Prows, Paddles, Hooks, Posts, Bowls, Drums, Textiles, Panels, Figures, Masks, Bark Paintings, Staffs, Ornaments, Jewelry, Daggers, Spears, Shields, and more. First rate paper, binding, photographs and presentation. If you have any interest in the art of Papua New Guinea, this book is worth seeking out.

title: The Nowhere Man shows his humanity
text:
The Nowhere Man shows his humanity
Evan Smoak is a one man vigilante force. A former covert assassin, Evan now seeks redemption by being the ultimate vigilante. Dial his secret Nowhere Man phone number and simply say “I need Help!” That’s all it takes to bring the Nowhere man to your aid. A fast moving novel, Hell Bent shows the personal side of Evan Smoak. By the end of the story you experience the entire humanity spectrum of just who is The Nowhere Man and why does he do what he does.
Excellent character development. Mr. Hurwitz fleshes out the totality of protagonist Evan Smoak into a very complex man. I Liked all the additional characters especially the shadowy Tommy Stojack and the enigmatic female Orphan V Candy McClure. Lots of fertile story ground to plow here!
No gratuitous sex but plenty of F-bombs and violence.
Evan Smoak assassin turned vigilante is turning out to be a superb series. Plenty of action tied to ever expanding character development. Eagerly looking forward to the next Evan Smoak adventure.

title: Four Excellent Modesty Blaise Adventures
text:
This excellent Over-sized Trade Paperback is actually volume 28 in Titan Books Complete Modesty Blaise, This volume reprints British Comic Strips from 1997 and 1998. Since the strip ended in 2001, I assume it will be 30 Volumes in total. This Book is NOT in the Landscape format (wider then tall) that most recent comic strip collections have adopted. Instead they use a traditional "portrait' format with four strips to a page. While I would like to see them in larger size they are still readable and the reproduction is sharp. Since they use 4 strips per page rather then instead of the 2 or 3 per page that the American Library Of Comics or Hermes Press employ. Sine the stories do not conclude with a multiple of six daily strips you get two stray strips (on the page) that conclude each adventure.

Peter O'Donnell's writing is brilliant and the adventures are tightly plotted with every story beat intricately calculated. When reading some other adventure strips, you get the feeling that the plot is being created as the story goes along. That never happens in a Modesty Blaise story. Everything is carefully crafted.

Enric Romero is back with realistic but sexy fine line art. The man has knack for showing Modesty and her female cohorts in various states of partial nudity and making it seem integral to the plot.

British Writer Rebecca Chance does the introductions and does a good job. I love how they do an introduction for the general volume and then each of the four story-lines gets their own introduction. This is a great concept that I wish other strip collections would emulate.

1) THE MURDER FRAME. In this story Willie, Modesty's trusted right hand man, is framed for murder by a neighboring socialite. This is a very traditional murder yarn, make enjoyable by how well it is done.The story features a pair of returning strong women Lady Janet and Maude Tiller.

2)FRASER'S STORY. This story brings the spotlight onto one of the bit players in O'Donnell's Opus. We dig into Fraser's past as he tries to murder an agent who has destroyed something very valuable to him.

3) A TRIBUTE TO THE PHARAOH. This is easily my favorite story of the volume. it provides us with new information on the childhood of both Modest and Willie. It is set on the banks of the Nile and explores ancient burial tombs an the legends of Kush. We get a flashback of Modesty as
young teen. And find an elderly woman who helped raise Willie. We also meet a plucky young girl who is modern version of young Modesty.

4) SPECIAL ORDER. Speaking of plucky young woman, this features another one. Sam is another Strong woman whom are heroes had previously encountered before. Now she gets abducted by a group who specialize in "special ordering" just the perfect Sex Slave. Can she plot here an escape from the slave ship, before Modesty and Willie help out?

This Volume gets My Highest Recommendation.

title: Tangled Web AR Torre Weaves!!!
text:
The masterful storyteller strikes again. If You Dare is the 3rd book in the Deanna Madden series. This series is suspense and intrigue and darkness at its finest.

I can’t tell you how many times I have wanted to transport myself into Deanna’s apartment and just hug her and love her and tell her that she can “have normal”. I believe that Deanna Madden is a psychotherapist’s dream. There are so many facets to Deanna……….her personality and her actions could be dissected for days, weeks, and definitely months. She is beyond strong but she is so very isolated in her own darkness that even when the light, aka Jeremy Pacer, tries to enter, she only allows the light to peek in so it never fully takes over the darkness. Deanna’ psychiatrist, Derek, has tried to help but can one really help when your sessions are done over the phone? And then there is Mike, Deanna’s techie that keeps her safe and isolated. Jeremy, Derek, and Mike are all champions of Deanna in one form or another but they all have some sort of disconnect as well. It’s such a tangled web the author weaves………its utter perfection!! I can’t forget to mention Simon…..he serves a purpose but he’s not a champion.

We know that Deanna goes to jail but why is the question. I won’t tell you anything more because to do so would be to spoil the journey. The journey is one that keeps you breathless at times, makes you sad at times, has you rooting at times and mostly it is one that makes you feel all of the time. A.R. Torre knows how to weave a brilliant story and add just the right amount of twists and turns to keep you captivated.

I will say that the ending took awhile to sink in for me. As I discussed with others, talked about what had happened, I decided that the ending was in fact perfect (for me). As whenever I open a book by this amazing author, I go into a book hangover where her books just affect my psyche for a few days. Her writing is visual and detailed and completely mesmerizing.

If you have read the first 2 books, get ready for a wickedly dastardly ride and if you haven’t read the first 2 in the series- GO GO GO and one click The Girl in 6E and Do Not Disturb. I promise that this series does not and will not disappoint.

title: A page-turning, thought-provoking adventure
text:
I have read very few books that manage to be both fun and thought-provoking. Princess Holy Aura is a rare breed of novel, one that keeps you engaged, hanging on the end of every word, needing to know what happens next while also making you pause and reflect. Far from a simple riff on the tropes present in magical girl series such as Sailor Moon, this is work that touches heavily on themes of sacrifice and identity, intertwining them into a narrative about a man who makes the willing choice to sacrifice his identity and sense of self to save the world, along with all that entails. And I can't help but ask myself, could I do the same if it were asked of me? And if I were able to summon the courage to give up my identity as an adult male to become a teenage girl to protect the world, what would that do to my psyche? Would I stubbornly cling to my original identity or find myself slowly but surely identifying more and more as the seemingly frail yet powerful magical girl warrior I had become? How much of it would be natural and how much of it would be due to the magic involved altering my perception and way of thinking?

I will say that there are certain elements of the story that could have been fleshed out more. The Cataclysm Knights are woefully undeveloped, for starters, and I feel like there was more that could have been done with the character of Dex and the OSC. The book is broken up into four sections, but it honestly feels like each section could have been expanded into its own book to make an entire series.

The bottom line: If you're a fan of magical girl anime series such as Sailor Moon, or simply want a fun, page-turning adventure that also makes you think, then read this book! You just might find yourself asking "What would I be willing to give up to save the world?"
