title: Easily among Ito's most creative, engaging, and grotesque
text:
While I'm very familiar with Junji Ito's work, and have been for a few years, Tomie is a series of his that I never knew of until recently. Being that really only Uzumaki and Gyo were well known in the states at the time, I had no idea how much more excellent material he'd done over the years.

After hearing about Tomie's American release, I googled pictures of the series, and initially wasn't very interested, since it looked more tame than the beautifully disgusting Uzumaki and Gyo, but when I actually ordered the book, I found that it's actually more gruesome than anything else I've read from Ito. Joy!

Now, in case you have yet to look at the length of this release, I'll just say outright that it's a TOME compared not only to previously released Ito work, but to most manga you'll find in your local bookstore. The reason for that being that Tomie has been going strong, as a loosely connected series of one shots, for decades now. As you'll find in this collection, Ito improved immensely over the years, and seeing his initially amateurish art style evolve from chapter to chapter is a joy for an avid reader of his like myself. Reading through this book is a more daunting task than something like Uzumaki, but the increasingly "out there" ongoing plot, as well as the standalone stories, make the journey very worth the time spent.

A huge part of what makes this series so engrossing is Tomie herself. As readers will quickly realize, she's a truly awful human being (or monster, if you prefer), to the extent that it's addictive seeing how she's going to screw over her victims from page to page, as well as how she'll get her occasional comeuppance. Her deplorable personality is often the heart of what makes so many of these tales work as well as they do (in particular Little Finger, which has a brilliant and dark (and I mean dark) fairy tale style to it that puts it near the top of Ito's work for me).

Since the book is so huge, of course not every chapter is equal to the last. Most of the book is excellent throughout, but there are some that are subpar, simply because they're so random and/or weird, despite their creativity. Luckily, said lesser stories are few and far between, and most of the ongoing chapters and the true one shots are often equal in their high quality, although the episodic story does get simply insane about halfway through, but not necessarily in a bad way. Overall, though, the compilation is extremely engaging and horrific throughout, so I'm very happy to have bought it.

If you're a horror fan looking for their next fix, I'd recommend the previously mentioned Ito works before this one, simply due to their accessibility and length, but if you're well versed in his grotesque and darkly humorous world already, you owe it to yourself to give this a look.

title: Exciting Historical Fiction
text:
Another enjoyable read by Teri Brown. Ms. Brown is a wonderful historical fiction writer, and this book finds her exploring outside the Roaring Twenties setting she mastered in the Born of Illusion series. This book takes place during WWI. I didn't feel like the sense of time and place was quite as good as the Born of Illusion series, but it was still an excellent story.
Teri Brown does an excellent job of portraying the intricate webs of espionage and intrigue, especially at a time when countless lives depended on being the first to know. I particularly liked the chapter headings with espionage terminology and definitions, and I think the book was very insightful and well-researched in the area of female espionage in particular.
The twist in this book was quite unpredictable, and I found it to be a very fitting and satisfying wrap up for the plot.
I will certainly continue reading further historical fiction by Teri Brown.

title: Pay attention to which edition you buy
text:
My rating above is on the text as a whole. If you are a student looking to buy this for a class, consider the note at the end of my review. I do NOT factor that content into my rating, but it may keep you from making the same mistake I did.

Ain't No Makin' It is an ethnography following the lives of two groups of boys growing up in Clarendon Heights, a public housing development in Massachusetts. Jay MacLeod considers the differing aspirations of the two groups of boys: one composed primarily of blacks and one composed primarily of whites. He began his studies of these boys in the 1980s and follows up again with them in 1991 and finally in 2006. Applying sociological techniques, he both documents the specific actions and comments of the boys and also considers these observations in the light of various social reproduction theories.

The book contains raw, honest documentation of the boys' lives. It is clear that MacLeod spent an incredible amount of time with the subjects and built deep relationships with them. It is particularly useful to gain a perspective of the challenges faced by the urban poor trying to make their way in the job market. However, at times the book feels repetitive and drawn out. MacLeod seems to restate some points excessively.

The book contains substantial portions of dialogue, which are full of profanity. While he is only accurately quoting the boys, the language does make it difficult to read at times.

----------

For STUDENTS looking to buy this for class: You can frequently get by and save money by purchasing a slightly older version of a text. Not so here. I purchased the 2nd edition thinking I would cleverly beat my bookstore and save on costs. Unfortunately, I did not research my purchase well. There are major differences between the 2nd and 3rd edition. The second edition is about 200 pages shorter and ends with MacLeod's 1991 field study. The 3rd edition adds follow-up fieldwork that MacLeod did with the boys (now men) in 2006. Buy the requested edition for your class.

title: No Way Back
text:
Not just another Spider-Geddon tie-in, this issue is also the start of a new series staring Spider-Gwen. This character was created in the build-up to the original Spider-Verse event, and she's been a fan-favorite for the most part since then. Jason Latour, the character's creator, recently finished his run on her series. Now writer Seanan McGuire seems to be following in that series footsteps perfectly. This issue takes place after Spider-Geddon#2, so spoilers ahead for those who haven't read that comic yet. The story is really told in two parts. The first catches up with Gwen after the events of her previous series, giving us an introduction into her and her world. I haven't read all of the previous series yet, but it's not too difficult to fill in the gaps in spite of that. The second part is where spoilers follow. After her fight with The Inheritors, Gwen finds herself stranded on an Earth she doesn't know, without her teleportation watch. While searching for a way back to the fight she comes across some familiar yet different faces who may be able to help her. I'm really glad I got this comic, McGuire has a very similar humor and style to that of Latour that really let's the main character shine. Rosi Kämpe is the artist for the issue, and her work is absolutely great. It's the perfect balance between a stylized and realistic look. This comic doesn't really tie-into Spider-Geddon all that much beyond using the scenario it set up for it's story, which is fine. This was really good start to this series, and I await the next issue.
4/5

title: Gourmet Fare
text:
Too Like the Lightning (Hardcover) by Ada Palmer

This book is quite the ride! It is set in the mid 2400's, yet narrated as if in the 1700's? This means that the reader doesn't get the luxury of our 21st century sound byte chapters of two or less pages. It also means that you need pay attention. The artifice of a future that is described as if in the past is well thought and developed contrivance. It simultaneously gives excruciating detail, while also avoiding the topic at hand.
Thus, the plot seems to be dragging, while in fact it covers only a few days. But you get an in depth relationship with the narrator that is rarely achieved in first person voice. And while you get this deep level of story telling, there is so much more that you ask along the way.
As each chapter is turned, you slowly become drawn in, and by the time you finish this tome, you realize that you simply must preorder the next one!
The author does a great job of having the characters, and their various relationships, drive the plot. So much so that at times you forget the miracles that are being done elsewhere?
but worry not, for the author does an admirable job of pulling yet another rabbit out of the hat, and you (yet again) applaud.

title: An economic tipping point
text:
A Review for Amazon by Jerry Woolpy of Saving Capitalism for the many and not the few by Robert B. Reich
Our economy is not sustainable because as the ninety percent become poor the other ten percent will not have consumers to make a market. If we fail to address inequality by changing the laws by which government regulates markets we are finished. Stockholder capitalism that ignores the interests of stakeholders including labor, customers, and the public interest will fall of its own weight. Since 1980, and especially during the Reagan and Clinton administrations, as a result of campaign financing of presidents and legislators beholden to wealthy and corporate interests, we have made patent law, labor law, inheritance, bankruptcy, contract law, property (what can be owned and for how long), merger law (anti-trust law), and tax law that regulates markets to advantage the accumulation of great wealth for the few at the expense of the many. Hard work and merit are not sufficient for upward mobility. CEOs are in control of their own compensation at three hundred or more times the average worker and they have become independent of stockholder intervention. Unlike the 1950s and 1960, when increases in productivity were linked to wages, now productivity increases while wages are flat or decreasing. Research and development has slowed as capital is being used for enormous salaries and the buyout of competitors in order to provide competition-free enterprise. Banks have been freed to invest as they see fit. Banks are financing distortions with people’s money by extending credit to feed the fantasies of folks who cannot afford it. Banks are insuring each other’s bad loans ultimately backed by government bailouts. But all of this can be fixed by reversing the political changes that disallowed the fair distribution of profit to all stakeholders. Money is not going to be free speech. Corporations are not going to be people. The majority parties won’t be able to set the boundaries of their districts. There will be no revolving doors for legislators to retire to. Campaign spending will be kept low, donors will be identified, and the regulations will be enforced. Reich believes that we are reaching the tipping point of inequality that will result in substantial changes for the better. It is an optimistic book.

title: Adoptive Parents
text:
Five Portraits (2014) is the thirty-ninth Fantasy novel in the Xanth series, following [[ASIN:1624670865 Board Stiff]]. The initial volume in this sequence is [[ASIN:0345347536 A Spell for Chameleon]].

In the previous volume, Kandy went to a wishing well and introduced herself. She explained her problems with men and says that she was board stiff. She presented her wishes and gave the well a pretty stone.

Then she fell down flat on her back and stared up at the sky. She could not move, because she wais a piece of lumber. She was a board with two knotholes as eyes.

After some time, Ease came to the wishing well. He introduced himself and stated his wishes. Then he gave the well an old knife. The knife sank to the bottom, but nothing else happened.

Ease saw the board lying by the well and took it as a weapon. It would be perfect for bashing dangerous animals in the snout. It worked very well, especially since Kandy steered it to the right place.

In this novel, Irrelevant Kandy is a good looking woman of Xanth who is usually only eye candy. She wants adventure, excitement and romance.

Astrid Basilisk-Cocktrice is a deadly basilisk who has been magicked into a beautiful woman. She has to wear sunglasses at all times to protect those near her.

Truculant is a troll. He is rough, tough, and hungry.

D. Fornax is a Demon from another galaxy. She is contraterrene and therefore cannot touch any normal matter without destroying it.

In this story, Astrid woke earty one morning -- as was her habit -- and left her husband sleeping. She spies a spectacle bush and folds her glasses. She takes a pair of rose-colored spectacles.

As she is walking around, she sees a large elf kneeling in front of a grave. The tombstone reads JONE. The elf introduces herself as Jenny.

The elf is friendly and explains that Jone had been her last baby daughter. A prophecy had said that Jone would help someone save the earth from destruction. Jone had died in a terrible accident.

Then Astrid meets a troll named Truculent. He offers a five step process to her. First, he will chase her down, but doesn't see much work in that since she is confined within his glade. Second, He will rape her. Third, he will kill her. The fourth and fifth processes are moot after that.

Astrid tries to talk the troll out of his plans, but he is adamant. He gets irritated at Astrid and strikes her in the head. Astrid loses her glasses and he looks her in the face. Then he falls dead.

Astrid finds an exit covered by an illusion and wanders down the path. It ends at the mouth of a cave. She finds three young goblin maidens in the cave. They try to run her off with warnings of the troll.

The goblins have three trolls prisoners. Astrid negotiates a swap of prisoners between the trolls and the goblins. Then she leaves the goblin den and returns to her tent.

Kandy has received a message from the Demon Fornax. The Demoness wants to be her friend, but Kandy she has already agreed to handle her business matters. Kandy sees a possible conflict of interest in such a relationship.

Kandy asks Astrid is she could be Fornax's friend. Astrid has no objections, but doesn't know how to be friends with a Demoness. Kandy points out that they have some common traits. So Astrid agrees to try.

This tale sends Astrid into the future to get orphaned children. Each of the five children has a different talent, but together they have the ability of Communing. This talent guides them through Xanth.

Astrid is trying to save Xanth. The next installment in this sequence has not yet been announced on Amazon.

Highly recommended for Anthony fans and for anyone else who enjoys tales of parenting styles, adult relationships, and types of love. Read and enjoy!

-Arthur W. Jordin

title: Mutual love for music and mysterious pasts...
text:
First off, let’s take a moment to admire the cover because wow, it’s so gorgeous! I love the fading colors! It’s so pretty to take pictures with, too! 😉

Overall, I enjoyed this book, but I did have some minor problems with it that I will address. This book was self-published, but it was well edited. Truthfully, I don’t read many of those but when the author approached me, the synopsis intrigued me. Normally, I’m not one to pick up the whole “we were childhood best friends but grew apart for X reason and then we meet up again later in life.” But there was a hint of mysteriousness in this, and a mutual love of music that I appreciated.

There were some scenes that could have done with a few more edits. Because I am a bit of a fangirl, I noticed the off things: using “Samwise Gamgees” in one paragraph and then “Samwise Gamgee” in another some pages later. Along with the lack of “The” in front of The Hunger Games. There are a variety of references to other fandoms and some early 2000s pop songs (John Mayer! <3) that made me smile. (It also makes me feel kind of old.)

As for the characters, I liked both of them. Trevor and Charlie are 18 and freshmen in college. As the story progresses, we see they’ve done many things, not because they wanted to, but because their parents wanted them to. I’m also intrigued how parents push many of their hopes and dreams onto their children, and how we, as the children, come to terms with it. We want to make our parents happy, but where’s the line? Where do my parents’ dreams end and ours really begin? The two characters also have a rough home life, in similar and different ways. There are many moments when their interactions with their parents, and the outcome, become a shaping force for the character to determine what or how they respond. It’s also a look at how individuals handle grief in the aftermath of horrific events.

I appreciated how Trevor gave Charlie space. When she needed to figure things out on her own, he wasn’t hanging around, nagging her. He truly let her figure out who she was (see what I did there? 😉 ). With everything that Charlie went through and the guilt and blame she placed on herself, it’s a lot to sort through. One of things I wasn’t sure about was the brief mentions of Charlie have panic or anxiety attacks. I’ve never dealt with those, but I was unsure how people reacted to physical touch while they’re having an attack. Everyone isn’t the same, but Charlie allowed Trevor to help her by touching her and simply being near. Charlie’s dad, we come to learn, has bi-polar disorder. I don’t have experience with this mental illness, so I can’t say if this was well-represented and handled, but I do appreciate Charlie’s willingness to work with her father. I disliked her mother’s lack of compassion in this area though.

Trevor and Charlie’s friendship grew stronger. The last time they saw each other, they were fourteen. A lot has happened and changed in the last four years, and what possibly started out as an infatuation was in desperate need to develop into something else. It’s a lot of misunderstanding that needed solid communication, and I think the two did that and handled it well.

Towards the end I did feel it dragging a bit. I appreciate Sam and Darcy’s openness, but I felt it turn into a sort of “Hey, I thought my life was kind of crappy too because of my parents…” thing. I understand we all have our own story to tell, but with everything going on with Trevor and Charlie’s families, I thought adding another one was too much.

title: Interesting, Impressive Achievements - Central to Today's L.A.
text:
I'd seen 'Chinatown,' and toured L.A. This book presented an opportunity to learn the real story (his granddaughter estimates that only half of existing literature on the topic is reasonably accurate) of how a single individual was so central to the growth of a major population center. (But how do I know Standiford's version is accurate?)

By 1890, it was clear that L.A.'s main water source was tapped out. In 1904, a 250-mile journey north to Owens Valley took place. William Mulholland, despite never completing high school, then initiated and directed the 233-mile-long L.A. Aqueduct between 1907 and 1913. The St. Francis Reservoir, about 50 miles north of L.A. had been completed in March 1926, with water diverted for storage there from the L.A. Aqueduct. Two years later, on March 7, L.A. Water and Power director William Mulholland ordered the impoundment to cease - there then were 12.5 billion gallons held back by the 195o-foot-high dam, sufficient to cover 60 square miles one foot deep.

The process of acquiring the rights to the water and the rights-of-way for the aqueduct had divided California's citizens as nothing ever before. Unfortunately, worrisome cracks and leaks quickly developed in the structure. Mulholland assumed they were due to normal settling. Then the waters exploded down the canyon (a hundred feet or so wide), 140 feet high. At least 450 lives were lost. Mulholland's response - 'I'm the one responsible.'

In the spring of 1878, returning to L.A. from a prospecting trip in Arizona, Mulholland took a job as ditch tender for the L.A. City Water Company @ $1.50/day. On the side, he began reading 'Elements of Geology.' Others followed. In 1880, he was placed in charge of a pipe-laying crew, and given a raise ($65/month, and a higher -grade of shack). In 1886 his superintendent resigned to become city engineer, and Mulholland was assigned to build a five-mile conduit that protected the L.A. River water from polluting nearby settlements. The conduit was largely built of wood and lined with concrete. November brought the superintendent's position to Mulholland. At the time L.A. had a population of nearly 50,000.

The L.A. water system had been started with 3 miles of wooden pipe and 1 mile of iron pipe; by 1896 there were 325 miles of water pipeline within the city - owned and managed by a private company. By 1900, L.A. population reached 102,000. By the end of 1901, a $2 million bond to buy the water company assets was approved 5:1, and it was decided that an elected board of water commissioners would oversee the system. After requesting a raise (as a civil servant, he would no longer be able to do consulting), Mulholland recommended installing water meters for every user because he believed they would reduce consumption. Water rates were cut 50% for every customer who agreed, on top of an across-the-board 10% cut. The water department will netted $1.5 million, and this was plowed back into operations. (The meters cut per capita consumption from 300 gallons/day to 200.)

Mulholland estimated existing supplies would support a population of 250,000, and that would not arrive until at least 1950. But by 1905, the city had nearly doubled in size again. Mulholland banned lawn watering, turned off the flow to ponds in the parks, and added pumps at his new underground reservoir. Per capita consumption dropped to 144 gallons/day. Success, but the handwriting was on the wall. Mulholland asked for and received 3 weeks leave. That time was used to finish acquiring Owens Valley land that would support claims to its river water.

title: Mysteries explained
text:
One of the more frustrating aspects of being interested in Titanic and Lusitania are the conspiracy theories. The internet has helped them take on new life and has gained more followers who repeat them as if they are facts. These rumors and theories get repeated in books, newspapers, and documentaries. Some will look at the facts presented to counter the rumors and change their mind. Others will double down and accuse people of not wanting to accept "the truth." Author J. Kent Layton decided to pick some of the more lingering conspiracy theories and debunk them in his new book, which runs over 300 pages. What makes his books a valuable resource to researchers are that they are meticulously end-noted. Also helpful, are photos of the participants in various chapters. Putting a face with a name helps the reader visualize what they are reading.

The following material is covered:
RMS Titanic
Bad Design? Bad Materials?
The Wrong Twin? The Olympic/Titanic Switch
Ships that Pass in the Night:The Californian and the Titanic
Churchill the Scoundrel: Did Winston Churchill sink the Titanic?
The Villainous Chairman: J. Bruce Ismay, the Most-Hated Survivor
The Telegram Conspiracy: Withholding the News?

RMS Lusitania
Masquerade: Disguising the Lusitania
Scoundrel's Encore: Did Churchill Conspire to Sink the Lusitania?
Secret Cargoes & Armament: Guns, Munitions, Guncotton, & Clandestine Cargo
The Second Explosion: What was the Cause?
Surfacing: Did the U-20 surface after the attack?
Destroying the Evidence: A Cover Up of Damning Forensic Evidence on there Wreck?

This book will definitely be a handy tool, not only when debating someone on the above topics, but also when learning new information about the ships.

title: Uneven pacing and difficulty level: sometimes just fine, sometimes too hard
text:
Perhaps too rigorous! I'm teaching to a 10 year old 5th grader and a 12 year old 7th grader. We previously completed the Nancy Larson Science series, which was a bit too easy for the kids, but RSO Biology 2 goes WAY in the other direction. Some of the chapters are simple enough, but some are CRAZY advanced, and all take way too much time. I have about 4 hours a week to spend on science with my kids. Many of the labs alone take 2-3 hours, and there are two labs a week. Add to that the Famous Science series, studying for the weekly reviews, and test with questions that are sometimes unclear and usually demand perfect recall of long lists of esoteric words... I'm just not seeing how this is likely to make kids excited about science. Heck, I love science and this daunts me!

For instance, this week we started the 1 week long unit on cell division. The key words for this week are: zygote, daughter cells, somatic cells, interphase, mitosis, cytokinesis, G1 phase, S phase, G2 phase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, centrioles, spindle fibers, centromeres, chromatids, ploidy, haploid, diploid, reproduction, asexual reproduction, binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation, and regeneration. And those are only the NEW terms that the children are supposed to learn in one week. These terms all need to be prepared: "chromatid" appears once in an aside in the text, but it is mentioned twice in the end of week test. And if they don't learn it now, they will also have trouble with the end of unit test.

At this point I'm just going to use the text as a basic guide and start ignoring the tests, which is a shame because I feel that quizzes are helpful to learning. I feel it is much more important for my children, at this age, to have a *functional* understanding of how cells divide rather than burying them under terms that will turn them off to science and which they will forget in a month.

Update: Having gotten further into the course, we are now running across week-units that are really short and that my kids and I can cover easily in 2-3 hours. The difficulty level of these chapters is solidly middle school, which is great (though making a lemon-battery for the lab on the nervous system is a stretch -- how about testing reflexes or something?). It is just so frustrating that the pacing and level is so crazy-uneven! I really feel like this book is a beta that needs major feedback and revision.

title: What A Delightful Book- Been Designing for Years, But Good For Beginner's Too
text:
I know that the title of this review might be off putting to some who would view this book, but let me explain. When I first began to sew and design clothing, I wanted to do it right. I didn't care about the shortcuts or the quickie solutions to just slipping by with creating clothing. I wanted to make high quality designer level fashions eventually. With this in mind, all of my sewing pursuits were based upon building one concept upon another and getting each one right as I went along until I learned a new one.

With this in mind, I recommend this for veteran sewers as well as beginners who want to learn how to do things right from the beginning. Yes it will take more time at first, but in the end, you will be glad you took the time to learn it correctly. HOWEVER IT IS NOT A HOW TO SEW BOOK. You will need other resources to compliment this one for basic sewing information.

WHAT IS THIS BOOK LIKE?
Author David Page Coffin breaks down the shirt types in terms of modular thinking. Each style has a particular look to the basic form of the shirt, which he calls blocks. Then there are sub blocks which mean that specific design shapes of shoulders, armscye, and center front and neckline, for example. The garment industry uses these blocks as generalized means of making a shirt to fit a wide variety of people. This book attempts to show you how to make your OWN PERSONAL block to fit YOU. These blocks are used to spin off of to make any type of shirt that you desire- adding details and interesting changes which reflect your personality.

This book has a large variety of photos of processes for things such as collars, plackets, cuffs, and anything that would apply to shirts. There are sections on specific styles of shirts with featured details laid out in progression. There are also designers featured in the book with examples of what they have done with shirts.

There are a lot of resources listed in the book, such as other books with good designing information in them so that you can build your own library of sewing reference- something that I have always found invaluable for my own sewing and designing pursuits.

He gives examples of each type of shirt block (think style here) and then places you can find these types of styles in patterns, books, and online.

The pages of the book are thick and durable (think good text book weight) and easy to read. The binding is not spiral and won't lay flat easily on a table unless weighted down.

HOW WOULD THIS CONTRIBUTE TO AN EXPERIENCED SEWER?
This book is an invaluable resource for any experienced sewer who wants to make high quality and good looking shirts that equal or excel beyond what is found in the general marketplace. The photos are well laid out, and the many tips in here offered will apply to many different types of patterns that you might develop or encounter. You can design your own shirts, or just use the many tips in the book to make excellent patterns from that are commercial patterns.

HOW WOULD THIS BOOK HELP A NOVICE SEWER?
This book might have some parts which are overwhelming for a novice sewer such as how to copy an existing shirt or perhaps designing, but if you are highly motivated as I was, it might be right up your alley. If you tend to be a bit more hesitant to try going out on your own, I would say that this book has enough in it to help you do one good thing for every pattern you try to sew. You can use a tip or two for your patterns and incorporate them into your daily sewing over time. When you are ready to do more, this book will provide it for you.

WHAT I LIKE
-lots of photos
-designer pages inspire greatly
-LOTS of references for more information
-breakdown of tips for all aspects of sewing
-diagrams helpful
-photo profiled garments, online patterns, and online articles are clearly marked in the text for easier reference

WHAT I DON'T LIKE
-flow of the book seems a bit jumbled -takes time to plow through it to find what I need
-spiral bound might make it easier to work with at the sewing table/machine

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you have ever wanted to make nice shirts of any kind, this book is an excellent resource to have. The information contained in the book is invaluable for improving sewing technique and making high quality durable clothing that looks designer. Even novices can use many tips in here until they find their grounding in the sewing world. Experienced sewers will find plenty in this book to keep them busy improving and learning and challenged. The designer cameos are very inspirational and encourage me to want to branch out into designing new things. All in all, although I wish it were spiral bound or bound so it stays open better, and the lay out of the book was a little less jumbled, this book is a huge winner! I highly recommend it to anyone who truly wants to sew and do it well.

This book will have a center place in my library for years to come. It is a jewel- not always easy to find these days. FIVE HUGE STARS !

ONLINE CONTENT
At the time of this review, I have not had a chance to work with the online content enough to evaluate it so I will update in the future as that opportunity presents itself to let you know about that aspect of the book as well.

title: Star Wars: Abysmal
text:
Abysmal. Horrible. Not fun. Not entertaining. Not enjoyable. Awful.

I'll go ahead and say it so people can argue that I'm not giving this book a fair chance. I LOVED the now "Legends" set of Star Wars EU novels. Tell you what though, although I am admittedly deeply saddened that the "Legends" are no longer existant and I will greatly miss those stories, I was excited to start all over. I was excited about this book as if it were a new entry in the "Legends" set. I love reading, I love Star Wars. While disappointed that all the previous Star Wars novels may as well not exist, I still eagerly looked forward to this book and starting the new, now official canon, EU. Honestly, the people who read the EU novels before, are the same people who will read the EU novels now. Just because it's been reset doesn't mean there will be a huge increase in EU fans. Those of us who liked the "Legends" are the same people that Del Rey is targeting with the EU novels now. Our opinions are of great importance.

The writing style... It felt like I was sitting at a Dungeons and Dragons table listening to the Dungeon Master describe everything. "Something is happening. Here, in the space above Akiva. Or maybe down there on the planet's surface. If he dies here-nobody will know what it is. Which means he has to play this right. He powers down the torpedos. He has another idea." Wedge rolls the dice, dice value of 1, Wedge is immediately captured.

If that sounds like something you want to read, then you'll enjoy this book tremendously. Everything in quotes was taken right from chapter 1 and the entire rest of the story goes on like that. The writing style is like nothing I can think of in any previous Star Wars novels except for "Chose Your Own Adventure" types (which aren't novels anyway).

While the Dungeon Master was very keen to describe the environments, his lack of character explanation and description left me with a fleet of new characters that I honestly struggled to even like. By the end, I was honestly hoping that all involved (aside from Wedge anyway, though I'll admit that's only due to my love for him from "Legends", this version isn't super impressive just yet...) would just eat a proton torpedo and call it a day.

Disappointing. Extremely disappointing. I really hope that the future novels put the EU novels back on the right track.

title: My Five-Year-Old Twins LOVE These Books!
text:
My five-year-old twins LOVE it when I read to them and they've been sitting through more and more stories lately, which makes this bibliophile mama so happy! We first heard about the Elephant and Piggie books by Mo Willems from school (they are in 4K) since they are popular books in classroom libraries, along with the Pigeon books. We borrowed all of the them from our public library and my kids loved them so much that we are working on buying our own copies!

I Broke My Trunk! is another wonderful book in the Elephant and Piggie series by acclaimed children's author Mo Willems. As usual, Elephant and Piggie are hilarious and the friendship between the two of them is perfect for young kids to read about. I'm not going to provide a synopsis of the book since I don't want to give the story away. You are going to want to buy this book. Buy all of the Elephant and Piggie books! Trust me!

This book is a Theodor Seuss Geisel Honor Book. It is a beautiful hardcover with thick, paperback pages so they will withstand many, many readings through the story (which will happen!). The book is 57 pages long. We can generally read these books in about five minutes.

I cannot tell you how much our whole family enjoys these books! Even my husband and I find them hilarious! They are short stories and some pages only have a couple words on them but they are stories kids will want to read over and over again. My kids are even starting to read and these books have helped a lot. There are plenty of opportunities to spell words and point out sentences and pretty soon, your kids will be reciting them back to you. What an amazing thing to find a series of books that help your kids read!

These books are perfect for the four to eight-year-old crowd but there is no reason kids younger and older wouldn't enjoy them either.

Overall, buy this book. You won't be disappointed at all! Kids love Mo Willems and discovering these books has impacted my twins so much! They are wonderful stories of friendship with plenty of humor. We are Mo fans for life (or until my kids outgrow these books)!

title: Please be careful!
text:
I'm an average 44 year old runner that's on a quest to run faster at all distances. I've read just about every book I can get my hands on. This book was highly rated so I gave it a try. I did everything the author recommended. I read the book straight through first and then went back and did the drills. I skipped nothing.

I considered the "running pose" common sense. Leaning forward and feeling the point that you begin to fall... um ok. I did every drill countless times but didn't learn anything I didn't already know. If you over-stride and heal strike then you should do the drills. If you already land with your feet under your hips then you will probably roll your eyes at most of the drills.

The 'Preparing to Move" routine that he recommends you do before each drill was absolutely WRONG for me! It made my runs slower and my runs took much more effort. He calls these flexibility stretches but most of them are simply static stretches. It took me several days to realize my slower times were due to the recommended stretches. I then Googled, "Should I stretch before running" and read several studies that basically said, "Hell NO!" Also, why do I need to stretch my wrists before running??? After about a week I stopped doing his stretches and it took me another 2 weeks to recover from the damage. I rarely do anything before running unless it's a short 5K or 10k race. For these shorter races, I jump up and down in place a few times and jog slowly up and down the sidewalk for about 1/2 - 3/4 mile. Half marathon and above are long enough for me to warm up by taking it easy for the first mile or two.

This book is also a terrible guide for anyone who's new to minimalist running. This book says to simply go out and buy flat shoes. I'm not kidding, that what it says! It then says to stand in them and do some of his poses before buying them. Doing the poses is OK but if you've never ran in minimalist shoes, don't go straight out and buy flat shoes. Standard shoes have a 10 - 13 mm heal to toe drop. If you go from that, directly to a flat shoe, you WILL injure yourself. You should buy an 8-10 mm drop shoe first. Then slowly transition to lower drop shoes ( 6mm, 4mm, etc). Eventually you will work your way down to flat shoes. At that point you can even try transitioning (slowly) to barefoot running if you want.

I did like the suggestions about being your own coach and I also learned a lot from video taping my running as the author suggested. I have since found an even better book about being your own coach. It's called "Run Faster from 5K to the marathon" by Brad Hudson (2008).

title: Great book for understanding the inner workings of R, but not for the novice!
text:
As advertised, this book is for advanced intermediate R programmers who want to know more about the inner workings of R. The author gives broad coverage of many aspects of the language and often points out differences and similarities between R and other popular programming languages such as C, Python, C++, etc. Programmers transitioning to R for the first time will find this book a handy reference to understand many things (e.g., scoping) which in R are different from many other languages.

What this book is not is a cookbook of how to do things in R. The examples require some sophistication in R programming to follow and are not for the eyes of R newbies. Once understood, however, they usually point out nuances of R that are missed in explanations in other books. (For those looking for “how to” information, I recommend the O’Reilly Series book, ‘R Cookbook’). If you have plowed into R programming from another language and you are unsure of issues like global vs local variables (scoping), the lack of pointers, the inner workings of data frames and other R data structures, or the way R handles array arithmetic, this is the book for you. If you are looking for a book on how to do things in R, this is probably the wrong book, although the reader will certainly be a better R programmer for having read and understood the material in this book. Recommended!

title: Female fossil hunters make a significant find
text: This is a historical fiction based on the real life women, Mary Anning and Elizabeth Philpot, set in the early 19th century in Lyme Regis. Elizabeth has a passion for collecting fossils and meets the young Mary and her family when she asks Mary’s father to build a cabinet for her collection.  Mary has the eye for finding fossils to sell to support her family’s income and the two strike up an unlikely friendship. Mary makes an unusual discovery of the skeleton of a large creature, initially identified as a “crocodile” but what we now know as a dinosaur. Her find causes great controversy among both the scientific and religious communities and being a young, uneducated female leads Mary to be discounted and shunned. While the two have a falling out over Mary helping a “scientist” whom Elizabeth finds to be untrustworthy, they eventually come back together and help make significant scientific achievements.

title: Wonderful little allegory
text:
I've now re-read this wonderful little allegory about Jonathan Livingston Seagull.

Jonathan is a seagull beyond the ordinary. The other seagulls in the Flock spend their time, and are only interested in, finding, and fighting for food, and squalling. But Jonathan loves and lives to fly, so he spends all his time perfecting his flying skills until he becomes a true master at these.

Eventually, he is shamed by the Elder for reckless irresponsibility and “violating the dignity and tradition of the Gull Family”, and becomes an Outcast – all the gulls close their ears to him and turn their backs upon him.

Now he spends his days alone; his sorrow is not solitude, but that the other gulls refuse to believe in the glory of flight, and refuse to open their eyes and see.

At one point, Jonathan is taken by two brilliant gulls to what he thinks is Heaven, His feathers also glow brilliant white now. In this new place there are magnificent gulls who think as he thinks and spend all day practicing advanced aeronautics. Their purpose for living is to find perfection and show it forth. “We choose our next world through what we learn in this one. Learn nothing, and the next world is the same as this one.”

The place he has come to is not Heaven, since Heaven is not a place, and not a time. Heaven is being perfect.

Jonathan learns that he can travel anywhere he likes instantly by simply knowing that he has already arrived!

The trick is to know that his true nature lives everywhere at once across space and time.

He learns that the gull sees farthest who flies highest.

He begins to train other Outcasts, and, finally, forgives the Flock for their harsh treatment, and returns.

He understands that “each of us is in truth an idea of the Great Gull, an unlimited idea of freedom.” He teaches that “your whole body is nothing more than thought itself, in a form you can see. Break the chains of your thought, and you break the chains of your body, too”.

It is the rule of the Flock that Outcasts never return, and at first Jonathan and the other returning Outcasts are ignored, but, finally, curious gulls come to him and ask to learn how to fly. A gull with a broken wing learns to fly, and another who should have been dead, lives. They say in the Flock that Jonathan is the Son of the Great Gull, or perhaps he is the Devil.

Jonathan moves on, vanishes, while another gull, Fletch, takes over his teaching work. The two have realized that there are no limits.

This is an amazing little book that reminds us of who we really are, and I highly recommend that you read or re-read it!

title: OS X Yosemite: The Missing Manual
text:
I have been a Windows user since the first Windows OS came out. I have always been supportive of the company until they came out with Windows 8. It was enough of an issue to move me over to Apple OS, especially since I have been using iPads for a number of years now and have been very happy with them. So, I went out an purchased a new MacBook Air with OS X Yosemite and found that I really needed a guide on how to use the computer. Too many years with Microsoft so things just did not seem to work for me. So, when this book became available I figured that I had found a possible solution to my problem and ordered it. Here is what i found:

1. If you are looking for a very quick how to guide, keep looking! This book is over 800 pages and it covers absolutely everything you can think of. While it probably has what you need to get started, it is not the easiest form for that.

2. This is basically a "user's bible" where you go to look for answers to any of your questions on the OS. It is well organized and does a very good job of providing you everything you need to get things running and to be able to change things to fit your style. It just is NOT a fast read.

3. There is a wonderful section in the back that basically helps a Windows user transition to a Mac OS by providing terms commonly used in Windows and then giving the equivalent in the Mac OS.

4. There is even a section listed as "the missing CD" that tells you how to obtain all of the referenced information that used to be put on a CD in the back of the book. It is very easy to get the page for this manual up as long as you do not take the instructions for how to get there too seriously. The instructions give you the website and then tell you to click on the icon when in fact it should tell you click on the section for missing manuals, then click on the first letter of the book title. When you do that, you will find the manual that you have and there is the link for the CD. Just a few more steps than the Author listed. Oh, in case this bothers you, there is a link to fill out an errata sheet if you want to tell them about their error!

I found the manual to e very helpful in answering questions that i had on settings i wanted to change (such as backing up to a network drive with Time Machine) and a lot of helpful suggestions on various aspects of the OS. It also provided a nice transition tool for me as I migrate from Windows to Mac OS X. This is just NOT a quick "just do this" type of manual.

If you are looking for an excellent reference book that really SHOULD have been included with the OS, then this is the book to order!! I would highly recommend it!

title: The thrillers in Claire Stibbe's Temeke series just get better and better and for four reasons
text:
The thrillers in Claire Stibbe's Temeke series just get better and better and for four reasons.

First, she populates her stories with relatable PEOPLE. Temeke is superbly drawn. The fact that he's a Brit in NM brings some terrific points of cultural contrast and conflict.

Secondly, her PLOTS are always full of unanticipated twists and turns. These are never telegraphed, nor are they overly obfuscating or complex. In 'Dead Cold, I was left with both hot as well as cold flushes as the plot proceeded with the suspense and intensity of the very best fugitive narratives.

Thirdly, she always creates an enticing sense of PLACE. No one makes the landscapes of new Mexico as present to the reader's imagination as she does. Her delineation of settings makes for a constant reboot of the pathetic fallacy, without ever having the crassness to say 'this is so.'

Finally, PROCEDURALS. With Claire Stibbe we have an author who has researched the police procedures of the APD with unparalleled care, even to the point of joining the department in a voluntary capacity. Few authors I know show this level of commitment.

I guarantee that these four factors, among many others, will mean that the Temeke collection will one day be up there with the best, and companies like HBO will be lining up to sign up this emerging, brilliant talent.

Can't wait for the next challenge for the flawed Brit detective!

title: War, Cooperation, & Competition: The Dynamics of History
text:
In Ultrasociety: How 10,000 Years of War Made Humans the Greatest Cooperators on Earth, Peter Turchin has another book that translates his sophisticated models of historical dynamics into a prose exposition that non-specialists can enjoy. As in his previous work, War and Peace and War, he has succeeded in his task by mixing accounts of historical (and pre-historical) incidents and epochs with lessons about the science of evolution. Having admired his accomplishment in War and Peace and War, I held high expectations for this book. He has met and exceeded those expectations by addressing a set of topics of even greater and wider import than those of his first (popular) book. He does this by following the course of most academics whom I admire: they transgress departmental boundaries to explore new connections and arrive at new insights. In his case, he moved from an academic specialization in population dynamics to helping found the new science of Cliodynamics, the study of history using large data sets to create mathematical models of historical dynamics. Although already a fan (and thanks to the internet for allowing groupies like me to follow along with new thoughts and trends between books), I almost shouted “Amen!” aloud when I read:

The situation [of competing theories] is made worse by the division of social science into “tribes” of anthropologists, sociologists, political scientists, and economists. Each discipline tends to emphasize its own set of theories while disagreeing with others (and even among its own adherents). Social scientists are the blind men touching different parts of an elephant and drawing different conclusions about it. -- Peter Turchin, Ultrasociety: How 10,000 Years of War Made Humans the Greatest Cooperators on Earth, Location 567.

The thesis of Ultrasociety is simple: over the course of human evolution, we humans have become the most cooperative species on the planet, outpacing our nearest rivals, the more numerous and highly cooperative ants. As Turchin points out, several factors account for this distinction, including two factors that take humans beyond the biological. First, in addition to biological evolution, which is slow and random, humans developed culture, the transmission of information via representation. The transmission of information by culture from generation to generation allows changes in human behavior to occur much more rapidly than any change in the human genome would allow. As a practical matter, the lives of humans, especially in the last 10,000 years (since the advent of agriculture) have changed by orders of magnitude far beyond anything that biological evolution by itself could have allowed.

Turchin identifies a second crucial spur to changes in human ways of life, and it may come as a shock to readers. It’s war. Particularly in the last 10,000 years, war is—for all its horrors—the most potent source of cultural evolution. War compels change and change occurs through cooperation within groups. As humans developed societies beyond those of hunter-gatherers, as they developed civilization (a society based on cities), war became more organized and pronounced, and increasing competition for survival ensued. The seeming paradox is at the heart of Turchin’s analysis.

By the way, Turchin notes that the idea of the "noble savage" leading a bucolic, pastoral life is a fantasy; in fact, hunter-gatherers have shockingly high rates of violent death from warfare and other forms of homicide. Note that Turchin is not a war-monger. He concedes the horror of war and that it entails destruction—often vast destruction. He is not, as some--especially during the period before the First World War--who think war a fine tonic for whatever ails society. Not at all. However, he recognizes war as a competitive environment that spurs intra-group cooperation.

Competition between groups and cooperation within groups, whether hunter-gatherer tribes or highly developed and coordinated nation-states ​are traits that evolutionary theory explain. The controversial (but increasingly accepted) theory of cultural multilevel selection is a key concept for understanding the dynamics involved in these competitions that require so much cooperation. To explain this, Turchin provides a brief history of evolutionary biology and the controversy about whether groups can evolve and undergo a process of natural selection. As recently as the 1970s, with the publication of Richard Dawkins's book, The Selfish Gene (and more recently in some of Steven Pinker’s work), mainstream biology believed that evolution occurred only on the level of individual genomes and not among groups. Turchin points out that there was an early, naïve theory of group selection that did not hold up to scrutiny. However, in work conducted by David Sloan Wilson and colleagues, the theory of multilevel selection became more sophisticated. This theory now provides a persuasive—albeit not universally accepted—theory of how groups compete and evolve.

Part of what makes Turchin's work fascinating is that he translates the highly theoretical and mathematically modeled work of evolutionary biology (his native field) into commonplace examples taken from anthropology and history. For instance, he draws upon his academic home at the University of Connecticut, which has a phenomenally successful women's college basketball program (and a successful men's program as well) to frame the problem of cooperation and competition within a group. He uses examples of sports teams as a microcosm of the problem of cooperation and competition. As a member of numerous sports teams and now as a boys varsity basketball coach, this issue has long intrigued me. How does one promote competition within the team to draw out the best individual performances and determine playing time, while requiring those same individuals to coalesce and cooperate unselfishly at the highest level to defeat an opponent? To the extent the team succeeds in cooperating against an opponent, the team will likely win. Maximum success depends on individuals putting aside their selfish interests (glory, pay) for the benefit of the team. Moreover, what applies to something as inconsequential as sports (at least at bill level of high school sports), applies to the level of intergroup competition in something as deadly serious as war. (Of course, this leads one to speculate on the relationship between war and sports, but that's a subject for another time). Turchin explains the dynamics involved and provides some revealing information about how relationships and status among members of a team affect team performance. Studies have shown that wide disparities in pay between professional players correlates with poorer team performance. Those teams with the greatest equality of pay tend to be the most successful. Although Turchin does not mention this directly, one has to wonder how this applies to society as a whole. With an increasing awareness of a growing inequality in American society since the 1970s, one can't help but notice the increasing social and political polarization that occurred during the same period. We have become an increasingly less cooperative polity and society as inequality has grown. Turchin also notes the triumph of individualist philosophies espoused by Ayn Rand, Friedrich Hayek (which is a selective reading of his total work by some proponents), and others who emphasize a highly individualistic and laisse-fair ideology. Turchin quotes the "greed is good" speech by the fictional character Gordon Gecko in the movie Wall Street as an exemplar of the ascendant selfish ideology that began running amok in the 1980s. Turchin makes clear that an undue emphasis on individual accomplishment and selfishness hurts the society as a whole.

Turchin can claim to be the founding father of Cliodynamics, a discipline that works to discern patterns in history and prehistory based on the quantification of data through mathematical modeling. Attempts of this sort in the past have been failures. Through the lens of philosopher like R. G. Collingwood (of whom I've been reading a great deal lately), this endeavor doesn’t qualify as history properly understood. For Collingwood, History is the history of thought and not the history of behavior. But Turchin's work and the work of others in Cliodynamics demonstrates the weakness of Collingwood's position. When Collingwood emphasizes history as the history of thought, including the thoughts behind human actions and choices, he limits history to examining the tip of the iceberg. Just as humans are the result of eons of evolution layered one upon another to arrive at our current state, with most of the functions of our bodies running involuntarily and without our conscious knowledge or decision, so with many of the actions of society. Many actions seen together, aggregated over large groups, display behaviors that are not the result of a conscious decision. Often they are the aggregate of individual decisions that reveal a larger pattern. We deal with this every day when considering market "decisions." (But note our personification of markets often leads to poor analysis. The “market” is not a conscious individual; it’s an abstraction of many individual actions aggregated for the convenience of analysis). Turchin analyzes data from the past to better understand the past. (Note: the only source of knowledge is the past!) To me, Cliodynamics is a welcome addition to the field of history. Although I retain my prejudice for history as the history of thought, with an emphasis on political and intellectual decisions, we simply cannot ignore the fact that human beings are both a part of Nature and apart from Nature. To understand the totality of the human past—the highest intellectual endeavor—we need to take advantage of all the tools available. Looking at history through different lenses provided by of social and natural sciences is a resource that we are foolish to ignore.

Indeed, in this book, Turchin suggests that perhaps we humans can move another step forward on our evolutionary journey and make war obsolete. The massive improvements in warfare and killing efficiency epitomized by atomic weapons make this more than a utopian dream. It's a practical necessity. The next logical—even necessary—step in cultural evolution must be increased cooperation, or we run the risk of regression to a less cooperative, must more barbaric (in the worst sense of the term) reality. Turchin uses the international space station as an example of the level of cooperation that nations are capable of attaining. He suggests that perhaps economic competition can replace war as a means of spurring cultural innovation without suffering the horrors of war. Paul Krugman, another social scientist inspired by Isaac Asimov’s vision of “psychohistory” outlined in his Foundation books, suggests we need an attack of aliens to foster an economic growth and cooperation, which is much in keeping with Turchin’s direction of thought. I believe that with the imminence of global climate change, we—as a species working through nation-states—will either ratchet-up our levels of peaceful cooperation to combat (by abatement and adaptation) what will become an increasingly alien environment—or we will suffer an increasingly deadly level of social and political conflict.

One mark of a successful book is that it leaves you wanting more. You hear yourself saying, “telling me more about this and that.” So it is with this book. The number of issues that it raises, the number of possible areas of explorations it suggests, are too numerous to list completely. But to name just one area of where I’d like to know more: Turchin describes the idea of “cultural evolution” as a scientific theory “based on mathematical models [that] are empirically testable.” Id., Location 330. Moreover, there is a tradition within sociology of social evolution and development theory, as well as theories of history (addressed by Turchin in War and Peace and War). However, I’m wondering about connections with theories of cultural evolution (or change) based on language and other symbolic systems, such as the work of Owen Barfield, Walter Ong, Jean Gebser, William Irwin Thompson and Ralph Abraham, and Clare Graves and Don Beck (an eclectic list, I admit). None of these thinkers, I believe, would necessarily disagree with the biologically based theory of cultural evolution espoused by Turchin, but it would be interesting to determine where they mesh and where they conflict.

So, I’ll stop here. With an outstanding book, the temptation is to go on and on about it. I’ll not. Go read it yourself.

title: Helicopter Money
text:
Give People Money examines the pro and cons of providing people with a universal basic income (UBI). The books presents Lowrey's research, interviews with experts, and descriptions of countries and even cities that have provided people with a guaranteed income. She also delves into the philosophical, moral, and cultural concerns and road blocks to UBI. She interviews people living in poverty to get their views on the matter as well.
I thought this book to be insightful, balanced, well researched and well written. UBI flies in the face of conventional wisdom. When I first heard of "helicopter money", I thought the idea absurd. Now I'm not so sure. Lowry gives several examples here and throughout the world where giving people cash instead of benefits is more pragmatic. UBI gives the poor a stake and a say in their existence. A basic income allows them to purchase things they need instead of benefit providers giving them things they don't need. Many times it is the most efficient way to lift people out of poverty. However, judging by the current political atmosphere and some of the other reviews, I don't think it's anything we'll have to worry about soon. I enjoyed the read.

title: "An American in Paris" - a misguided page-turner
text:
Pros: Page-turner that quickens the pace by alternating between two sisters who forge different paths
Cons: Predictable, lacks emotional heft, and culturally lazy

I'm an average person who has had the luxury of reading sixty novels during my commute this year. Because of that, I couldn't help thinking of all the books that outperform this book in every way.

- Want to read an incredible book about a double agent coping with ethical ambiguity? Read The Sympathizer by Viet Thanh Nguyen.
- Want to get an idea of the horrors and turmoil of war?: Half of a Yellow Sun by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
- Are you hung up on World War II in particular?: The Gift of Rain by Tan Twan Eng, The Narrow Road to the Deep North by Richard Flanagan
- Family dynamics during WWII for European Jews?: The Glass House by Simon Mawer
- "But no, seriously, France during WWII?": All the Light We Cannot See by Anthony Doerr
- Books that are linguistically and culturally immersive: The God of Small Things by Arundhati Roy, The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao by Junot Diaz, The Lowland by Jhumpa Lahiri, The Garden of Evening Mists by Tan Twan Eng, And the Mountains Echoed by Khaled Hosseini, Purple Hibiscus by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie

Despite the dramatic setting, I felt almost nothing from reading this book. I loved that it focused on "everyday" heroism, and I loved that it told the story of a young woman who refused to accept that she couldn't contribute during wartime. Even so, it is incredible to me that a book with such dark topics felt like an emotionally "light read." Having characters repeat warnings to each other did nothing to build up tension. "Yes, but if you get caught..." and, "you can't expect any mercy from them, Isabelle" over and over felt redundant and skimmable.

The lack of cultural immersion was also frustrating for me. It felt like the work of a Francophile who only learned the words "Yes", "Thank you", and "S***". Starting sentences with "Oui" in italics doesn't make it feel like we're in France. Upon hearing the phrase "Les Pyrénées", most French people wouldn't say something like, "Ah yes, the mountains?" Even as a French-American who grew up in New Jersey, this was painfully obvious - I can only imagine how easy it would be for a French person to stop reading this book mid-sentence. "Schnell" and "Mein Gott" were the only German additions to the book; this might have been excusable a century ago, but all of this can be easily Googled and wound up feeling lazy.

If you're already a fan of Kristin Hannah, you'll probably enjoy this book. If you're looking for a book that's emotionally compelling and culturally immersive, look elsewhere.

text: This is a fantastic book for anyone interested in the geology of the American west. It's also a great overview to geology in general. It is definitely geared towards people with a college degree. It covers basic geological terms and processes. It also walks the reader through the creation of North America with beautiful, GIS-rendered, paleogeographical maps and photographs of representative outcrops of the formations described. My only complaint is that it frequently has figures with multiple illustrations, e.g. Figure 1a, 1b, 1c, etc. that run over multiple pages and the caption is found on the first page. Thus you have to turn back to read the caption for many of the figures, despite the fact that there is ample white space on each figure's page to situate a caption. Also, some of the paleogeographic maps are quite small, again in spite of the fact that there is ample white space in the book. I hope that future editions will correct this annoying flaw. Nonetheless, this is the best overview to the geology of western North America that I have found for the educated non-specialist.

title: The Best for Learning Basics
text:
This is without question the best language program to getting started in almost any language, specifically any romance or germanic language, from English as a base. As others have noted, this program is different from all the others in that it focuses nothing on memorization, there is no note taking, no homework, and Thomas spends no time on things like counting numbers, or formal names. Instead, he tells you that most languages use only about 600-800 words, and then over the course of the program, shows you how to put together sentences using most of those words, some of which are similar to English. This gives you a very quick grasp of how to at least think a little in Spanish. So if you find yourself a month or so away from a trip to a Spanish speaking country, this will get you prepared more than any other program, period. You'll be able to put sentences together, if somewhat clunky, and start thinking in the most practical way about Spanish. The same I believe would apply to his programs for French, Portugese, Italian, German, Dutch, etc. though I have not tried those.

There are some things to know about this, mild criticisms. To me the first is that you can get through a disc or two here and have a false sense of accomplishment. Even getting through all discs here, you're still going to be a novice, and need plenty of practice. Yes, it's amazing how far he can quickly get you, but it will not make you conversational, let alone fluent. That will take practice, and time. Any program will. Next is that Thomas spends very, very little time having you listen to anything, even a sentence in Spanish, to where that part of your mind gets used to understanding the language aurally. Compare this, say, to Pimsler, which breaks down sentences this way, having you listen, then learn how it's said. You could find yourself getting through this entire set, then listening to someone speak Spanish and be flummoxed. The key of course is to go out and listen on your own, watch Spanish speaking TV, movies in Spanish, etc.

I agree with the others who say one of the students on the discs is a bit of a slow learner, and Michele focuses a bit too much on pronunciation, which can slow things down a little. This is peculiar as I have also heard that since Michel himself was Polish who learned French at an early age (then many other languages, including Spanish obviously), himself has an accent while speaking Spanish that a native Spanish speaker would notice. I wouldn't worry too much about any of this. While another program, such as Pimsler, or Rosetta Stone, does indeed focus on native speakers with perfect, and neutral accents, this a very minor issue for most people just trying to learn the basics of language.

Finally, I recommend you go through this program twice. First, the way Michel says. In one push over the course of a few days, with as few of distractions as possible. Then, take a break, watch some Spanish TV, maybe even try some vocabulary learners (books, CDs, online), or another teaching program even. Then, come back to this and go through it again. From there, you'll have a very solid base, and feel confident you can go to almost any Spanish speaking country in the world and least feel comfortable, certainly putting the most common sentences together, even if you struggle at times.

title: Should be Kept and Referred to By Active Campaigners.
text:
This is a very well done and thorough book on what works and what doesn't relating to Get-Out-The-Vote efforts. The book scores high in terms of credibility in that it references, describes, and summarizes research that has been undertaken on varying GOTV tactics. Also, the author appears to be a full-time professor, not engaged in consulting and presumably without financial ties to any of the industries that provide GOTV services.

The book scores very high in terms of readability and accessibility in that at the beginning and end of each chapter the author outlines the conclusions as to the efficacy and efficiency of various GOTV tactics. His work underscores how little effect most GOTV efforts have on turnout (even those with a positive effect are almost uniformly slight) and identifies those which tend to produce the greatest effect according to studies.

This is a serious book for any politico who will be organizing or running campaigns. It will be a great aid if practitioners are willing to be convinced that some "conventional wisdom" is largely anecdotal and often the product of those who have a service to sell. The book does reveal better and worse tactics and also dollarizes the choices in terms of cost per likely voter so that resource allocation can be a factor in assessing which tactics to emphasize. Although the author touches some on persuadability and the effect of message on GOTV tactics, that is not a focus of the book. This lack of attention to message that might be married with given tactics is a shortfall of the work, though in fairness to the author it appears beyond the scope of his effort. It is a valuable addition to any campaigner's bookshelf.

title: Hopeful view of AI that is also honest about the potential pitfalls
text: The main thesis of the book is that AI will greatly affect our future, in mostly positive ways. However, I greatly appreciate how honest the book is about our need to tackle certain issues with AI to ensure that humanity as a whole benefits. Many detractors of AI point out the threats that AI can pose: fears about autonomous weapons, loss of employment, and malicious software bots spreading fake news, to name a few. This book addresses all of these issues head on, but still manages to convince the reader that embracing AI is the key to humanity's future prosperity. AI is not going away, but the best way to solve some of the problems it will create is with AI itself. The book states that the AI genie is out of the bottle, and it is foolish to assume that malicious actors will halt development of threatening AI technology. Therefore, it is incumbent on Computer Scientists to anticipate these threats and proactively develop technologies that will defend against such malicious action. I especially appreciate the perspective of the author regarding the purpose of humanity. Many fear AI because it will steal their jobs, and I think that this fear is justified in the short term. However, once the world is completely transformed by AI, there will not be much need to humans to do many jobs. In the long term, this is only a problem if we truly believe that work gives our lives meaning. This book indicates that once AI frees us from toil, we might be able to find new purpose in our lives. I certainly hope this is the case.

title: A Delightful Set of 10 Children's Storybooks
text:
"One Sentence Storybooks" is a delightful set of 10 children's short story books. Each book starts out with one sentence and adds a new sentence for the next three pages. The story ends with four sentences that explain each Bible story. There is an illustration on every other page of the part of the book that contains the stories, each illustrating all the sentences that are used. There are some review pages at the end of the book consisting of the main words used in each story, a page about truths, verses, and prayers that apply to the story, and a look back into the story where the children can find colors, shapes, and words that sound like pictures that are shown.

I really liked reading these books which brought Bible stories together in four sentences for children. To me they are more like pamphlets, although I believe they are short enough to keep a child's attention throughout all the stories. If all 10 books were combined I think it would also make a good mini-book of Bible stories for children, and some people might look at it that way. I like that all of the books are numbered; this makes it easy to keep them all in order. The 10 stories came together in a nice paperback/cardboard case with Velcro, to keep the case closed when the books aren't being used.

I think this will be a great collection to children's' libraries, and that it would also be good to be placed on tables or stands to be readily available to read at different times.

I received this book free from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. The opinions I have given are my own.

title: Like Rapunzel, this is a fun
text:
Calamity Jack is the sequel to the graphic novel Rapunzel’s Revenge and gives readers the backstory on Rapunzel’s buddy, Jack. Like Rapunzel, this is a fun, new take on the Jack and the Beanstalk fairy tale geared to attract older readers.

When readers first meet Jack in Rapunzel’s Revenge, he’s a guy on the run. Calamity Jack tells the story of why he’s on the run and who he’s running from – a kid who can’t stay out of trouble, Jack ends up getting himself, and by extension, his mother, into trouble with the local giants that run his town. He steals a goose that he hears is due to lay a golden egg and goes on the run, hoping that any golden eggs will pay for the destruction of his mother’s bakery. After his early adventures with Rapunzel, she accompanies him back to his hometown where they hope to reunite Jack with his mother – and find the town under siege by giant ants, his mother a prisoner of the giants, and a sneaking suspicion that the giants are at the heart of all the town’s problems.
Anyone who enjoyed Rapunzel will enjoy Calamity Jack. Written in the same fun spirit, the authors give equal time to the main male and female characters with their own adventures. Graphic novels are a good way to reach male readers, and turning a fairy tale into an adventure tale is a smart way to draw in those readers who may feel they are “too old” for these books.

title: Perk up your lunchbox!
text:
This is among the reviews where I urge you to ignore the number of stars I give the item, because the cookbook's usefulness depends very much on what you're looking for. It's not a great fit for my needs, but it may be superb for you.

The Paris Picnic Club is about 100 recipes from two friends who -- as the title suggests -- began a tradition of creating weekly picnic lunches in Paris that ultimately attracted 80 guests at a time. As "picnic" implies, their menus emphasized portable food, such as sandwiches and carry-able desserts. There are chapters for small plates; sharing platters; bread, etc.; tartines (think "open faced sandwiches"); desserts; and drinks.

The "Paris" in the title should not suggest that this is all French food. Much of it is, because the authors are locovores, but really it just means, "We're in Paris." So there are quite a few ingredients that may be easy to find in France (such as fresh chestnuts or sorrel), but also plenty of dishes that incorporate international flavors (such as "Casablanca couscous" or "Korean chicken salad with pickled cabbage, cucumbers, peanuts, and cilantro").

I think it's best to think of the cookbook as options for improving your own lunchtime options with more exotic flavors. The tartines section can be treated as "interesting sandwiches," though the authors also suggest you can leave off the bread and turn several of the recipes into salads. That worked well for me. First I made the "cold oven chicken," which is sort of a garlic-and-lemon chicken dish that (as the name implies) you shove into the oven without even preheating it first. (YAY for convenience! It wasn't exotic, but it was simple and tasty.) Then I used leftovers to make a tartine-for-one (minus the bread) following the book's recipe for "roasted chicken, bacon, tomatoes, and avocado with mayo and baby gem lettuce" (wherein the list of ingredients is pretty much the recipe). Hey, I was looking for something simple.

...and that's kind of where I stalled. Some of the recipes sound delicious but aren't friendly to my low-carb diet (for example, "squash, chestnut, and ricotta ravioli with sage brown butter and almonds" or "apricot and rosemary tarte tatin"). Others require ingredients that are hard to find; I'm not sure where to get Toulouse sausages for "fennel, leek, Puy lentils, and sausages with basil pistou."

But mostly... quite a few of these are time consuming or require so much effort that you rather NEED to feed a crowd to justify them. I don't mind doing things that are cook-ahed, but I'm unlikely to actually make "pork belly with roasted red kuri squash and pistachio parsley pesto." I try to be honest with myself about my personal weaknesses. And while "porchetta with caramelized apple and fennel sauce" sounds like an awesome tartine -- you spread an herbed cream cheese on bread, then the pork, a layer of sauce, and arugula with a hazelnut oil vinaigrette -- I'm not up for making a big roast just to make it possible.

There are, however, lots of delicious-sounding meals, and some of these may come to fruition: a tartine of smoked ham, brie, and onion jam; or gravlax, capers, sorrel, and cervellle de canut (another spread made with herbs and cheese or yogurt).

So, ultimately, this isn't the best cookbook for me. That doesn't mean it won't be helpful to you, though. Hopefully I've given you enough information to make a better decision. ...and if you make that porchetta recipe, invite me over.
